job description: Ricoh Hong Kong Limited is a printer company, and the report states that about 90 percent of HKU printers come from Ricoh. The paperless trend has pressured the firm to transform its business model, with AI as a major part of that shift. The Sustainable Growth Department integrates intelligent systems, including AI agents, into workflows. InnoAI Hub, a proprietary large language model platform from the Beijing research center SRCB, is central to that effort. The AI Developer Intern role was to brainstorm, develop, and fine-tune agents and to turn those capabilities into client-facing business value.
job duties: Brainstormed, developed, and fine-tuned AI agents on InnoAI Hub; created presentation decks and refined AI-integrated consultancy tools used with clients; redesigned the AI Experience Center flow and drafted a tour revamp that added successful agent cases and third-party AI tools while keeping the tour simple, and collected content from stakeholders; changed Excel input settings so a completed questionnaire produced charts and could be sent to an agent that generated a consultant report within about a minute; fine-tuned cybersecurity assessment tools and joined a tutorial that briefed consultants on the updates; attended client meetings, including with IKEA and MUJI, to collect pain points, expectations, and concerns about AI; revised an ecosystem demonstration slide after testing showed the interactive whiteboard could not play the planned animation.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started by reading the job description and matching personal strengths to the requirements. Mock interviews with friends covered self-introduction, previous work, project experience, and extracurricular roles. Selection was a single interview followed by an offer, with no qualification test. The interview lasted about ten minutes, shorter than a typical fifteen minutes, and the offer arrived one week later.
what have I learned: Coursework on transformer logic was used to refine agent workflows and to explain large language models to colleagues who did not know them. Client meetings supplied first-hand requests and led to new use cases, including retrieval-augmented generation and other technologies. An Excel and agent workflow that produced consultant reports in about a minute showed how AI can remove repetitive manual work. The Experience Center revamp showed the value of checking each draft with the project leader and of changing a design when the display hardware could not support it. Slides made proposals easier for decision-makers to follow.
what do I need to improve: Most assigned work stayed inside existing abilities, so the internship did not push beyond a comfort zone. The Experience Center tour revamp was difficult because there was no prior tour-design experience and the previous plan was unfamiliar. More skill is still needed to build stronger AI tools for business problems that current technology does not solve.
post-internship reflections: The career aim is a product-manager role that turns client needs into technical plans and sits between front-end and back-end teams. Building demo agents for client discussions confirmed that this direction fits, while also showing that more technical skill is still required. The collaborative culture, called the Ricoh Way or the Three Loves, made a future return to Ricoh feel welcome.
advice for future interns: Apply early when positions open, prepare thoroughly for interviews, and stay calm because the conversations are professional and conversational. Be ready to learn quickly, adapt, and build relationships with people in the workplace.
technical skills: Work used large language model agents, transformer workflow design, retrieval-augmented generation, agent fine-tuning, Excel questionnaire visualization, and automated consultant report generation.
soft skills: The report describes explaining technical ideas in plain language, checking plans with stakeholders, communicating in client and internal meetings, and using slides so decision-makers could follow a proposal.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Tools named in the work are Excel, PowerPoint, and the InnoAI Hub platform.

job description: Harman International is a global audio and automotive technology company whose brands include JBL and Harman Kardon. It designs portable Bluetooth speakers, PartyBox systems, home audio products, and headphones. The internship was in the Portable Audio Business Unit, on the Algorithm Team in the Digital Signal Processing division of Advanced Audio Engineering, and focused on AI-driven processing. The role supported music source separation models: organizing audio data, improving open-source models, testing performance, documenting workflows, and carrying a guitar-separation project through a TFC-TDF framework over a six-month internship.
job duties: Organized and improved music datasets; installed and optimized open-source models, compared their performance, and documented workflows and results; reproduced the DTTNet baseline from the ICASSP 2024 Dual-Path TFC-TDF UNet paper and adapted the pipeline for guitar removal; added guitar-specific data augmentation and changed the training setup; raised uSDR and cSDR by about 10 percent with an internal testing package; cut the parameter count by almost 50 percent while improving SDR by nearly 0.7; trained models on Linux GPU servers over SSH using bash scripts; gave weekly progress talks that helped the team choose what to optimize next; contributed literature review, experiments, drafted sections, and statistical analysis for a research paper and related patent work on AI music source separation.
pre-internship preparation: With no formal signal-processing course completed yet, preparation covered digital signal processing, music source separation, and recent deep-learning methods for audio, plus a review of earlier coding and machine-learning projects. Three interviews followed. Human resources asked about education, employment, and the company. A technical round with the Advanced Audio Engineering director and the DSP team head covered convolutional networks, recurrent networks, transformers, attention, the Fourier transform, and Python deep-learning frameworks. A line manager then discussed expectations. Guitar and band experience came up because the project involved guitar removal.
what have I learned: Deep learning and computer vision from the Applied AI curriculum transferred to model pipelines, loss functions, evaluation, and experimental design, and earlier Python, Linux, and remote-server experience made the move onto company GPU machines faster. The first two weeks were confusing because audio-processing experience was limited, which pushed the work from clearly defined classroom tasks toward independent engineering. Large gains came from many small changes in data, architecture, and training. A smaller model that still improved SDR showed that an industrial algorithm must also meet memory, latency, hardware, and cost limits. Weekly presentations, help from teammates, documentation, and the paper and patent process added a practical view of product constraints and research accountability.
what do I need to improve: Experience with audio signal processing was very limited at the start, and the first two weeks included confusion about priorities and about how single experiments served the project. Further obstacles were unfamiliar model components, implementation problems, disappointing results, and new audio-analysis tools.
post-internship reflections: Finance or another business path had been under consideration. The six-month internship shifted interest toward engineering and product development in audio algorithms, including music source separation, speech enhancement, noise cancellation, and real-time spoken-language translation. The study plan moved toward a computer science minor, including software engineering and databases, with a longer aim of starting a company that develops algorithms. A return to Harman after graduation is of interest, and the company asked for six more months of part-time work on the same project.
advice for future interns: Be confident, and do not treat limited experience as a reason to avoid applying. An undergraduate should not expect to arrive with every answer. Curiosity, asking questions, and a willingness to grow matter more than already knowing the field.
technical skills: Technical work covered deep learning, convolutional and recurrent networks, transformers, attention, the Fourier transform, music source separation, DTTNet and TFC-TDF models, data augmentation, uSDR and cSDR, model-size reduction, experimental design, and training on GPU servers.
soft skills: The internship required weekly presentations that framed results for team decisions, asking colleagues for help, and communication and trust with teammates, including on a team trip to Fujian.
courses mentioned: Classes chosen for a computer science minor are named as software engineering and databases. Deep learning and computer vision from the Applied AI curriculum were used on the project. A formal signal-processing course had not yet been taken.
tools and software: Named tools and environments are Python, Linux, SSH, bash scripts, and GPU servers, plus an internally developed testing package.

job description: The host organization is not named. It operates in supply-chain management, international shipping, and consumer-goods trading, where profit depends on sourcing costs, factory cycles, and multi-currency trades. The report describes a relationship-based business in which client and factory communication still relies on manual judgment, while repetitive invoice reconciliation creates inefficiency. The internship built an automated pipeline to cross-check factory payment records against statements of account, and later started a model to estimate how many days a client invoice would take to be paid.
job duties: Built a data-engineering pipeline to cross-reference factory payment databases with statements of account; wrote cross-file handling steps and audited poorly structured spreadsheets for anomalies; used a heuristic, auditable model because the financial checks needed to be exact; designed a simple interface for non-technical staff and allowed for imperfect input; first split the work into validator.py and merge_tool.py, then merged them into unified_tool.py after openpyxl cleared cached Excel formula values on save and later steps read empty or zero cells; tried writing precalculated values into formula cells, then dropped that approach because prices and amounts can still change; on 30 July started a days-to-payment analysis aimed at deployment by 21 August, tested multiple linear regression, and moved toward a support vector machine because of multicollinearity, holiday seasonality, and a modest amount of data.
pre-internship preparation: This was a first job interview. Preparation reviewed Applied AI prerequisites COMP3340, MATH3904, and STAT3612, and used a conversational generative AI model to simulate industry questions and comment on the answers. Across two weeks, the assessment had two parts: a timed proposal on how AI could help the company, answered with a supervised logistic-regression score of supplier trustworthiness from trade count, price stability, and company scale, then an interview focused on clear communication and a past COMP2113 coursework project.
what have I learned: The main gain was seeing the gap between clean academic datasets and messy corporate spreadsheets. The program had to be usable by non-technical staff and tolerant of input errors. Debugging, including printing each step when one bad index stopped the run, and the openpyxl cache failure that forced a single in-memory program, showed how design choices affect daily operations. Multiple linear regression was a poor fit for days to payment, which led toward a support vector machine for nonlinear patterns and smaller data. The work strengthened an interest in data engineering and in automation that frees people for work that still needs human judgment.
what do I need to improve: Replacing formula cells with stored cached values was described as unwise because amounts such as unit price can be edited later. Limited knowledge and time also left many other procedures unautomated, including further work on the support vector machine model.
post-internship reflections: The long-term aim is to work as an AI engineer focused on predictive intelligence and on algorithms that automate slow, repetitive processes. Remaining credits are being shifted toward machine-learning model design, automation, and optimization. A return to the host company as a full-time engineer is of interest, in order to extend the automated pipelines and continue the payment model.
advice for future interns: Accept the difference between academic machine learning and industry deployment. University tasks often provide clean data and center on fitting a model, while business files are sparse and contain typing errors. Cleaning and validation can take as long as development if bad inputs are to be kept out of the pipeline.
technical skills: Technical work included heuristic data pipelines, spreadsheet auditing, interface design for non-technical users, multiple linear regression, support vector machines, and a supervised logistic-regression proposal for supplier scoring.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: Courses reviewed or discussed are COMP3340, MATH3904, STAT3612, and COMP2113.
tools and software: Named tools are Python, through validator.py, merge_tool.py, and unified_tool.py, plus the openpyxl library and Excel workbooks.

job description: Lingyange Semiconductor Incorporated, also referred to as LYG or LYG-SEMI, was originally funded by Foxconn's semiconductor division. Its core business is chip development and design, with later expansion into artificial intelligence, automotive electronics, biomedicine, and smart cities. The internship was in the Embodied Intelligence Lab, on the AIAG Intelligent Agents group, as a large-model algorithm intern. The main task was a financial agent for the internal finance department, built on a private large-scale model, to turn Excel spreadsheets into charts and written summaries and cut the time staff spend writing reports.
job duties: Built a financial agent with a separated front end and back end, natural-language queries, and text-to-SQL, together with data processing and large-language-model integration; used NumPy and Pandas while working with Excel data; met finance colleagues to learn workflows, pain points, and which metrics and charts mattered; spoke with a former finance intern about dashboard practice and learned that software such as UFIDA already automates part of the work; limited the agent to a defined set of actions so its behavior stayed predictable; wrote a comparison of chat delivery through Lark or DingTalk against a standalone web front end and database, covering development time, user needs, reliability, maintenance cost, and scalability; built a minimal demo and presented the report and demo at a weekly meeting, after which the team leader approved the standalone format.
pre-internship preparation: From March to May, preparation included studying projects, polishing a resume, and practicing coding for agent and full-stack roles and for algorithm roles in multimodal systems, embodied intelligence, and large models. Open-source GitHub projects, some reinforcement learning, and hands-on work with Git, Docker, and AI agents built a base that was not all tested in interviews. Hiring ran from a resume on a job platform, to review by the technical lead, to scheduling by HR, to a one-on-one interview with the future supervisor. The hardest prompt was to design a question-answering assistant over a document portal using a large-model API and retrieval-augmented generation, with query rewriting, embedding search, BM25, business-tag filters, merging, re-ranking, and cited answers. The interviewer noted that the design skipped a local edge-case test set and a phased rollout.
what have I learned: The largest change was moving from clearly specified coursework to vague requests from finance users who are not engineers, which meant turning those requests into a concrete plan. Talks with finance staff and a former finance intern clarified metrics and charts, and showed that tools such as UFIDA already cover part of the process, so the agent was given strict boundaries. A written comparison and a small demo moved the delivery plan from chat-tool file drops to a standalone web front end and database. A senior engineer with a microelectronics background encouraged learning hardware as well as software, because models still run on chips.
what do I need to improve: Finance knowledge was thin at the start, so it was hard to tell when the team would use the agent, which metrics needed charts, and what kinds of charts to use. The interview answer on the document assistant also missed a testing stage and a phased release before full launch.
post-internship reflections: The career goal remains large-model algorithms, with more hands-on engineering and an open mind about direction. Year 4 courses stay in the AI Technology concentration and also explore the AI in Business and Finance concentration. A return to LYG-SEMI after a master's degree is possible if a suitable large-model or agent role is open, and applications to larger technology companies are also planned. The choice would depend on the role, room to grow, responsibilities, and the overall package.
advice for future interns: Know the projects on a resume well enough to explain how they work, not only which technologies they list. Prepare for scenario questions by thinking about how a small practice project would behave in production, including real user needs and heavy traffic, and where it would need to change.
technical skills: The project used large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, text-to-SQL, separated front-end and back-end design, prompt and workflow design, and NumPy and Pandas processing of Excel data. The interview design also used embedding search and BM25.
soft skills: The report describes face-to-face talks with finance staff to clarify vague needs, taking on product-style translation of those needs into a technical plan, and presenting a proposal and demo to the team.
courses mentioned: Courses named as most helpful are COMP3278, STAT3612, and COMP3340. Year 4 study mentioned the AI Technology concentration and the AI in Business and Finance concentration.
tools and software: Named tools are Git, Docker, GitHub, Excel, NumPy, Pandas, UFIDA, Lark, and DingTalk.

job description: Swire Resources Limited is part of the Swire Group under Swire Pacific and retails sports and outdoor products. Brands including Catalog, Marathon Sports, and GigaSports authorize it to sell in Hong Kong, Macau, and Mainland China. Imported goods are distributed to stores, so logistics and customs declarations are essential, and supplier formats differ enough that much of the translation between documents is still manual. The AI Summer Intern role began on 15 June 2026, was planned for eight weeks, and supported the warehouse team by automating trade declarations to Hong Kong customs.
job duties: Built an AI agent so warehouse staff could upload shipping files, request a declaration, and download a Tradelink Excel file; pulled fields from bills of lading, invoices, packing lists, cargo receipts, debit notes, and photos of handwritten documents; looked up Hong Kong HS codes by fuzzy matching goods names to a cleaned database and to official descriptions; calculated goods value and estimated net weight or value when source data were thin; validated entries in Python so the model would not fill gaps unchecked, and called extraction, data, and form tools through an MCP server, using multimodal models on images and PDFs; asked users to confirm missing or unclear fields; used parallel processing and dropped top-n filtering after accuracy fell; deployed the tool and wrote guides for non-technical users.
pre-internship preparation: The opening was found on the HKU CDS Careers Portal in mid-March, and the application went in through the company website. The company then asked by email for a resume, academic transcript, and an account of hands-on AI experience, projects, and coursework. An online selection set combined an aptitude test with a written proof of concept for an AI pilot. The interview was with the General Manager of IT and Digital. A short wait before the meeting was used to look up that person's background on LinkedIn. A question about using generative AI on the written test was answered by saying it had been used to pick out key points and draft a framework. The interviewer then introduced the company and asked about a start date.
what have I learned: Real shipping documents pushed the work past a classroom proof of concept toward a tool that could be deployed, including guides that warehouse staff could follow without reading the code. Talking with the manager and with users made the trade-off between full automation and reliability concrete, because a wrong declaration has operational effects and some handwritten inputs cannot be read automatically. Colleague feedback supported a simple upload and download flow with less training. Senior staff and a flexible-hours policy were part of how the product was delivered.
what do I need to improve: NA
post-internship reflections: University courses and projects were seen as unable to stand in for a real workplace, so the study plan adds independent learning on current AI practice, with a focus on large language model systems, agentic AI, and enterprise deployment. Rejoining is under consideration. The summer contract was extended by two weeks, and the company invited part-time maintenance of the product during year 4. The Swire Group setting is viewed as a stable path after graduation.
advice for future interns: Keep learning current AI topics independently, because the field moves quickly alongside university courses. Put at least as much effort into communication as into coding. Knowing the real user requirement prevents simple mistakes and mismatched expectations, and matters more than memorizing programming practice when tools can help look up code.
technical skills: The role used agentic AI, multimodal models for image and PDF extraction, fuzzy HS-code search, Python checks against hallucinated values, MCP tool calling, human-in-the-loop review, parallel processing, deployment, and user guides.
soft skills: The report highlights communication with the manager, warehouse users, and other stakeholders, collaboration on real business problems, and explaining the trade-off between automation and reliability.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Named tools and platforms are Python, Excel, Tradelink, an MCP server, and LinkedIn, which was used to prepare for the interview. Generative AI was also used on the written selection task.

company: Rating and Valuation Department of the HKSAR Government
job description: The Rating and Valuation Department of the HKSAR Government assesses properties for rates and government rent, keeps accounts, issues demand notes, advises other bureaux, publishes property-market statistics, and helps with landlord and tenant matters. The summer internship joined a Computer Division project on how machine learning could assist surveyors and valuation officers. Work discussed in the report is limited to ground-floor street shops in Hong Kong and combined prediction, walking-distance analysis, and reading on spatial statistics, with colleagues from surveying and urban studies and with the departmental data analyst.
job duties: Reproduced earlier tests of 14 models, from regressions and trees through XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and generalized additive models; traced a 0.99 XGBoost score to leakage from next-year rateable value, dropped those fields, and brought scores to about 0.85 to 0.94; added multi-seed tests and Optuna tuning; prototyped a feature-tokenized transformer on a small dummy set but could not run it on the full data because locked, offline PCs blocked installs and torch failed to import; built a Python shortest-walk script with Dijkstra on pedestrian data using GeoPandas, NetworkX, and Shapely, drew routes in ArcGIS Pro, and checked 16 cases against Walkin' HK and GeoInfo Map; scored interpolation with R-squared, MAE, RMSE, and error bands using terms such as Reduced Zone A; presented a Whittle-Matern review and looked at R packages for later use.
pre-internship preparation: The opening was found through HKU CEDARS and matched a concentration in AI in smart city. Stated duties were data cleaning, predictive modeling, and evaluation of machine-learning algorithms. Preparation used the department website and definitions of rating and valuation terms, and linked AI, computer science, and geography coursework to physical and spatial features that might affect value. The interview covered technical skills, valuation concepts, and workplace integrity, and was followed by an offer.
what have I learned: Terms such as rent, rateable value, and Reduced Zone A had to be understood before a model fitted valuation practice. Documenting functions and variables let colleagues reuse a performance script. Explaining methods to people from surveying and urban studies mattered as much as the algorithm. Locked machines, with no internet installs and a failed transformer run, showed why the department restricts computers in order to protect public data. After the leakage fix, tree-based models, especially XGBoost, sat in a more realistic range for this tabular data.
what do I need to improve: There was no prior knowledge of rating and valuation or of the department's functions. A further gap was a habit of focusing on technical complexity and of working mainly with technical peers, while giving less weight to domain knowledge and to cooperation with non-technical colleagues.
post-internship reflections: The internship shifted attention from technical complexity alone toward domain knowledge, documentation, and communication across disciplines. Time in a government department clarified why civil servants balance accountability, public transparency, and new technology. Beyond the public sector, the aim is to use the same computational and spatial skills in other industries.
advice for future interns: NA
technical skills: Technical work covered tabular machine learning, including XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, k-nearest neighbours, support vector machines, multilayer perceptrons, and generalized additive models, plus leakage checks, Optuna tuning, a feature-tokenized transformer, Dijkstra walking distances, and interpolation metrics such as R-squared, MAE, and RMSE. Independent reading covered Whittle-Matern fields on metric graphs.
soft skills: The report stresses communication with surveyors, valuation officers, and interns from other disciplines, translating algorithms into intuitive explanations, and writing documentation so colleagues could adapt the code.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Named tools are Python, R, Optuna, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, torch, GeoPandas, NetworkX, Shapely, ArcGIS Pro, Common Spatial Data Infrastructure data, Walkin' HK, and GeoInfo Map.

job title: Tencent Tech Product Intern (Cloud and AI)
job description: Tencent is described as a major technology company in mainland China. The Tech Product Intern (Cloud and AI) role supported the launch of WorkBuddy, a new AI agent with over 20 million active users in mainland China, into Hong Kong and overseas markets where products such as Claude Code and Codex already compete. A second stream, called AI for Good and including Tencent Foundation work in Hong Kong, used Tencent products to help local non-governmental organizations and social enterprises. The work was on the product side: design, launch, promotion, and fitting tools to how people actually work.
job duties: Compared similar AI agents, tracked their updates, and proposed layout, default skills, and prompts for an international WorkBuddy, showing the ideas in demos; met the development team with a mentor to explain the requirements and the reasons for them; built event websites that introduced WorkBuddy and encouraged people to try it; visited about ten Hong Kong NGOs, identified repetitive funding paperwork, and helped design a WorkBuddy flow to fill forms from application requirements; built skills and automations so NGOs could use the product; for a requested phone chatbot on funding and events, proposed retrieval-augmented generation together with OSR and TTS models; built a skill that uses AI agents to publish NGO needs on a website designed for that purpose.
pre-internship preparation: There were five interviews over about a month, each roughly an hour with two or three interviewers, including one face-to-face round. Preparation used an AI tool fed with the job description, company information, and background, asked to act as the interviewer and to draft questions. Some questions on products and culture later appeared in the interviews. The first three rounds covered technical topics and personality. The fourth asked for a vibe-coded demo, using Tencent's AI agent, on a social issue, plus an explanation of the concept, motivation, skills, and tech stack. The last round, with the vice president responsible for Hong Kong public affairs, focused on communication and on views of AI and startups in the Greater Bay Area.
what have I learned: The launch work clarified how a technology product is designed, released, and revised from user feedback. NGO visits showed that useful tools come from interviewing people and checking that a feature matches real work, such as repeated funding forms. Coursework supported discussions of model limits and algorithm choices with developers, and supported a retrieval-augmented design for a phone chatbot. After a mentor pointed out confusing wording, explanations were split between technical terms for engineers and analogies for colleagues without that background. Vague tasks, including how NGOs could state their needs, required a design with no sample answer.
what do I need to improve: Communication was a major gap. Requirements were hard to state precisely to the development team, and terms such as RAG or MCP confused colleagues without a technical background, which a mentor pointed out. Tasks with no clear definition of success were also difficult, because university assignments had come with instructions and reference answers.
post-internship reflections: The internship was still in progress. The plan is to take the return-offer interview and to rejoin if it succeeds, because the product role matches a goal of using AI in ways that affect daily life. If that happens, the next step is to deepen product-management skill and, later, possibly start a company. An earlier uncertainty between research or development and product work settled on the product side: deciding what to build and why it matters.
advice for future interns: For large companies, do not rely only on public resume channels such as LinkedIn, where an application is easy to overlook among many similar ones. Join events and competitions, meet people at the target companies, and let them see the work so they make contact.
technical skills: Product work used competitor analysis of AI agents, demo building, retrieval-augmented generation, OSR and TTS for a proposed voice chatbot, workflow automation for form filling, and judgments about what models can and cannot do.
soft skills: The report describes communication with technical and non-technical colleagues, user interviews at NGOs, switching between jargon and analogies, and working with a mentor and a development team under ambiguous tasks.
courses mentioned: APAI4011 is named as the course where retrieval-augmented generation was learned.
tools and software: Named products and platforms are WorkBuddy, Claude Code, Codex, Tencent's AI agent, and LinkedIn. MCP is named as a technical term used with engineers.

job description: The internship was with the Asset Liability Management team at Prudential Corporate Asia, on economic scenario generation. Daily interest-rate monitoring collected government bond rates, swap rates, credit spreads, and indicators such as VIX and PMI for several countries, then sent visualized summaries to internal and external stakeholders for market risk, investment strategy, and regulatory needs. Data came from the Bloomberg Terminal and were compiled with R into HTML. When the internship began, the chain was largely manual and took about 40 to 50 minutes. The main project turned it into an automated run of about 10 minutes that other analysts could maintain.
job duties: Learned the manual chain of updating dates in the Interest Rate Monitoring Downloader and Auto Control Workbook, running Excel macros, pulling remaining points from Bloomberg, maintaining a cross-currency swap tool, knitting two R Markdown files into internal and external HTML, and pasting a summary into separate emails; built a Python script that asks for the report date and sender name, triggers the extraction macros, updates the database file, calls the R reports without a manual knit in RStudio, and sends both emails with the summary included; replaced hard-coded comparison dates with dates read from the database so weekends and holidays are respected; redesigned HTML tables with clearer double headers; added spike detection that flags percentage moves against thresholds from historical statistics and regulatory requirements and highlights them on charts; wrote documentation of the process and its limits for later interns.
pre-internship preparation: NA
what have I learned: Python and R were extended beyond lecture examples to automate a multi-step reporting process and to connect several data sources. Clear charts mattered for readers who are not specialists. The project also required planning for later maintenance, tracing errors to their source, and explaining technical steps to a non-technical audience. Moving the manual process into a documented workflow linked risk-management and finance study with a live reporting cycle and reduced both typing errors and dependence on one analyst.
what do I need to improve: NA
post-internship reflections: The experience is tied to a continuing path in risk management and finance. Linking classroom ideas with a live asset-liability process is described as a central takeaway, and the automation and domain skills are expected to carry forward in that career.
advice for future interns: Documentation of the whole process, its limits, and ideas for later development was left for the next interns so the tool can be maintained and improved. The recommended next step is to add another data source and bring the remaining manual tickers, especially cross-currency swaps, into the automated flow.
technical skills: Technical work used Python and R automation, R Markdown HTML reports, Excel macros, Bloomberg data, spike detection from percentage changes, and thresholds set from historical data and regulatory requirements.
soft skills: The report names project management with attention to later maintenance, problem-solving, and communication of technical ideas to a non-technical audience.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Named tools are Python, R, R Markdown, RStudio, Excel, the Bloomberg Terminal, and HTML report output.

job description: FWD Group Management Holdings Limited is described as an innovative insurer providing pan-Asian insurance services. The report frames insurance work as including back-office valuation, reporting, and analysis, not only product sales. The intern joined the Embedded Value Team, which measures the value of shareholders' interest in distributable profit. The role consolidated data from business units into standardized valuation reports. Much of the work was repetitive grouping, file updates, and formula templates, and part of the contribution was to automate steps that had been done by hand.
job duties: Consolidated business-unit data into standardized valuation reports by grouping records, updating files, and creating formula templates; proposed VBA automation to cut manual handling, and saw that automation pass testing and move into production; updated links in the input cells of an existing reporting program, doubted the output, kept a backup, compared format and logic with the previous year's template, fixed the issues, and had the manager accept the changes for production; merged and grouped data and maintained reporting templates during a peak period that included overtime; returned to training notes whenever a new or repeated task connected to earlier material.
pre-internship preparation: The application followed an actuarial internship at AIA and was aimed at seeing more manual analysis and a full process in a smaller company. Preparation used the STAR method from an HKU session for questions on difficulties, strengths, and weaknesses, and reviewed technical knowledge from the AIA work plus IFRS 17 handouts. There was one online interview with the hiring manager, who had previously worked on the same AIA IFRS 17 team. The conversation became a discussion of that team's recent projects and enhancements.
what have I learned: Coding and statistics from the Decision Analytics major supported VBA automation of repetitive reporting, and a template that reached production gave a concrete sense of adding value. A faulty update taught independent checking: keep a backup, test against last year's logic, and confirm quality with the manager. Compared with AIA, where instructions and weekly development conversations were clearer, FWD expected more independent work, so issues were investigated first and feedback was requested after each task. Across assignments, the reporting cycle became a fuller picture of how the team creates value, and professional contacts proved useful again later.
what do I need to improve: An early gap was hesitation to question an existing setup, and a tendency to wait for instructions when a result looked wrong and the manager was busy. Another was uncertainty about expectations in a team that gave fewer guidelines than the previous internship, which called for a more self-directed way of working.
post-internship reflections: Two actuarial internships confirmed a goal of becoming an actuary and of starting as a graduate analyst, with extra effort because the major is not actuarial science. The plan is to pass four SOA exams by graduation and to shift a second major in finance toward insurance electives. FWD is valued, but limited hiring of fresh graduates led to a start at Deloitte for wider consulting exposure. An offer to join Deloitte as an actuarial consulting intern in the final semester, interviewed by its embedded-value team, is already in hand, with the hope of a later return offer as a graduate consultant.
advice for future interns: Show strong soft skills when applying for an actuarial internship. Candidates often share similar academic knowledge, so attitude, willingness to learn, and a professional manner are what stand out. Being self-motivated, careful, and well connected helps secure opportunities.
technical skills: Technical work used VBA automation, consolidation and grouping of valuation data, embedded-value reporting templates, IFRS 17 material, and checks of formula links against a prior-year template.

job title: Intern in the Risk Management Division
job description: The Bank of East Asia is a Hong Kong-based bank offering wealth management, retail banking, and corporate banking. The report describes the industry as changing through financial technology, digitalization, artificial intelligence, and big data, including an internal project to automate credit rating. The one-year internship was in the Risk Management Division. The main duty was to maintain the bank-wide risk data warehouse, described as the single source of risk data drawn from different countries and institutions, including exchange rates, stock prices, credit ratings, and customer information. After extract, transform, and load processing, the data feed regulatory reports such as BASEL and IFRS9, so errors or delays affect compliance.
job duties: Maintained the risk data warehouse and checked that market, credit, and customer data flowed into BASEL and IFRS9 reporting; ran user-acceptance tests on upgrades, checking field values and whether results made sense in risk terms such as probability of default and value-at-risk; took end-to-end enhancements across loan, derivatives, and securities projects, including requirement discussions, scheduling, acceptance testing, and health checks after go-live; prepared updates for meetings every two weeks with risk, finance, and IT, and answered in business language; investigated a source-system data-quality issue that was distorting a credit-risk report, measured the fields, frequency, and volume of errors, and recommended a fix so management could make a risk-based decision; studied documentation and lineage maps, searched online, and asked colleagues when the table structure was unclear.
pre-internship preparation: Before the interviews, preparation covered the bank's background and trends in banking. There were two rounds. Human resources focused on the resume and on duties and lessons from a previous internship. The division's team head and manager then asked about risk-management concepts and about SAS and SQL. A situational question asked how to urge colleagues on other teams to finish work. The reply was a polite email one or two days before the deadline, then a phone call or another direct contact if there was still no reply, together with clear communication about urgency and any blockage.
what have I learned: SQL and SAS moved from school knowledge into daily warehouse work, along with a view of the full data flow and the regulatory reports it supports. Working with IT staff and presenting to senior colleagues sharpened the ability to turn a technical fault into business language. Projects across loans, derivatives, and securities gave a wider view of the risk architecture than a single product area. The biweekly meetings required fast, careful answers for audiences from several departments. Early on, the number of tables and the transformation logic were the hardest part of the system to absorb.
what do I need to improve: At the start, the volume of tables and the extract-transform-load logic were overwhelming, and it was difficult to see how data changed or how to extract and validate the right fields. The response was to study lineage documentation outside immediate tasks, search independently, and then ask experienced colleagues.
post-internship reflections: The internship strengthened a plan to work in banking, especially in risk. Further study is aimed at the technical side, with priority on machine learning and data mining because of fintech, and on Python libraries for data analysis and statistical modelling. Rejoining the bank after graduation is strongly considered because of the trust given on projects and the exposure across risk domains.
advice for future interns: Build a solid technical base, and learn the programming languages that data roles use day to day. Ask about the idea behind each assigned task so the new setting is easier to absorb. Practice explaining a complicated technical issue clearly to people from different backgrounds.
technical skills: Hands-on skills were SQL and SAS, warehouse extract-transform-load processes, user-acceptance testing, and reading outputs with risk concepts such as probability of default and value-at-risk, in support of BASEL and IFRS9 reporting.
soft skills: The report names sharper communication from working with IT professionals and presenting to senior colleagues, translation of technical issues into business language, and cross-team follow-up under time pressure.

job duties: Compiled public information and registry details on ownership, management, compliance, and media coverage, and reconciled figures on industry size, prices, users, and channels; wrote short English and Chinese pieces for proposals and clients on Hong Kong stablecoin laws, Web 3.0 and digital assets, and the licensing setting for a possible crypto gift-card business, plus a public-source brand case on weak growth, demand forecasting, and data-driven distribution; checked scope with a mentor before delivery; researched Yunnan restaurants, including Kunming versus prefecture cities, central kitchens, delivery, and short-video marketing; screened the brand Qiezi Qiaqia on review sites, social media, registries, and news, and judged whether criticism looked isolated or systemic; built a slide deck mapping licensing, disclosure, and reserve rules to operations; extended the Hong Kong crypto study to pan-Asian exchanges, including custody, retail access, and stablecoin or fiat on-ramps.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation covered both the industry and the firm. The consulting work linked risk ideas to growth choices, such as market entry and partnerships with licensed custodians and payment firms. Internal studies of restaurants and of crypto licensing added practice that the report expects to reuse in later jobs.
what do I need to improve: A reputational survey had to be rewritten because the data were collected for the wrong time period, which was described as negligence. post-internship reflections: Near-term goals are consulting and risk management, including regulatory impact assessment, compliance frameworks, and scenario planning in fintech and digital change. The longer aim is to become a risk executive or risk strategist who connects risk modeling with business execution. Study is aimed at regulatory technology, financial risk management, corporate finance, and data engineering, with capstone work on management, data quality, and scenario modeling, plus qualifications in risk and compliance. Working at Frost and Sullivan after graduation is of interest because the firm's industry coverage fits that path.
advice for future interns: Build a joined-up base of industry structure, regulation, and business measures. In interviews, state expectations clearly and be ready to justify them. On the job, standardize deliverables and keep steady communication with supervisors. Research a company's background thoroughly before applying.

job description: Grant Thornton is described as part of a large independent audit, tax, and advisory network and as one of the earlier accounting firms in China. The summer internship applied a statistics and risk-management background to audit sampling, analytical review, and tracing source documents through the financial statements in that financial advisory setting.
job duties: Used statistical sampling on accounts receivable instead of checking every transaction, paying more attention to items with a higher risk of misstatement such as high-value invoices; compared period expenses with the prior period and the budget, and flagged outliers and large departures from normal values so substantive testing could be targeted; traced purchase contracts and invoices to fixed assets, current-period depreciation, and investing cash flows, found equipment that had been scrapped but not removed from the books, and corrected the journal entry across the three statements; on an office-rent jump, reviewed payment vouchers, compared old and new leases, set out dates and amounts in the working papers, and calculated the contract change for the supervisor.

A certification-training institution recommended the application. The interview was with a human-resources team manager and the Financial Advisory Team. After a self-introduction, a situational question asked what to do if the student alone spotted discrepancies in a client's data. The answer was to confirm the finding, state the problem clearly, and report it to the supervisor in a respectful, factual way, emphasising the risk to the audit opinion.

what do I need to improve: The student says the hardest gap was not the volume of work but a lack of structured audit thinking: unfamiliar terms and testing methods, scattered knowledge, and difficulty considering credit risk, revenue recognition, and bad-debt provisions at the same time for accounts receivable. Statistical sampling and regression analysis learned at school were initially hard to apply to the financial-consulting information.
post-internship reflections: The student does not want to do this job for the long term. Financial consulting relates to the studies, but the audit work is not interesting as a career, so the student is still looking and would like a winter-break internship in a bank investment department. The study plan is to learn more accounting and combine it with the risk-management background. Grant Thornton's supportive and professional atmosphere was enjoyable, but a return after graduation is unlikely while the plan is banking investments and securities. The student remains open to roles that match that interest.
advice for future interns: Improve the resume and do not be discouraged by an imperfect GPA. Show analytical ability through contests, certifications, or personal projects. Enter the internship as a learner, because early work can look dull while the basic principles still matter. Improve communication so professional analytical results can be explained clearly.
technical skills: The student used statistical sampling, risk-based selection, analytical procedures, outlier and standard-deviation checks, and tracing of journals through the three financial statements. Regression analysis is named as a school method that was difficult to apply at first.

job description: The internship was Market Risk Management for Global Foreign Exchange at HSBC. In the secondary market the bank is a market maker, posting bid and ask prices so the market has liquidity, and it also offers brokerage that executes trades for clients. The student describes trading as fast and continually changing. The job was to monitor and manage market risk from trading activity. That meant following market moves so the consequences of scenarios could be anticipated, then managing risk by setting limits on factors such as value at risk, stressed value at risk, conditional value at risk, Greeks, and liquidity.
job duties: Monitored and managed market risk from trading, including foreign-exchange and rates moves, and worked with limits on value at risk, stressed value at risk, conditional value at risk, Greeks, and liquidity; took a large VBA automation project from the line manager despite having no VBA background, using a beginner tutorial, code left by previous interns, and daily tests of small modules; when a project seemed to require pulling a large data set from an intranet site, showed that the files were already stored and wrote Python to loop through them in parallel, extract the fields, and process them under set conditions, which saved about 90 percent of the time; used the market framework to interpret the early-August carry-trade unwind, when USDJPY moved from about 150 to 140.
pre-internship preparation: The student prepared for Market Risk Management (Global Foreign Exchange) at HSBC on two fronts. Behavioural preparation covered motivation for the market-risk role, strengths and weaknesses, and a walkthrough of experience. Technical preparation reviewed foreign exchange, derivatives, and market news. The process was an online application, a one-way virtual interview, and a final interview with the line manager. A difficult final question asked how to price a digital call option. The student reasoned from Black-Scholes and a bull call spread: long and short calls in a quantity of one over the strike gap, then a zero-gap limit, so the digital price equals the derivative of the call value with respect to the strike.
what have I learned: The student gained a practical reading of foreign exchange and rates: policy rates and interest-rate parity, export strength, geopolitics, the dollar smile, the yen as a funding and haven currency, SOFR as the secured repo rate, and the federal funds rate as unsecured overnight lending between banks. Risk-management courses mapped onto the desk, especially value at risk from STAT3609 and option valuation, Greeks, market-maker economics, and exotic options from STAT3618. VBA was learned on the job, and a Python file loop replaced a slow manual extract. The August carry-trade unwind, after a Bank of Japan hike and expected Federal Reserve cuts, became a worked example, including the related sell-off in Japanese exporters.
what do I need to improve: The named difficulty is VBA. University courses had covered Python, few colleagues knew Python, and the team preferred VBA because it was easy to run inside Excel. The line manager still assigned a large VBA project when the student had no VBA background.
post-internship reflections: The career goal is to become a trader. The study plan is to learn more financial products, because many structured products are still unfamiliar. The student would consider rejoining HSBC after graduation, citing its culture and work-life balance.
advice for future interns: Fully review the financial and statistical knowledge learned at school, and think carefully about how statistics can be implemented in finance in order to manage risk.
technical skills: The student monitored market risk and limits on value at risk, stressed value at risk, conditional value at risk, Greeks, and liquidity, interpreted foreign-exchange and rates markets, learned VBA for Excel automation, and wrote Python to extract and condition data from many files. Digital-call pricing in the interview used Black-Scholes and a limiting bull call spread.
soft skills: The student proposed using Python to loop through files already held in a folder and extract the data automatically, and colleagues regarded that approach as innovative. VBA was learned from a beginner tutorial, code left by earlier interns, and daily practice on small modules.
courses mentioned: STAT3609, covering value at risk, market efficiency, the capital asset pricing model, and arbitrage pricing theory; STAT3618, covering option basics and trading strategies, binomial-tree and Black-Scholes valuation, Greeks, the market-maker role, and exotic options.
tools and software: VBA, Excel, and Python.

job description: The student joined a Group Asset-Liability Management team, in the economic scenario generation sub-group, alongside portfolio monitoring and strategic asset allocation. That sub-group generates investment scenarios, estimates the time value of guarantees, checks solvency coverage, and tries to reduce portfolio risk. Its macroeconomic and market scenarios are used for internal forecasting, regulatory stress testing, and asset strategy, and the results pass to local business units and a group heavy-model team for valuation and capital assessment. The six-month internship sat across daily monitoring, system operations, automation, and the production modelling pipeline.
job duties: Took a turn at daily interest-rate monitoring, pulling key index data from a Bloomberg terminal to support asset allocation; managed virtual machines that deploy production tools, using Windows command lines and fixing compatibility problems, and logged recurring program failures for colleagues; upgraded Moody's Scenario Generator and the Python environment, ran user-acceptance tests, and updated outdated VBA and Python; translated selected production features from VBA to Python, in some cases speeding runs by up to 45 percent, and for tools that stayed in Excel moved cell formulas into central VBA functions with macro buttons; embedded HTML and JavaScript in Python to dashboard scenario results; sanity-checked raw data from local units, loaded assumptions, and helped produce cash rates, inflation indexes, zero-coupon bond prices, equity returns and dividend yields, risk-free and risky bond returns, and credit spreads, using bisection, secant, and Newton methods.
pre-internship preparation: Because the student was not majoring in actuarial science, time before the applications and interviews went into the insurance and actuarial industry, the teams along the actuarial life cycle, and the technical skills those roles ask for. Online research and talks with actuarial-major friends were used to polish statistics knowledge and common coding, and the resume was updated to highlight Python and VBA. In the interviews the student was at first unsure about detailed actuarial practice and asked the interviewers for the expected answer. The student says that approach led to nine offers from eleven interviews.
what have I learned: The student saw the asset-liability pipeline from daily market monitoring through scenario production, including how to keep tools working across upgrades and how bisection, secant, and Newton's method show up in production models. Practical gains were self-teaching, asking a precise question, and keeping notes so a successor could take over. Speaking with both technical and non-technical stakeholders about development plans and delivered code taught the student how to build trust and make teamwork smoother. Dashboards made scenario output easier for non-technical readers. Moving logic out of scattered cell formulas reduced manual errors.
what do I need to improve: The greatest challenge was the number of tools to learn at once: VBA, Python, multi-instance Excel, command-line scripts, and virtual-machine management. The learning curve was steep. A second difficulty was cross-department communication, because development plans and coding results had to be explained to both technical and non-technical stakeholders.
post-internship reflections: The student values the professional culture but does not plan to stay on this path. The next interest is product engineering and AI applications. To get there the student intends to go deeper in full-stack development, cloud computing, and machine learning, and to join more open-source projects and hackathons.
advice for future interns: Strengthen coding and Excel, especially Python and VBA, because most of the workflows now run through automated programs. It also helps to understand the fundamentals of asset-liability assessment, which the team uses every day. Stay curious and proactive, which the student says makes growth during the internship faster.
technical skills: The student used Python, VBA, Excel, a Bloomberg terminal, Windows command lines, and virtual machines, upgraded Moody's Scenario Generator, refactored workbooks, built HTML and JavaScript dashboards, and applied bisection, secant, and Newton methods inside the scenario-production pipeline.
soft skills: The student names cross-department communication, building trust, and smoother teamwork, plus self-teaching and writing notes so knowledge could be passed to a successor.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Bloomberg, Python, VBA, Excel, Moody's Scenario Generator, HTML, JavaScript, and Windows command line.

job description: SEA YA YA LIMITED focuses on individual wealth management and asset allocation and builds personalised financial solutions from each client's income, assets, risk tolerance, and long-term goals such as retirement and children's education. The student says those strategies need both statistics, for prediction and risk assessment, and business judgment about client needs and how the market works. The data-analysis internship followed that mix: learning the product set, measuring return and risk, building client-specific models, and explaining the results so a client could choose a portfolio.
job duties: Learned the firm's asset-allocation products and calculated annualised return, internal rate of return, and risk-adjusted returns, then set out data-driven comparisons and a risk-return classification framework; from the third week, built customised models, for example combining capital, duration, and expected return for a child's college costs and presenting a lower-risk, lower-cost suggestion in slides and charts; for a client hesitant after past losses, compared the current portfolio with a principal-guaranteed product that had a minimum guaranteed return; after a client who had bought a five-year 4.5 percent principal-guaranteed product faced a 15 percent early-redemption fee, started including short-term liquidity and explaining liquidity differences; replaced unexplained use of internal rate of return and standard deviation with plainer wording and line charts; built an Excel tool that, from amount and term, generated decade expected returns and comparison charts.
pre-internship preparation: For the Data Analysis Intern interview at SEA YA YA LIMITED, whose work is asset allocation and financial data analysis, the student reviewed risk-management course material on return models, probability distributions, and investment-risk statistics, self-studied the return and risk of common allocation products, and practised organising data in Excel and R. Selection was resume screening and a 45-minute technical assessment. One question asked how to turn a request to invest safely with returns above a savings account into a quantifiable project. The student proposed a minimum acceptable annualised return, a maximum tolerable annual loss, and an investment duration. Another asked how to explain model results to clients without a finance background. The student proposed everyday analogies, such as comparing volatility with changing grocery bills, plus bar and line charts.
what have I learned: The student gained practice in financial data analysis, from collecting client data and clarifying requirements to models that affected decisions, and in explaining technical points to non-professionals. Recommending a principal-guaranteed product to a cautious client, and later seeing another client hit a 15 percent early-redemption fee, showed that short-term liquidity and the client's situation matter as much as the risk-return numbers. An Excel calculator cut repeated manual comparisons and errors. Communication and the ability to tailor a solution are the soft skills the student says deepened.
what do I need to improve: A five-year principal-guaranteed product with a 4.5 percent expected annualised return was recommended from overall risk tolerance and long-term goals, with too little attention to short-term liquidity. When the client needed cash, a 15 percent early-redemption fee meant a large loss. Early meetings also used internal rate of return and standard deviation in a way that confused clients without a professional background.
post-internship reflections: The internship pointed the student toward financial statistics, especially asset allocation and personal wealth management, using statistical tools to help individuals decide. The revised study plan has three parts: advanced courses in financial statistics and financial machine learning, the CFA Level 1 exam for a broader view of financial markets, and an internship at a larger organisation. The student would consider returning to SEA YA YA LIMITED, where intern ideas were welcomed and the supervisor gave regular feedback and harder projects, but also wants a wider platform and a more diverse industry.
advice for future interns: Start with a clear objective, whether that is a specific industry, a skill, or the difference between teamwork in a corporation and a start-up. Use the university's resources, including faculty job postings and referrals from professors or alumni. Large firms give a broader industry view and more standardised division of work, while smaller firms often allow more hands-on responsibility and faster confidence. Treat an internship as a learning journey even when it is not an ideal long-term fit, because it still shows how a workplace runs, how to manage time, and what to want from the next role.
technical skills: The student calculated annualised return, internal rate of return, and risk-adjusted returns, built risk-return frameworks and client-specific financial models, and used charts to compare portfolios. Excel was used for an automated product-comparison tool. R and Excel were practised for data organisation before the internship.
soft skills: The student explicitly says the internship deepened soft skills, especially explaining technical concepts to non-professionals and shaping a solution around different client requirements. Listening to why a client distrusted investing after past losses is part of that account.
courses mentioned: Risk management courses, covering return models, probability distributions, and investment-risk statistics; planned advanced courses in financial statistics and financial machine learning; CFA Level 1.
tools and software: Excel and R.

job description: The internship was at a wealth management firm which, on its website, presents the values of security, inheritance, and persistence, acts as a risk-management consultant and an intermediary for insurance companies, and has offices in the United States, Singapore, mainland China, and Hong Kong. Services include insurance, tax planning, and residential planning. The three-month internship was in the broker management department. The student was responsible for customer service and support, compliance training, and cost management, and describes the setting as insurance brokerage.
job duties: Helped about ten groups of new employees complete required compliance courses and exams and checked progress every day; signed contracts, opened accounts, and archived documents, including customer-identity checks and anti-money-laundering rules; applied for budgets and reimbursements for company events and compared supplier prices; assisted a mentor through a first full client signing, including taking the client to a bank to open an account and make a payment, after asking for each step, writing a checklist, and rehearsing it; reorganised a messy annual departmental spending statement, looked at how other companies presented similar information, designed two clearer versions, and had one plan adopted by the department boss.
pre-internship preparation: After the interview invitation the student read the company website and financial reports for background and industry trends, compared personal skills with the job, and organised projects on risk and financial decision-making to show problem-solving and communication. Common questions were predicted, including why the student wanted the job and what the goal was, and answers were prepared so the logic would stay structured. There were two rounds. The first, with human resources and department leaders, covered past experience and motivation, and they introduced the company and department. The second, with the department director, focused on understanding of wealth management. Asked what to do if a customer does not trust a product, the student said they would ask why, listen, and then explain the product with facts and real cases so the risk level was transparent, relying on honesty and professionalism.
what have I learned: The student learned how a wealth-management and insurance-brokerage firm runs day to day, including compliance training as a control on business and reputation risk, identity and anti-money-laundering checks, and contract and account-opening steps. Class ideas about finding and controlling risk were used on those tasks. A rehearsed signing process, with questions to the mentor whenever something was unclear, got through a nervous first client bank visit. Redesigning the spending statement showed the value of proposing a clearer layout rather than only filling the old form. Cross-department work practised passing information accurately and cooperating with other people's demands.
what do I need to improve: Before the first full signing and bank payment the student was very nervous and had little experience, so each step had to be asked of the mentor, listed, and practised.
post-internship reflections: The student wants a management role in insurance and finance, for example managing brokers or improving how a business runs, and enjoys clear goals such as collecting and analysing information, sorting large amounts of data, and finding problems. A mentor asked about returning after graduation. In the short term the small team gives direct contact with the business. In the long term the department's scope is narrow and the main work stays with the same senior employees, so new joiners have less room to grow. The preference is a company with more services and career paths.
advice for future interns: Learn the basic concepts early. For this kind of insurance firm, know insurance knowledge, the relevant rules, and the business processes. The industry touches risk management, compliance, and finance. Solid theory from school makes the workflow and the reason for each task easier to understand, and makes customer problems easier to handle with more efficiency and confidence.
technical skills: The student tracked compliance-course completion, checked customer identity and anti-money-laundering requirements, handled contracts, account opening, and archiving, compared supplier prices, and rebuilt a departmental spending statement into a clearer layout.
soft skills: Problem-solving and communication were prepared for the interview and used with clients, including listening before explaining product risk and relying on honesty and professionalism. The student also describes information transmission, coordination, and cooperation with other departments.
