job description: The internship was at Hang Seng Insurance, under Hang Seng Bank. The student describes insurance as risk management: the insurer groups clients with similar pure risks so that, by the law of large numbers, actual results move toward the expected result, and people can transfer risks such as the cost of serious illness. The role was to assess the firm's solvency through the Prescribed Capital Amount and the Minimum Capital Amount. The Prescribed Capital Amount is the capital needed to survive a 1-in-200-year event within a year. If capital falls below 100 percent of that amount, the position is described as relatively dangerous and the regulator can require a restoration plan even if the firm is still operating.
job duties: Ran stochastic models over 1,000 economic scenarios to test whether policyholder obligations and claims could still be met in extreme events; calculated charges for market, insurance, credit, and operational risk and how different economic environments affect assets and liabilities; stress-tested solvency across market conditions; ran validation checks and sensitivity analyses and enhanced the Excel workbook before results were submitted to the Insurance Authority; requested quarterly valuation data from other departments by email; used VBA to automate Excel tasks; used Prophet to model risk and financial projections, including interest rates, equity returns, inflation, the present value of future claims and expenses, and the behaviour of a new product before launch; after several meetings on a workbook problem, worked with seniors to simplify some calculations.
pre-internship preparation: The student read the job description and matched it to school projects, then practised explaining those projects with the STAR method because paid experience was limited, stressing interest in the actuarial industry and willingness to learn. Scripts were written for a self-introduction in Chinese and in English and for common interview questions. Industry research covered what actuaries do and why the work is interesting. Questions prepared for the interviewer included a typical day, what an intern is expected to achieve, and whether progress on a Society of Actuaries exam is required. A recorded self-introduction was used to check clothes and flow, and the microphone and camera were tested.
what have I learned: The student learned how solvency is measured, including the Prescribed Capital Amount and Minimum Capital Amount, stochastic scenarios, stress tests, and checks before a regulatory submission. Excel became familiar within about a week, enough to take over the previous intern's work, and VBA was learned to automate tasks. Prophet was learned for actuarial projection. Writing emails to request quarterly valuation data was the stated communication lesson. A team-building event changed an expectation that a professional office would be only serious and competitive. After three months the manager assigned a harder workbook task, which was eventually simplified with senior colleagues.
what do I need to improve: At the start the student knew little about insurance and had never applied school learning to real work, so the material was entirely new. On a later workbook that the manager treated as important, several weeks of trying still left a problem the student could not solve. Seniors recognised it as a larger issue in that workbook, and the solution was to simplify some calculations.
post-internship reflections: The internship created an interest in what actuaries do and in a possible actuarial career. The student wants to look for more information on the Society of Actuaries exam and would like to rejoin Hang Seng Insurance after graduation. The reasons given are a friendly culture, seniors who teach new joiners, and seniors who will take an intern's advice when it improves a template.
advice for future interns: Prepare the CV and cover letter early, and recite a self-introduction and common questions such as why you want to join the company and what you know about the industry. The internship is described as a good place to learn technical skills and communication skills. Even if actuarial work is not the lasting interest, the Excel skills transfer to other industries.
technical skills: The student ran stochastic scenario models, calculated Prescribed Capital Amount and Minimum Capital Amount items and market, insurance, credit, and operational risk charges, and performed stress testing, validation, and sensitivity analysis. Excel, VBA, and Prophet were the tools learned or improved on the job.
soft skills: The student learned to write emails that ask other departments for quarterly valuation data, and discussed an unsolved workbook problem with seniors over several meetings. A team event is credited with showing that a supportive culture matters more than the student had expected.
courses mentioned: Society of Actuaries (SOA) exam.
tools and software: Excel, VBA, and Prophet.

job description: Tencent is a large internet technology company, best known for WeChat and QQ, with games as another major business. It has also increased investment in AI products and built its own large language model, Yuanbao. The student describes today's internet industry as a provider of everyday services and entertainment rather than a purely emerging field, while arguing that AI still opens further possibilities. From 31 July 2025 to 9 January 2026 the data-engineer internship centred on the Settings module of the Intellectual Knowledge Production System. That module stores user, tester, product, and group information and lets specified users manage group members and products.
job duties: Built the Settings-module database in MySQL and coded RESTful APIs connecting it to the front-end page; helped develop search so users can query specific groups, products, and users; during a system upgrade, found user information repeated across tables and cases where one ID matched two user names, then proposed a hidden ID that would not appear on the front end, plus relational tables between the tables; learned Go and wrote APIs in it, later fixing bugs independently; when a user-management API rendered chaotically, compared the code with the mentor's previous version and unified return structures and names so the page displayed correctly; traced empty search results for some Chinese product names to half-width parentheses, recorded the affected names, and argued that the mismatch should be fixed before the stored data grew.
pre-internship preparation: The job description required database knowledge, coding, and API calls. The student reviewed those topics on W3Schools, watched courses on YouTube and BiliBili, and did coding exercises on LeetCode, and also prepared answers on career plan and self-positioning. The resume went to HR through an internal recommendation. About a week later the first interview focused on the CV, followed by four more rounds that mixed technical understanding with improvising in workplace situations. Asked about PySpark in real development, the student said honestly that they knew little and were willing to learn. Asked about database-development experience, the student described a practice WeChat mini-program for exercise records, built while preparing, which used a lightweight database to store user data.
what have I learned: Technical gains were writing APIs in Go, which was new, developing a stable RESTful API independently, and fixing bugs. A statistics background is credited for attention to data structure, relationships, quality, and inconsistency, which led to the hidden-ID redesign and lower later maintenance cost. The stated soft-skill gain is clear communication in teamwork. The student also explored Tencent AI tools, including GPT, Claude, and DeepSeek, which could be used free, and was encouraged to build mobile apps, websites, and WeChat applets. The search-symbol bug was a case of testing a small issue and persuading the mentor it would matter at larger scale, even though the student did not make the final decision.
what do I need to improve: The student was not familiar at first with the team's coding specifications. A user-management API that seemed logically complete produced chaotic and sometimes wrong front-end output because the returned data's structure and field names did not match the expected format. The student also says they knew little about PySpark in the interview and had never joined a real database project before a small practice program.
post-internship reflections: The data-engineer role fitted the undergraduate studies, but the student does not want to work only as a programmer dealing with code all day. The stated interest sits between data analysis and business understanding, in roles such as industry research and quantitative analysis. Preparation will keep building technical skills and add finance and economics. The student has signed up for the CFA Level I exam. Rejoining Tencent is a possibility because of the working atmosphere, but it would depend on the specific position.
advice for future interns: Do not only recite textbook definitions when preparing for the interview. The student found the follow-up questions hardest: what was done in a project, which tools were used, what problems appeared, and how they were solved. Before the interview, go through past projects until those details can be explained.
technical skills: The student designed MySQL tables, wrote RESTful APIs, learned Go, built search, and debugged return payloads and inconsistent product-name symbols. Database, coding, and API practice before the internship used W3Schools, YouTube, BiliBili, and LeetCode. PySpark was asked about in an interview and was not something the student knew well.
soft skills: The student calls clear and effective communication, especially in teamwork, the main soft-skill gain. That included talking with colleagues about a broken page and making a tested case to a mentor for fixing a search mismatch.
courses mentioned: CFA Level I.
tools and software: MySQL, Go, W3Schools, YouTube, BiliBili, LeetCode, WeChat, GPT, Claude, and DeepSeek.

job description: From 2 July to 31 December 2025 the student was an Actuarial Intern at AIA Group, in Group Capital Management, Group Reinsurance. AIA is one of the largest independent Asian life insurance groups, offering life and accident insurance plus savings and retirement plans, with business units such as China and Malaysia under the group. Reinsurance is described as insurance for insurers: a company cedes part of its risk so large or uncertain claims are less destabilising, and both sides are typically actuaries, so premiums and claims must be set with care. The internship covered ceding thresholds, tendering, and treaty tracking, supporting transactions across units from the Hong Kong Island office.
job duties: Collected and summarised regulatory data, designed the database structure for reinsurance transactions, and wrote weekly progress reports; led a redesign of a database that had no unique search key and received inconsistent data from business units, including meetings to take unit feedback into the new structure; applied candidate keys and reduced redundancy so each transaction could be identified and queries ran faster; used regression to model reinsurance premium and claim distribution for the India business unit; filled in product type and line of business; turned raw annual-report figures into visual stories and wrote VBA macros so repeated report updates were faster; began writing down action items and details during meetings after forgetting instructions once the meeting ended.
pre-internship preparation: The student prepared for one week after invitations to first-round interviews with the Shareholder and Embedded Value Reporting team and the Reinsurance team. Both areas were researched online and notes were taken. Decision Analytics coursework was reviewed, especially regression analysis, Python, and R, and the student registered for the Society of Actuaries Probability (P) exam before the interview. The hard part was a 30-minute virtual interview with unexpected questions from the team leader. About 20 prepared answers, including why the student wanted to join, were never asked. The questions that were asked covered the typical structure of an insurance company and the main responsibilities of its departments. Prior industry research made those answers possible, and the interviewers' praise for that understanding helped secure the internship.
what have I learned: The student learned reinsurance ideas that reference books and slides introduced at the start, including lines of business, industry abbreviations, ceding, tendering, and treaty tracking. Decision Analytics and COMP3278 material was used on candidate keys, redundancy, and a regression for the India unit's premiums and claims. SQL, Excel quick commands, and VBA macros were learned from company resources, and a faster reporting process was the most enjoyable result. The workplace also required more independence than university, because a delay can affect teammates rather than only a grade. Writing action items in the meeting removed the need to ask the manager to repeat detailed instructions.
what do I need to improve: Newly learned reinsurance types and lines of business were at first hard to assign quickly and accurately, so the student reread a colleague's reference book during lunch breaks. In meetings the overall mission was remembered but the detailed instructions were forgotten, which meant asking the manager again until the student started noting action items and specifics during every meeting.
post-internship reflections: The goal after graduation is to be an analyst in data analytics. Colleagues' comments that actuarial jobs rarely have the same work-life balance pushed data science ahead of actuarial work, which is now a second choice. The student plans to pause Society of Actuaries exams, raise the GPA first, prioritise advanced data-analytics electives, strengthen programming and machine learning, and seek more data-driven final-year projects. Rejoining the AIA Group office is attractive because of the people, but suitable fresh-graduate roles are not currently offered, so the plan is to gain experience elsewhere and return at a more senior level. A last-day conversation with the department head included feedback and suggestions on preparing for an actuarial career.
advice for future interns: The student recommends this internship for real working experience, better communication, and contact with industry experts. Looking back, the student would have researched reinsurance concepts and related workflows more deeply before starting, because the early learning took a lot of time. If possible, live in a university hall or closer to the office. The daily commute between Kowloon and the Hong Kong Island office took quite a lot of time.
technical skills: The student used regression analysis, SQL, Excel, and VBA, and applied database ideas of candidate keys and redundancy. Python and R were reviewed from Decision Analytics courses before the interview. Reporting work turned annual-report data into visuals and automated updates with macros.
soft skills: The student describes a shift toward independent work and a stronger sense that delays affect teammates, and refers to these mindset changes as soft skills. Communication is also named in the recommendation of the internship. The meeting-note habit was the practical fix for forgetting spoken instructions.
courses mentioned: Decision Analytics courses, including regression analysis, Python, and R; COMP3278; Society of Actuaries (SOA) Probability (P) exam; planned advanced data analytics electives.
tools and software: Python, R, SQL, Excel, and VBA.

job description: The student completed a six-month full-time internship at HSBC in the Global Risk Analytics Department, on the Wholesale Analytics team, which monitors credit-risk models. HSBC is described as a global bank, and the placement showed bank operations and risk management at a global standard. The student also found the bank large: risk work is split across many teams, so the scope is narrow and the whole credit-risk picture is hard to see. Placement interns are hired for business-as-usual tasks, with a long written guide passed from one intern to the next. Alongside that monitoring, the student did ad hoc analysis, including a benchmarking of the slotting model.
job duties: Used an approximately 80-page Word handover that set out each business-as-usual procedure; from the first week of the month, took the report from IT, followed up default and resolution cases with other regional sites, including Australia, Singapore, and Indonesia, verified the reasons, analysed the report in Excel, SAS, and Python, and built a presentation deck for management; benchmarked slotting-model versions V1 and V2, an internal rating model that turns a relationship manager's client questionnaire into Strong, Good, Satisfactory, or Weak, by calculating the population stability index and a transition matrix in Python; when SAS programs were unfamiliar, used AI prompts to generate and explain code and then amended it from a basic Python background.
pre-internship preparation: Human resources called while the student was travelling in Vienna, asked about background, discussed the job duties, and scheduled a 30-minute online manager interview two days later, which fell at 4:30 am Vienna time because of the time difference with Hong Kong. Preparation at night covered HSBC's background and credit-risk model concepts, including the probability of default, loss given default, and exposure at default formulas, plus interview experiences shared on social media. The interview asked for a self-introduction, previous internship experience, and simple technical questions on the credit-risk model, which matched that preparation. Asked to rate Python ability from 1 to 10, the student said 6, noting no prior internship that used Python for data analysis but expecting AI to help with most tasks. An offer call came a few hours later.
what have I learned: The student learned bank administration, such as applying for access and reading knowledge articles, the risk-management framework, and how to catch up on assigned business-as-usual work and finish it on time. Communication improved through case discussions with sites including Australia, Singapore, and Indonesia. School statistics did not match every model formula, but it provided a base for reading the equations. Population stability index, transition matrices, and the slotting scale were applied on the benchmarking. A Global Risk Analytics networking session, with remarks from the Global Head of Risk Management, suggested that many risk managers start in a Big Four firm because direct hiring of fresh graduates into that department is rare. AI was used to draft and explain SAS code.
what do I need to improve: The student says risk-management studies gave little exposure to programming, even though the analysis depends on code. Basic Python had come from online courses, but the language used most for this HSBC work was SAS, and running SAS programs was difficult until AI-generated code could be read, explained, and amended.
post-internship reflections: After the internship the career goal changed to risk analyst, specifically risk advisory in a consulting firm, so that client contact and technical work sit together. Connecting with people was the most enjoyable part. The student would consider rejoining HSBC after graduation if a role with similar work exists. Preparation already includes a part-time internship at TransUnion on credit analytics for banks and financial institutions, and a plan to take the FRM Part 1 exam for industry knowledge.
advice for future interns: The student says an internship is the most direct way to understand an industry and one's own strengths and weaknesses, and that talking with practitioners helps career planning, so fellow students should build a CV and broaden their view by doing an internship. For a risk role, learn the industry knowledge attached to the job, read other candidates' interview experiences on Glassdoor, and prepare stories for behavioural questions. Technical preparation matters most. Knowing languages such as Python, SQL, and R is a large advantage. Interviewers are not expected to assume a student knows everything, but they do expect visible preparation and motivation.
technical skills: The student used Excel, SAS, and Python on default and resolution cases, data extraction, and report analysis, and calculated the population stability index and a transition matrix for a slotting-model benchmark. Credit-risk formulas for probability of default, loss given default, and exposure at default were reviewed before the interview. AI was used to generate and explain SAS code.
soft skills: The student says workplace communication improved, especially when discussing and verifying cases with colleagues in other regions, and also mentions managing the time needed to finish assigned tasks. A department networking event added ideas about career paths in risk management.
courses mentioned: FRM Part 1.
tools and software: Excel, SAS, Python, and Word.

job description: Hannover Re Hong Kong Branch is a life and health reinsurer and an Asia-Pacific hub for insurers in Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan, Singapore, the Philippines, Indonesia and Mongolia. Its services cover product design, underwriting and claims support, sharing risks such as mortality and multiple diseases. The business is described as relatively stable because income comes mainly from life and health insurance. The intern's work had three parts: reviewing claims against treaty terms, managing the claims database, and drafting confirmation letters, later including an automation of that drafting, plus some discounted-cash-flow help for the valuation team.
job duties: Checked claim applications against signed treaty terms using Excel functions such as IF, SUM, VLOOKUP and FILTER, plus pivot tables; sorted the previous quarter's claims by treaty code into a common format, merged them, imported the file with SQL, and adjusted claims from earlier quarters that needed correction; used SQL to total claims by policy, document date and currency and cross-checked those totals with underwriting statements; completed this database work for the second and third quarters of 2025 and updated the process notes; filled confirmation-letter templates with contact details, company names and customer statements of account, and compared them with the company statement; built a contact list and a VBA routine that generates letters from treaty code and term; calculated some discounted cash flows and volatility for the valuation team; linked cells into an urgent Hong Kong Risk-Based Capital table.
pre-internship preparation: In sophomore year the Corporate Mentor Program, run by the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, led to conversations with practicing actuaries at SCOR Re and to later applications in actuarial and insurance work. Interview preparation included reading about actuarial-department roles, duties, skills and partner departments, mock interviews with the CMP mentor, and practice on likely questions. Selection was a written test on Excel, SQL and financial mathematics, then an interview. One question asked for three words or phrases and how they fit the role; the answer given was communication skills, attention to detail and creativity.
what have I learned: The clearest gain was proposing and finishing automation of confirmation letters, after the drafting work had been manual copying of customer details, period changes and statement checks. A mentor and underwriting colleagues agreed after a meeting, and later users only needed to enter items such as treaty code and term. A separate lesson was to weigh how often a task occurs before optimising it: an urgent quarterly Hong Kong Risk-Based Capital report was delayed while a better linking method was explored. Daily notes, simpler steps, and clear titles for the next colleague also became working habits. Putting an idea to a mentor early was treated as important to staying motivated.
what do I need to improve: VBA had not been learned before the confirmation-letter project. On the Hong Kong Risk-Based Capital table, time went into looking for a better method instead of finishing an urgent manual link, and the report was late. The supervisor's point was that saving an hour or two on a once-a-quarter task, and asking colleagues to learn the new method, was not a good trade.
post-internship reflections: The career aim is to become an actuary in insurance. Plans include the qualification of the American Association of Actuary and further insurance courses. The working atmosphere at Hannover Re is viewed positively, with a hope of working there again.
advice for future interns: For an actuarial application, pass one or two actuarial exams beforehand and join activities of the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Sciences, such as the Corporate Mentor Program, so there is direct contact with practicing actuaries before interviews and career planning.
technical skills: Excel functions (IF, SUM, VLOOKUP, FILTER), pivot tables and charts, SQL, discounted cash flow and volatility calculations, VBA, and Python as a bridge into VBA.
soft skills: Communication, attention to detail, creativity, teamwork, and raising ideas with a mentor.
courses mentioned: STAT1600; STAT3615; COMP3278; STAT3612; COMP2119; actuarial exams.
tools and software: Excel, SQL, VBA, Python.

job description: Earnst Young, also called EY in the report, is a professional services firm providing audit, tax, consulting and advisory services. The five-month internship was in the actuarial team of the risk consulting department, which guides other insurance companies and is expected to keep current technical knowledge. The work centred on auditing IFRS 17 reports, auditing Hong Kong Risk-Based Capital reports, and using Alteryx. IFRS 17 is described as an insurance-contract standard that discounts future cash flows, spreads revenue through a contractual service margin, and adjusts non-economic assumptions. HKRBC is described as a capital rule tied to the size of an insurer's risk.
job duties: Audited IFRS 17 reports, covering discounted future cash flows, contractual service margin and non-economic assumptions; audited Hong Kong Risk-Based Capital reports; learned Alteryx, relating it to SQL and R; wrote a VBA macro that cut a manual task of about 30 minutes to under 20 seconds, and asked managers for more Excel work, including overtime; reconciled life-catastrophe-risk figures using the client's non-economic data and economic data from online sources, compared the result with the client's, and reported a gap that was traced to minor errors on the client side; asked questions immediately and recorded meetings when industry terms were unclear.
pre-internship preparation: The interview had an HR phone round and a one-to-one virtual round with a senior. Both were prepared with a 30-second self-introduction delivered while smiling. The HR round was practiced around strengths and weaknesses, leadership, teamwork difficulty and how it was handled. The second round was prepared with industry terms, recent industry news, and questions written from the resume, including prior internships. An unexpected question asked about Alteryx, which had not been used; the reply listed C+, Python, SQL, R, SAS, Power BI and Tableau and argued that overlap would speed up a new tool. An offer came a few days later.
what have I learned: Excel was the stated goal, after a December course on functions and VBA macros taken because a previous actuarial internship had offered little Excel work. During this placement a VBA macro reduced about 30 minutes of manual work to under 20 seconds, though more Excel practice still felt necessary. Alteryx was learned quickly by comparison with SQL and R. Accounting ideas such as the balance sheet, income statement, liability measurement and pension income recognition, plus insurance courses from the Decision Analytics major, made IFRS 17 and HKRBC easier to follow. Choosing team lunches, instead of studying alone for an exam as in a previous internship, made day-to-day communication easier. A life-catastrophe reconciliation that did not match the client was checked, escalated, and found to reflect client-side errors.
what do I need to improve: Excel still felt short of the level needed, so more Excel tasks were requested. Industry wording and concepts, rather than Excel, were the usual block, so questions were asked at once and meetings were recorded. Compared with actuarial science majors, actuarial concepts were described as a gap because interest in the field started only in year 4.
post-internship reflections: The career plan is to stay in actuarial work. Graduation is expected in May, followed by study for SOA exams SRM and PM and an MSc in Actuarial Science that has already been offered. The report says that degree would add two exam passes, for six SOA exams in total by the end of the MSc. A return to the firm is being considered; the manager was asked about a return offer, with the result expected in June.
advice for future interns: Use the SAAS internship website. Both actuarial internships came from that site, and one application round usually produced about three to five interviews.
technical skills: Excel, Excel VBA, Alteryx, IFRS 17 and HKRBC audit work, financial reconciliation, and prior use of C+, Python, SQL, R, SAS, Power BI and Tableau.
soft skills: Communication, team engagement, and asking questions early to avoid misunderstanding.
courses mentioned: SOA Exam SRM; SOA Exam PM; MSc in Actuarial Science; Decision Analytics insurance courses; Excel technical course.
tools and software: Excel, Excel VBA, Alteryx, C+, Python, SQL, R, SAS, Power BI, Tableau.

job description: MCM Wealth Management (HK) Limited is a locally registered insurance broker. It sits between clients and insurers such as AIA and AXA and earns commissions on products it distributes, so relationships, documentation, client due diligence and legal compliance are central. The intern joined as a risk management and compliance intern, expecting product and client risk assessment, data collection and monitoring. The work that followed was operational: internal due diligence files, external due diligence for partner insurers, Know Your Client and anti-money laundering checks, and contact with regulators including the Insurance Authority.
job duties: Located documents against a checklist and filed reports, financial statements, compliance policies, training manuals and transaction papers into a consistent folder structure; collected items on checklists sent by insurers considering a partnership; for KYC and AML, recorded occupation, income level and source of income and checked clients against the HK government terrorists list; telephoned the Insurance Authority after a license was cancelled because a renewal payment was not on the system, until a second payment cleared the record; listed the files needed for due diligence, agreed where each one lived with the mentor, and wrote a standard operating procedure so later requests could be completed with less help.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started from the firm's role as a broker between clients and insurers such as AIA and AXA, and from an expectation that a risk management and compliance internship would include analysis. Recruitment was one informal interview with the managing director about background and five-year goals, with no case or quantitative exercise. An early start was encouraged, which was read as a preference for availability and willingness over technical skill. The process also showed that a role labelled risk can be operational, especially in a smaller firm.
what have I learned: A main lesson was that data quality and file structure have to be settled before analysis, and that small firms often lack the routines of larger ones. Sorting documents was treated as a form of data cleaning. Partner checklists showed how trust is judged from paperwork. KYC and AML classification had no scoring system and depended on manual judgment, which was seen as a source of inconsistent decisions; a standardised score was suggested as a remedy. Writing a standard operating procedure after a meeting with the mentor cut repeated questions about where files were kept.
what do I need to improve: At the start, file locations were unknown and the database was unstructured, so each new document type meant asking the mentor. For a later quantitative risk role, the stated gaps are data and statistics skills, including Python, SQL and Excel VBA, plus Value at Risk and Greeks, and more practice on real cases.
post-internship reflections: The internship changed both study plans and career aims. The preferred path is quantitative risk management in a bank or fund where transaction data exist, rather than operations and compliance. Python, SQL, Excel VBA, Value at Risk and Greeks are the study targets, together with real-world cases. Staying with this firm would be weighed against other employers, based on qualifications and how the firm develops.
advice for future interns: Before applying to a similar internship, find out what the job actually involves, especially if it is labelled risk or compliance, and whether the work is operational or analytical. Operational work can still build useful skill if the process itself is examined.
technical skills: Document structuring, checklist-based due diligence, KYC and AML information checks, and writing a standard operating procedure.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: NA

job description: The three-month internship was a data scientist role in the digital and data team at Zurich Insurance, shared between the AI-Automation and customer Analytics sub-teams. The work followed products on the company's AI platform through the software development lifecycle, including optical character recognition, a document AI agent and sentiment analysis. A large part of the coding used assistants such as Copilot and ChatGPT rather than fully manual coding. One concrete product turned uneditable PDFs, such as bank slips, into Excel files sent by email.
job duties: Implemented architectures designed by senior data scientists for an OCR project; built a Streamlit application where users upload a PDF and an email address and receive an Excel file by email; helped build the Databricks pipeline that runs after submission; tested Azure Form Recognizer, which was weak on poorly aligned bank slips, and proposed ChatGPT-4o-mini to read layout and extract fields, adding plain text from the PDF into the prompt, with about a 20 percent accuracy gain; split the flow so structured slips stayed on Azure Form Recognizer and unstructured slips used ChatGPT-4o-mini; migrated a workflow by developing, testing and deploying feature branches in Azure DevOps; debugged Python notebooks for configuration, package and deprecated-function errors.
pre-internship preparation: After the interview invitation there were only a few days to prepare. Time went to the company website and its AI platform, review of Pandas and NumPy, hypothesis testing and machine learning, daily LeetCode practice in SQL and Python, and rehearsal of behavioural questions. The selection was a one-hour interview: HR behavioural questions, then two senior data scientists on resume topics, including traditional machine learning versus deep learning and the inputs and outputs of a model from a previous internship. They also described team culture, structure and recent projects.
what have I learned: The law of large numbers from HKU statistics courses was linked to risk pooling in insurance. Git, SQL and database work carried over into the AI platform, while automated machine learning and Azure were in demand beyond classroom regression and clustering. Problem solving was practiced by splitting work into develop, test and deploy steps in Azure DevOps, and by debugging notebooks in stages. On OCR, a language model and a cheaper form recognizer were kept side by side, with about a 20 percent accuracy gain on unstructured slips. Azure, Git and PySpark were strengthened, and data-scientist work was seen as overlapping newer AI-engineer and prompt-engineer roles. Adaptation, innovation, communication and critical thinking were named as necessary on tight business problems.
what do I need to improve: NA
post-internship reflections: Interest in data roles began in the first year and was followed by internships in data analytics, data engineering and data science across consulting, insurance and research startups. Data scientist work is the preferred stream because of AI and machine learning, and the Zurich projects added interest in financial services and banking. A banking data offer was received. Graduation was deferred by one year to take more internships before graduate applications in Hong Kong. The placement is described as redirecting career interests toward a data-scientist path in the Hong Kong job market.

soft skills: Communication, critical thinking, adaptation, and breaking problems into steps.

job description: Prudential Hong Kong Limited, part of Prudential plc, is a Hong Kong direct insurer offering health, life and investment-linked insurance and financial planning. The report cites the company site that more than 1.4 million customers have chosen its products, and Insurance Authority figures of HK$635.2 billion of gross premiums in Hong Kong in 2024. The intern chose the valuation area in order to learn IFRS 17, Hong Kong Risk-Based Capital and reporting, and spent six months on the Embedded Value reporting team. The role supported regular monthly and quarterly reporting, premium and value measures, model-point files, forecasting and ad-hoc spreadsheet work.
job duties: Calculated Annualized Premium Equivalent from finance-team data and fed it into the Channel Product Mix spreadsheet of sales and profits by channel; used DCS to prepare model point files and APE data for other teams; ran APE forecasts and business plans on horizons such as 6+6 and 9+3, combining actual months with forecasts for the rest of the year; for an ad-hoc request, merged separate product workbooks into one Pay-Term Mix file of APE and related data by pay term; supported measures including New Business Value, net present value and New Business Strain; traced wrong figures back to source cells when spreadsheet results did not tie.
pre-internship preparation: Before the interview the posted duties were read and a one-minute self-introduction was prepared around being detail-oriented and analytical with large spreadsheets, including university group projects and passed SOA Exam P and Exam FM. Probability, statistics and financial mathematics were reviewed. HR screened resumes, then an HR manager interviewed. One question was why Prudential Hong Kong Limited; the reply cited its reputation, openings for different majors, and the chance to learn. After the offer, the valuation team was chosen in order to see IFRS 17, HKRBC and reporting.
what have I learned: Excel use improved because the duties ran through spreadsheets, including SUMIFS and VLOOKUP. Problem-solving was practiced by drilling numbers and formulae back to source cells after early mistakes. Actuarial reporting became clearer, including APE, New Business Value, net present value and New Business Strain, which were linked to present value, discounting and interest-rate risk from STAT3615 and STAT3609. DCS was new; Python from STAT2604 and R from an exchange at Wilfrid Laurier University made its coding easier to approach. A further lesson was to ask for help when a deadline meant the team's data preparation could not wait on solo learning.
what do I need to improve: Early on, working alone took too long and colleagues still had to be asked, which slowed the team because the intern owned data preparation. Mistakes were also common at the start, before the reporting steps were familiar.
post-internship reflections: The aim is an actuarial job, preferably in an insurance company. SOA Exam P and Exam FM are already passed, Exam SRM is planned for September 2026, and there is a minor in actuarial studies at HKU. STAT3600 and STAT3622 are courses the intern would like to take for programming and Excel. Rejoining Prudential Hong Kong Limited and the Embedded Value team would be considered because of work-from-home flexibility and a team of similarly aged colleagues.
advice for future interns: For the Embedded Value reporting team at Prudential Hong Kong Limited, pass at least one SOA or IFoA exam, which the report says insurers expect as a sign of basic actuarial knowledge and commitment. Ask questions, because the office is different from class and supervisors are willing to answer.
technical skills: Excel, including SUMIFS and VLOOKUP, DCS, APE and related value calculations, forecasting, model point files, and prior Python and R used to approach DCS.
soft skills: Attention to detail, analytical work, problem-solving, asking for help, and teamwork when deadlines are close.
courses mentioned: SOA Exam P; SOA Exam FM; SOA Exam SRM; IFoA exams; STAT3615; STAT3609; STAT2604; STAT3600; STAT3622.
tools and software: Excel, DCS, Python, R.

company: Chubb Life Insurance Hong Kong Limited
job description: Chubb Life Insurance Hong Kong Limited is a life insurer. The report describes Hong Kong's high insurance penetration, life insurance's large share of gross premiums, demand from local residents and mainland visitors, and growing need for retirement, annuity and wealth-transfer products. The half-year internship was an actuarial role on the pricing team. Day-to-day work was special quotations, enquiries from agents and customers, and checks of annual statements. Extra tasks covered an experience-study impact analysis, a bond-yield update from 2022 to 2025, and user-acceptance testing for a premium holiday. Pricing is described as one step alongside agency, underwriting and claims.
job duties: Prepared special quotations for cases such as overage, face amount above the usual limit, and a specified withdrawal, by quoting a regular policy and adjusting it in Excel; answered enquiries on the refund and remaining cash value after a face-amount reduction, premiums for extra mortality, and cash value during a premium holiday; checked annual statements for policyholders; for an experience study, reviewed the prior year, rebuilt a similar Excel table, copied this year's mortality rates by product, imported the data into Prophet and evaluated the result; updated bond yields from 2022 to 2025 to compare high-yield bonds with the company's bonds; assisted user-acceptance testing for premium holiday; built enquiry templates with VLOOKUP, internal guidelines and present-value checks; after a quotation error, grouped past cases into a template that showed the IT department the calculation logic for automated quotes.
pre-internship preparation: The search was aimed at risk management and actuarial internships, using the Corporate Mentorship Program and the department internship system. After invitations, the business and the job description were researched. AI tools were used to simulate interviewers and draft questions, general answer patterns were looked up, and a mentor was asked about an intern's daily work. A question list was then written, with statistics review focused on financial mathematics, machine learning, and how those topics show up in insurance. Interviewers often asked about the actual duties; seniors in similar work were consulted so the answers were practical. That preparation is credited with getting the offers.
what have I learned: The placement gave a practical picture of pricing inside a process that also includes agency, underwriting and claims, and showed that pricing is revisited for existing products as well as new ones. Excel moved past basic functions into reading and correcting VBA already in company templates. Enquiry work, the part closest to the Risk Management major, led to templates using VLOOKUP, internal guidelines, present-value calculations and checks, improved against templates left by earlier interns. Abbreviation mistakes were written down for the next intern. With IT, past quotations were pulled into a template to speed automated quotes for specific clients.
what do I need to improve: Actuarial abbreviations in the company system were hard to match to calculation variables, and the first mistake was described as embarrassing. On a special quote, Surrendered Value was copied into the Death Benefit field. An Excel-and-PDF check did not catch the text, and the reviewer sent the quote to the agent. The lesson recorded was to check every case and not assume the previous template is right.
post-internship reflections: Actuarial work is seen as a possible path because of a clear career ladder, stable pay and fit with the major, alongside the burden of professional exams and limited contact with clients. Study would be aligned with exam content through related electives. Consulting or risk-management internships are also of interest because they involve more communication. If the actuarial path is taken, rejoining would be considered: the firm is described as still growing, and the department atmosphere as relaxed.
advice for future interns: Before a similar interview, ask seniors on a similar team about the real daily routine so the answers show practical understanding. After an offer, self-study VBA or the company system, such as Prophet. During the internship, ask questions, check the work carefully, and talk with the supervisor and colleagues.
technical skills: Excel, VLOOKUP, present-value calculations, reading and correcting VBA, Prophet, experience-study tables, bond-yield comparison, and user-acceptance checks.
soft skills: Asking mentors, seniors and other interns for help, and communicating with colleagues, the supervisor and IT.
courses mentioned: Statistics courses covering financial mathematics and machine learning; actuarial exams.
tools and software: Excel, VBA, Prophet, AI tools, Excel and PDF comparison tool.

job description: Wuhan Jingsheng International Logistics, applied to as Jing Sheng Logistic, provides cargo transport among provinces in China and storage services. Customers mainly move industrial raw materials, daily necessities and electrical products. The report says the industry generates many delivery records, so a data analyst has to handle complex data and find problems that raise efficiency and cut cost. The internship covered daily data processing, anomaly analysis and dashboards. The intern links that work to statistics and to risk management aimed at fewer disruptions in delivery.
job duties: Wrote morning SQL joining three systems, filtered by region, orders and delivery time, including a September 2025 Wuhan-to-Changsha seafood shipment over 48 hours; cleaned orders in Python, R and Excel by filling gaps and dropping irrelevant rows, raising accuracy from 80 percent to 95 percent; flagged weekly shipping-order changes above 10 percent in Python and traced a 12 percent Wuhan-to-Yichang drop to a closed road; built a Python dashboard of orders, delivery time and abnormal data from SQL extracts; set up finance and operations meetings plus a shared term list, cutting definition uncertainty from 15 percent to at most 5 percent; suggested the B12 route in rain for Wuhan-Changsha, later tied to a 20 percent punctuality gain, and a revised Wuhan-Nanchang road tied to a 2w cost drop in a month.
pre-internship preparation: The Data Analyst application was made in May 2025 and the interview call came within days. Preparation reviewed hypothesis tests, p-values and t-values from STAT1600, SQL multi-table queries and subqueries from online courses, Excel techniques such as VLOOKUP, and Pandas from STAT1005. The company site and other logistics reports were read for business scope, shipping cost and punctuality. Selection was an HR screen on background, past internships and challenges, then a technical interview with the mentor: two SQL questions and logistics operations. The hardest question was differing definitions of transportation cost across systems; the answer was to confirm scope with finance and operations and build a mapping table. A success email followed within days.
what have I learned: SQL moved from basic queries to more complex ones. A working habit was to open the related data, explain the cause, and propose a fix, as with a closed road behind a Wuhan-Yichang drop. Communication with colleagues improved through notes, looking things up before asking the mentor, and smoother joint work after an adjustment period. Agreeing definitions of delivery cost and punctuality with finance and operations reduced data uncertainty from 15 percent to at most 5 percent. A rain routing suggestion and a road change were followed by a higher punctuality rate and a lower delivery cost.
what do I need to improve: Communication and social contact with colleagues and leaders are described as still lacking. Excel is also described as a sticking point for real-time monitoring, which is why Power BI and Tableau are planned. Supply-chain reading is named as another gap so that analysis stays close to logistics practice.
post-internship reflections: The goal is to become a supply chain data analyst. The study plan is to learn Power BI and Tableau, read supply-chain management books, and spend more time talking with colleagues and leaders. Joining the company after graduation would be considered because of its growth, a patient team, a focus on data-driven decisions, and a chance to join important projects.
advice for future interns: For logistics roles, become proficient in SQL and other programming used every day, learn terms such as number of deliveries, cost of delivery and punctuality rate, and build communication across departments, because the data sit in more than one team.
technical skills: SQL, including multi-table queries and subqueries, Python, R, Excel, VLOOKUP, Pandas, data cleaning, anomaly checks, and dashboard building.
soft skills: Communication and cooperation with colleagues, note-taking, and working with finance and operations.
courses mentioned: STAT1600; STAT1005; STAT3600.
tools and software: SQL, Excel, Python, R, Pandas.

company: Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, University of Hong Kong
job description: The internship was a Research Assistant post in the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science at the University of Hong Kong. The tasks were closer to teaching support than to work in a private firm. The brief was to prepare learning material for an introductory statistics course aimed at students who are not in a statistics-related major. The intern chose a course they had not studied, in order to practice explaining statistics simply. The department was less structured than expected: most days the intern decided what to work on, how long to spend, and when the work should be done.
job duties: Built a multiple-choice question bank on sampling distribution, hypothesis testing, and correlation and regression; set wrong options from mistakes a student with weak fundamentals would make, an approach the supervisor requested and that later shaped questions across the course; wrote an applied hypothesis-testing item on GPA and hours of sleep; discussed approaches with other research assistants; after repeated LaTeX formatting and export errors, made a reusable template so new questions were not started from scratch.
pre-internship preparation: The Research Assistant application at the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science had no interview. The only step was a cover letter, rewritten in about five or six drafts. Preparation focused on what the role should teach, namely applying theory in an academic setting, and on what could be offered to the department. Doubt about academic background and about Python and LaTeX was met by study on DataCamp and by videos from online platforms, so the first day would not start from zero.
what have I learned: The Risk Management major was used to explain why introductory ideas matter in daily life, including a hypothesis-testing example on GPA and sleep. Writing multiple-choice questions turned out harder than solving them, because each wrong option had to match a plausible mistake so the answer was not obvious by elimination. That distractor method spread beyond the items written personally. A consistent LaTeX template reduced formatting errors. The loose schedule left time to study, talk with other interns, and see where each task sat, instead of only clearing a queue.
what do I need to improve: Before the start, academic knowledge and the required Python and LaTeX were felt to be too thin for the role. During the work, the question bank on sampling distributions, hypothesis testing, and correlation and regression was the hardest part, and LaTeX formatting and export errors kept recurring until a template existed. Setting one's own priorities, without regular checking, also took time to get used to.
post-internship reflections: The career aim is sports data analysis, where distributions, hypothesis testing and regression still underlie the models, and results have to be explained to coaches, players or other non-technical people. No single sport is fixed. The internship led to a decision not to specialise too early, and to strengthen core statistics and programming first, including the ability to explain fundamentals simply. A similar role would be taken again for that reason.
advice for future interns: Treat the cover letter as the only chance to show genuine interest and clear goals, because there is no interview. Expect the learning to come from explaining familiar ideas again in simpler words, not from research in the usual sense, and be solid on the fundamentals before chasing a specialism.
technical skills: Question design in sampling distributions, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression, LaTeX, and Python studied on DataCamp before the start.
soft skills: Explaining technical ideas simply, discussing work with other research assistants, and managing an unstructured schedule.
courses mentioned: STAT2602; STAT3600.
tools and software: Python, LaTeX, DataCamp.

job description: Chubb Life Hong Kong is the international life division of Chubb. It offers savings, accident, health and annuity plans for financial protection and wealth management, sold mainly through agents, brokers and online channels. A final-year statistics student joined as a Product Pricing Intern to see the logic behind product and pricing decisions. The role covered user acceptance testing for launches and riders, checks of system calculations and policy illustrations against specifications and Excel worksheets, cleansing of Economic Scenario Generator data for quarterly risk-based capital pricing, and automation of repetitive testing work.
job duties: Joined several UAT rounds for product launches and riders, preparing and executing 60 to 100 test cases across three to four products in each round; checked system calculations and policy illustrations against product specifications and Excel worksheets; trimmed and cleansed Economic Scenario Generator data for quarterly risk-based capital pricing; wrote Excel VBA macros to automate repetitive UAT steps; used AI to build a Python tool that extracts selected information from a document for the same process; agreed work splits with teammates and reported progress to the supervisor.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation began with the job description, then the Hong Kong life insurance market, the company and its products. Because the major was not actuarial science, basic terms such as profit testing, profit margin and IRR were studied, and major coursework in data analysis, statistical modelling and Excel was revised. The CV was reviewed and a self-introduction prepared. Selection was a Cantonese Zoom interview with a senior manager and a senior associate from product pricing, covering prior internships and Python and Excel, plus how to tell whether a product is profitable. The candidate also asked what qualities the interviewers wanted. An offer came after a few weeks.
what have I learned: Product pricing logic became clearer through UAT, illustration checks and ESG cleansing for quarterly RBC. Excel VBA was learned by reading teammates' code and debugging, and AI prompts for development work turned out to need specific technique. Random sampling informed test-case design, and statistical preprocessing informed ESG cleansing. company: Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, University of Hong Kong
job description: The internship was a Student Research Assistant post in the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science at the University of Hong Kong. Dr. Wat accepted the application and invited Dr. Kwan as a joint supervisor. The work was teaching support, done fully online, not commercial analysis. The team built a Moodle question bank for the introductory course SDST1600 so junior students could practice core ideas. Items started from lecture notes and long reference books and then had to be rewritten for the course. The intern drafted questions and a coverage list that instructors used when deciding what to keep, edit or replace. The time requirement was 160 hours.
job duties: Read each chapter's notes, compared them with reference-book examples, wrote four options, marked the correct answer and wrote the steps, then checked fit with the notes before adding the item; designed a Chapter 7 time-series graph question separating seasonal and cyclical patterns, with wrong options based on common mix-ups; rewrote items that were too simple, too long or too close to the book, sometimes using settings such as the 2026 FIFA World Cup or events at HKU; used artificial intelligence to find likely chapters in long books, then checked those pages; converted formula screenshots to LaTeX with AI and checked the symbols; kept a list mapping each question to a concept and recording source, chapter, page and edits for the instructors' review.
pre-internship preparation: The search began with data-analysis or actuarial internships for STAT4766, then moved to a Student Research Assistant notice, in particular Dr. Wat's post. The duties were compared with existing skills, the resume and cover letter were updated, and R, Python, Excel, SDST2601 and junior statistics textbooks were reviewed because the job was a question bank for junior students. Selection was a resume, cover letter and transcript, with no interview, written test or technical assessment. An email from Dr. Wat accepted the application and named Dr. Kwan as supervisor. An online briefing with teachers and other research assistants assigned the SDST1600 Moodle bank.
what have I learned: A clear multiple-choice item needs an unambiguous correct answer and distractors that still look possible, and a much longer option can signal the answer. The enjoyable part was revising questions that were too simple, too long or too close to the book, and tying them to daily life. A personal mix-up between seasonal and cyclical patterns was turned into a graph question. Artificial intelligence sped up finding chapters, while LaTeX was learned from scratch so formulas would display. A concept list showed too much weight on calculations and too little on concepts, graphs and explanations. Working from home became steadier after a weekly minimum and a calendar of topics, expected hours and deadlines. Explaining technical ideas and managing time both improved.
what do I need to improve: LaTeX was unknown before the internship. In the first days at home there was no timetable, so work was postponed and concentration was poor. Question sets also leaned too far toward calculations and left out conceptual, graph and explanation items until a coverage list was used.
post-internship reflections: After graduation the hope is banking, especially risk management or data analysis, and there is also interest in a statistician post at the Census and Statistics Department. The internship confirmed a preference for practical analytical work and improved explanation of technical ideas and time management. With the last undergraduate semester already done, the study plan cannot change much. Python and data analysis will still be practiced, and risk management and financial markets will be learned. A related master's degree may follow some work experience.
advice for future interns: Read the course notes and confirm the required format before starting. Learn basic LaTeX, because formulas may not display on Moodle. Artificial intelligence can search long books and convert formulas, but the output has to be checked. Use a plan and a work calendar. Aim for accurate, engaging questions rather than a large count.
technical skills: R, Python, Excel, LaTeX, Moodle question design, and time-series distinctions between seasonal and cyclical patterns.
soft skills: Explaining technical concepts, and time management while working from home.
courses mentioned: SDST2601; SDST1600; STAT4766.
tools and software: R, Python, Excel, Moodle, LaTeX.

job description: UOB Kay Hian is a financial services firm headquartered in Singapore. The Summer Research Internship was in the Private Wealth Management division, which serves high-net-worth clients in global markets and expects researchers to follow news and write quickly on macroeconomic, interest-rate, geopolitical and company-specific risks. The intern joined research and strategy meetings, reviewed US and China portfolios, prepared stock pitches and risk analysis, and attended a four-week Investment Consultant Summer Training Programme.
job duties: Attended daily, weekly and monthly research and strategy meetings and followed US and China markets; reviewed existing US and China portfolio allocations and reports; wrote stock pitches with add-or-reduce recommendations, downside scenarios and proposed portfolio changes; researched high-conviction themes and sectors in the US and China for risk-adjusted returns; applied standard deviation, tail risk, debt-to-equity, beta, diversification and the Sharpe ratio; used Bloomberg and iFinD to pull company data and news; made pitch books after the investment-consultant training; in a US and China portfolio review, flagged a concentrated technology allocation and helped persuade the team to change asset weights.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation for the UOB Kay Hian Private Wealth Management summer research interview covered financial basics, risk models and macroeconomic indicators, plus China and US stock-market trends. Asked about professional equity-research experience, which was lacking, the reply shifted to a STAT3609 group project, The statistics of investment risk, on the relationship between market-capitalization growth and revenue growth among US tech giants, using modelling and hypothesis testing.
what have I learned: Equity-research skills gained included market views, financial terminals and the parts of a company note: highlights, analysis, risk assessment, valuation and share-price catalysts. The fast pace and real-time dislocations were the enjoyable part, including sharp falls in single-stock leveraged ETFs on names such as Samsung and SK Hynix, which illustrated path dependence, liquidity and behavioural finance. Product-team training showed how to pair downside risk with asset allocation and turn it into pitch books. A glossary of meeting terms made discussion easier after a few weeks.
what do I need to improve: There was no professional equity-research experience at the interview. In daily meetings, the volume of market jargon and real-time updates was overwhelming, and academic ideas were hard to connect to practice until new terms were listed and revised against research reports.
post-internship reflections: The internship prompted a plan to work in equity research after graduation. Final-year study would focus on financial risk management and time-series analysis, and the Financial Risk Manager exam is planned alongside the Risk Management degree. Rejoining UOB Kay Hian would be welcomed, for the culture, training and coverage of Asian and global markets. A supervisor provided practical teaching and Bloomberg training.
advice for future interns: Apply academic theory to real market situations, follow the market daily, and read news on interest-rate decisions, geopolitical events and macroeconomic shifts. Do not treat university coursework as minor; connecting it to practice is what made market operations familiar.
technical skills: Equity research, modelling, hypothesis testing, standard deviation, tail risk, debt-to-equity, beta, diversification, Sharpe ratio, downside scenario analysis, valuation, and use of Bloomberg and iFinD.
soft skills: Interpersonal communication in meetings, and explaining a risk analysis well enough to influence portfolio weights.
courses mentioned: STAT3609 The statistics of investment risk; financial risk management; Time-Series Analysis; Financial Risk Manager (FRM) exam.

job description: Vistra (Hong Kong) Limited is a corporate services provider and part of the international Vistra Group. An AI tool was used to draft possible questions, which were practiced with friends and alone until the answers felt clearer. Selection used one-on-one interviews. Questions such as why this company, how much was already known, and what the previous role involved were described as predictable. what have I learned: Hands-on work covered corporate governance and risk management, with more care on compliance detail. Prior study of risk identification, assessment and control made the testing more systematic and showed why voting procedures matter. Recording plans, estimating duration honestly, and updating the team regularly were the practical lessons.
what do I need to improve: The AGM voting system, electronic or paper, was difficult to learn quickly in peak season, and colleagues were too busy to teach, so the start felt tense. post-internship reflections: The career aim is to stay in corporate services and risk management, which matched interests from the Risk Management major. Rejoining Vistra (Hong Kong) Limited would be welcome: coworkers were helpful, and the work, though sometimes complicated, involved real governance and risk practice.
advice for future interns: Be ready to learn quickly. Summer is busy with AGMs and EGMs, and the pace is high. Mistakes are treated as normal if they are learned from. Keep notes, both to remember details and to show colleagues that the work is being taken seriously. Willingness to learn, care with detail, and clear communication are the habits the report recommends.
technical skills: Testing of an AGM electronic and paper voting system, risk identification, risk assessment, risk control, and compliance reporting.
soft skills: Communication, collaboration, attention to detail, meeting deadlines, and precise wording.

job duties: Migrated seasonal-adjustment processing for eight service industries from SAS to Python, with batch scripts that read source data, call the X-12 engine, and write standardised PDF reports without manual steps; added per-industry parameter settings and an automatic backup so one industry can be rerun without a full batch; analysed legacy FoxPro code and updated the sampling process and data structure from HSIC V2.0 to HSIC V3.0; cross-checked Python output with a colleague against the original SAS results; built isolated FoxPro test programs before deployment; wrote environment-configuration instructions so colleagues could run the programs on their own computers.
pre-internship preparation: Selection used a written CV on the department template rather than a face-to-face interview, so the challenge was to show analytical ability and academic qualifications in writing. Essential IT Skills training covered the ideas behind processing data in Python and R and introduced SQL and Excel VBA. Because the Hong Kong SAR government mainly uses Cantonese at work, Cantonese was practised before the summer until daily conversation and simple communication were basically manageable.
what have I learned: The placement connected classroom models with production systems. Time-series coursework helped with the mechanism behind X-12 ARIMA, and statistical inference helped explain why the HSIC sample rotation keeps an overlap between cycles so long-term trends can be captured and sampling variance smoothed. Maintainable code, configuration notes, testing, and cross-checks were emphasised over one-off scripts. Flexible parameters and backups reduced operational risk and repeat processing. A sharing session was given in English because spoken Cantonese was not fluent, and colleagues and the Commissioner encouraged that choice.
what do I need to improve: Spoken Cantonese was not fluent enough for the sharing session. The X-12 trend-extraction mechanism and engine source could not be fully understood in the time available, so established methods had to be accepted in order to produce accurate output. FoxPro legacy logic required a different way of thinking, and small structural changes risked breaking existing departmental data.
post-internship reflections: The career goal is to become an actuary and quantitative data professional in financial risk modelling and product innovation. The study plan is to improve R and Python and to take core actuarial courses, treating theory and practical feasibility together. Error prevention and data validation from this placement are expected to help a later half-year corporate internship at Prudential. Rejoining the department after graduation is under serious consideration because of its digital-transformation work and its standard of data accuracy.
advice for future interns: Do not stay only at the theoretical and mathematical level. Think about how to validate programs and keep them reliable, and build tools that colleagues can actually use and maintain. Learn from old code, put detailed cross-checking first, and raise small problems in a setting where accuracy matters.
technical skills: Python, R, SAS, SQL, Excel VBA, X-12 ARIMA, FoxPro, batch scripting, sampling design, statistical inference, and time series.
soft skills: Communication with the supervisor and colleagues, and presenting technical work in English.
courses mentioned: Essential IT Skills; time series analysis course; core actuarial courses.
tools and software: Python, R, SAS, SQL, Excel VBA, X-12, FoxPro.

job description: The host is a multi-strategy hedge fund that trades stock derivatives and interest-rate derivatives. Assets under management are several billion Hong Kong dollars. Main products include vanilla options, snowball options, contracts for difference, and swaps. As an operations team member, the intern supported the trade life cycle from execution through settlement, including client onboarding, trade confirmation, and daily margin follow-up.
job duties: Helped onboard clients by checking identification, proof of address, and corporate registration documents before the compliance team did KYC and sanctions screening; updated the internal system for deposits and withdrawals and kept in contact with the finance department; acted as the link between clients and traders during trading hours; entered trade details, sent them to counterparties for confirmation, and followed up items with an abnormal status; tracked daily margin moves with the risk team, identified positions that might trigger margin calls, and reminded clients to add margin before the deadline; took corporate-action data such as dividends and stock splits from Bloomberg, recalculated contract multipliers and execution prices, and entered the updated values; wrote Python matching rules that pulled trade data from at least five sources into Excel, cutting reconciliation from about 1.5 hours to 15 minutes.
pre-internship preparation: Applications were selective and aimed at roles that needed statistical thinking and data analysis. Each resume was edited to the employer's terms, highlighting earlier data-processing work, a core risk management course, and Python and R. Feedback from rejections was used to improve later resumes and interviews. This offer followed two interviews. The first asked about fit for a derivatives operations position, prior internship work, OTC options, simple risk indicators, Black-Scholes pricing, hedging logic, and the difference between exotic and vanilla options, which had not been studied and was asked about openly. The second tested Python cleaning, aggregation, and outliers, then a task to pull real-time prices and financial indicators, clean and standardise them, value each company with a given formula, and compare stocks for a relative valuation advantage.
what have I learned: The placement covered the derivatives life cycle from execution to settlement, rather than only classroom pricing formulas. Bloomberg was used for stock and index data and historical volatility, and Python was used for a pipeline of gathering, processing, and analysis. In busy markets, work had to be prioritised by urgency and impact, with communication kept open to counterparties and clients. Internal training materials and daily notes built familiarity with terms such as knock-in, knock-out, and auto-redemption. Margin monitoring applied class material on counterparty credit risk, collateral, and initial margin.
what do I need to improve: At the start, derivatives terminology and business processes were unfamiliar, including knock-in, knock-out, auto-redemption, and over-the-counter life cycles, so colleagues had to help. Data-analysis skills are still being developed, and the HKSI Paper 1 exam is being prepared in order to qualify for securities work.
post-internship reflections: The experience gave confidence to continue in derivatives trading and risk management. Preparation for HKSI Paper 1 is underway, and data-analysis skills are being developed further. A return offer was made, and a full-time return is of interest because of the culture and the room to grow.
advice for future interns: NA
technical skills: Python, R, Bloomberg, Excel, data cleaning and aggregation, outlier identification, company valuation, and trade reconciliation.
soft skills: Attention to detail, communication with other divisions, clients, and counterparties, and working under pressure.
courses mentioned: Risk management course; HKSI Paper 1.
tools and software: Python, R, Excel, Bloomberg.

job description: Livibank is a digital bank funded by BoC and JingDong Group. It has no branch network, focuses on technology, treats SMEs as its largest customer group, and is supervised by the HKMA. Technology expertise also sits in a Shenzhen department, while this office was in Oxford House. The intern combined a daily large-exposure monitoring process for financial institutions and sovereigns with a project to rebuild a legacy reconciliation model that almost nobody remaining could maintain.
job duties: Each morning, downloaded raw exposure data, ran a Health Check file, grouped the results, compared them with the treasury department, and checked that limits sat within BELR and HKMA restrictions; rebuilt reconciliation and calculation after the colleague who maintained a legacy Microsoft Access model had left, moving the process toward Excel and Power Query; dealt with columns that did not line up across raw sources; traced Nostro mismatches to public holidays and payment booking days, asked how Deutsche Bank accounts and holiday dates were handled, and added conditional formatting plus a date-based check; used Copilot to unpack formulas and troubleshoot without loading large confidential files wholesale.
pre-internship preparation: About half a year passed between the cover letter to Livibank and the contract. An interview in early March had behavioural and technical parts. Preparation used the Livibank website for background, products, goals, customers, and what is distinctive about a digital bank, plus a list of lessons, strengths, and weaknesses from a former internship and practice interview questions. Spoken English, a stated weak point, was practised for more than two weeks. In the interview, handling raw data was discussed through a STAT3609 project. The bank did not follow up until late May.
what have I learned: Statistics and risk-management courses, together with earlier Excel and Power Query experience, were used for product types, customer segments, maturity tenors, grouping, and conditional logic. Data management, a stated weakness, improved through mentorship and daily practice. After many errors, the large-exposure report produced accurate numbers and later stayed inside a predetermined 2 percent range, so colleagues no longer spent the morning rechecking it. A further lesson was to mix independent troubleshooting with asking a supervisor before a costly mistake.
what do I need to improve: Effective data management was a particular weakness, and confidence in IT was low. English was the weakest point going into the interview. During the Access-to-Excel rebuild, Power Query logic and linkages were often wrong, errors were hard to spot, and Copilot was not always correct, which led to anxiety and several full redos.
post-internship reflections: The placement changed a view of statistical work as dry. Risk management and data work now seem engaging, and the field will be kept open. An FRM exam is planned this fall. The contract was extended to the end of summer, with plans to take advanced SQL and automation courses that build on the job.
advice for future interns: For aspiring risk management students, especially those who have struggled in statistics courses, do not treat a hard task as impossible. Putting full effort into work that felt out of reach, and finishing it, was one of the most rewarding parts of the experience.
technical skills: Excel, Power Query, Microsoft Access, conditional formatting, data reconciliation, statistical grouping, and Copilot-assisted formula work.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: STAT3609; FRM exam; advanced SQL and automation courses.
tools and software: Excel, Power Query, Microsoft Access, Microsoft Copilot.

company: Shanghai Semiconductor Equipment and Materials Industry Investment Management Co., Ltd.
