Its business is equity investment and fund management in semiconductors and other hard technology, including artificial intelligence, robotics, and commercial aerospace. Deals often take five to seven years from start to exit. The intern assisted the full private-equity and venture-capital cycle of finding and evaluating hard-tech companies.
job duties: Mapped domestic embodied-robot hardware and software and reviewed more than 100 embodied-AI companies; screened projects and wrote business analysis, due-diligence notes, initiation reports, and investment memos; joined project-initiation and investment-committee meetings; studied VLA and world-model paths, including JEPA and generative approaches, for Qianjue Tech; analysed Dexmal and recommended valuing it mainly on commercial traction as a logistics-robot provider, after which the firm invested at a valuation described as reasonable; interviewed Lumos Robotics on Ego and UMI data collection and dual-arm inspection work with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, then did not proceed because R&D looked slow and products homogeneous; evaluated Satabot, a lawn-mowing and photovoltaic operations firm, through interviews and field trips to Suzhou, and put it on hold; also reviewed Cimicro, Gewu Zhiyan, and Puyu Tech.

Financial answers covered crawling public contracts to check order backlog, financial modelling of core profits, and calculating a core price/earnings-to-growth ratio. job description: Guangzhou Xiantai is a manufacturer of tattoo stickers and UV gel nail stickers, especially semi-cured gel nail strips that customers harden with a UV or LED lamp. A typical order becomes a production sheet for the warehouse, then materials are issued, goods are produced and cut, and products are sold. Finance staff need to understand that process so the books match production. The intern, as a finance assistant, analysed a one-year trial of a 1688 online store and compared public nail-sticker market data with the firm's own products.
job duties: Compiled one year of 1688 store backend data and outbound delivery records, including SKU, product name, and outbound time, and calculated total sales revenue; separated new and existing customers by repurchase frequency and found that almost all orders came from existing customers; compared order quantities and amounts with outbound records and learned that replenishment, free gifts, replacements, and discounts can explain the gaps; collected public 1688 figures on sales rank, recent sales, price, repeat rate, supplier, and location for nail stickers and semi-cured strips, and compared comprehensive search rank with sales rank; compared price with sales while noting minimum order quantity and tiered pricing; compared the market sample with the firm's products and noted that two semi-cured products had low exposure but still had transactions.
pre-internship preparation: The application was meant to see how risk management works in daily operations and how a finance department checks information for management. Before the interview, company size, major products, and the general production process were reviewed. Selection was resume screening plus a company interview. The company explained Finance Assistant Intern duties. One interview question was why a risk management student would apply for a finance assistant job. The answer given was that business operations contain many risks and the aim was to see how a company handles them in practice.
what have I learned: Making two sets of numbers match was not always the end of the work. Some differences between orders and deliveries are normal business actions, so the business reason has to be known before something is called an error. Asking the team leader was usually faster than guessing. Public 1688 data come only from platform search results, sometimes as lower bounds or ranges, and cannot support market share or a firm conclusion. One indicator, such as a lower price, can mislead when minimum order quantity, tiered prices, and product differences also matter. Understanding a finance figure can require sales, warehouse, or production information. Spot checks of raw materials and finished goods were linked to finding problems before production is finished.
what do I need to improve: The habit of asking where a number came from, and what caused a difference, still needs improvement. Further gaps named for later study are financial accounting, corporate finance, data analysis, Excel, statistics, and other analytical tools.
post-internship reflections: The internship was not finished when the report was written. Interest remains in risk management, financial analysis, and business analysis, with a new emphasis on understanding the real business process before analysing data. Future roles that combine data with operations are preferred. Planned study includes financial accounting, corporate finance, Excel, statistics, and closer attention to applying class knowledge to business problems. In a later similar role, products and processes would be learned earlier and more questions would be asked.
advice for future interns: NA
technical skills: Sales-data compilation, repurchase analysis, reconciliation of orders with outbound records, and comparison of price, sales, and product exposure.
soft skills: Asking questions and communicating with the team leader.

company: Agricultural Bank of China, Hong Kong Branch
job description: The internship was in the Anti-Money Laundering Office of the Hong Kong branch of the Agricultural Bank of China, from 6 July 2026 to 31 August 2026. The branch is mainly corporate rather than retail. It serves cross-boundary clients and provides RMB settlement, and it does not offer retail banking in Hong Kong. The office monitors transactions for money laundering and terrorist financing, investigates questionable activity, and notifies the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit. The intern supported alert review, daily sanctions and AML news, and quantitative work on the monitoring system.
job duties: Reviewed first-level alerts from the monitoring system using transaction history and KYC records, wrote a disposition, and either closed the alert or escalated it to a second-level reviewer; after the second week handled about two alerts an hour; each morning used generative AI to collect sanctions and AML news from government releases and the media, organised it, translated it into Chinese, and presented it to colleagues; extracted alert and disposition data with SQL; analysed false-positive rates by detection scenario and ran threshold-tuning experiments; carried out statistical studies on AML applications, including ways to identify trade-based money-laundering tendencies.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation began about two months before the start. Because the Hong Kong branch of this mainland bank does not do local retail business, reading focused on cross-boundary corporate clients and RMB settlement, and on the HKMA Guideline on AML/CFT. Interview practice covered standard questions, questions for recruiters, hypothesis testing, Excel and R, and explaining statistical ideas in Cantonese and Putonghua. There were four stages: an online CV, a 15-minute HR phone screen checking resume facts and availability, an online test of numerical, logical, and computer skills, and a panel interview with the AML team head and a senior analyst. A scenario question asked what to do if the boss wants a report today but the data contain an issue. The answer was to flag the problem immediately, try to fix it, and if needed submit the original report with its limitations explained.
what have I learned: The office was under real quantitative pressure: regulators expect evidence that monitoring can detect money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk, so compliance work is also a data problem. The most useful personal lesson was to ask for help early instead of waiting. Threshold-tuning experiments were the most enjoyable work and once raised an abnormal flag that had been overlooked. An alert escalated by the intern was later filed as a suspicious-activity report. Reading HKMA text improved by treating defined terms as technical words and by asking colleagues to correct each draft.
what do I need to improve: In the first week it was hard to ask for help. Writing was a weakness, so long suspicious-activity reports were less welcome than tuning work, and the first report was slow because reporting terminology was unfamiliar. HKMA guidelines and legal provisions were difficult at first because of their formal language. As an intern there was no direct access to the private database, so data requests had to be precise and patient.
post-internship reflections: Career direction is still open. The placement confirmed an interest in work that combines data analysis, but not necessarily financial-crime compliance, because much of the standard paperwork felt uninteresting. Relevant modelling courses may be chosen later. Rejoining the bank would be considered: the team was supportive and the cross-boundary exposure would be hard to find elsewhere in Hong Kong. The preference would be the tuning and analytics side rather than staying in alert review.
advice for future interns: Read the HKMA AML/CFT guidelines and a few FATF reports before the interview so the daily work of an AML office is familiar. Expect routine paperwork and take it seriously, because attitude matters in compliance. Do not post or disclose work online. Information at the bank can be confidential and disclosure can cause problems for the intern and the employer.
technical skills: SQL, Excel, R, hypothesis testing, false-positive analysis, threshold tuning, generative AI for news gathering, and statistical study of trade-based money-laundering patterns.
soft skills: Asking for help, explaining ideas in Cantonese, Putonghua, and Chinese, and written reporting.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: SQL, Excel, R, generative AI.

company: Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, The University of Hong Kong
job description: This was a Student Research Assistant role in the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science at the University of Hong Kong. Unlike a corporate internship, it supported teaching, course development, and educational outreach. The main strands were a question bank for an upcoming course and preparation to help at a statistics workshop for middle-school students. A separate outside internship was held at the same time.
job duties: Developed and reviewed a question bank for the upcoming SDST2602 course, drafting questions at different difficulty levels, writing solutions, and checking alignment with learning outcomes; selected, adapted, and refined items from available reference materials; prepared to help at a workshop by planning statistics activities and games on probability, risk, and decision-making, and a sharing session about university life in the department; practised explaining those ideas in simpler language to a younger relative with no statistics background; kept this role alongside another internship by listing deadlines and planning the week so one job did not damage the other.
pre-internship preparation: The search began in semester 2 of the 2025-26 academic year. An email advertised a Student Research Assistant post in the home department. Preparation was to review the courses named in the email, especially question banks and lecture slides for the relevant instructor, and to refresh forgotten statistical concepts and problem-solving techniques. The application itself was a CV and cover letter. Another outside internship offer arrived during the process. Both sides agreed that both jobs could be done together if the workload stayed manageable. Acceptance followed soon after, with no further test described.
what have I learned: Writing the question bank showed the work behind usable teaching materials and academic standards, including the move from a student's view of a previously taken course to an educator's view. LaTeX needed more hands-on skill than a little earlier exposure. Explaining probability, risk, and decision-making without specialist terms was a separate skill. Balancing two internships built the habit of writing down deadlines and planning the week. Organisation, communication, and teamwork were described as the most valuable lesson, because statistical knowledge is not enough if it cannot be explained, including in outreach.
what do I need to improve: LaTeX was unfamiliar and had to be learned during the tasks. A long-standing weakness was overlooking small details, finishing too quickly, and leaving careless mistakes that could mislead a reader. Those mistakes showed a need to review and polish work before sending it to the supervisor. Explaining statistical terms to a non-specialist was also difficult at first.
post-internship reflections: Before this role, statistics and risk management seemed to apply mainly to research, banking, and corporate work. The internship added teaching and educational outreach as career paths. Future plans are to keep strengthening statistics and risk management knowledge and soft skills such as communication, research, and organisation, including through further projects or internships. Similar education or academic-support roles would be of interest. Seeing learners benefit from the materials was described as personally rewarding.
advice for future interns: Build a strong foundation in statistical concepts and keep a proactive attitude. For this research-assistant role, willingness to learn matters especially, because many technical and professional skills will still be unfamiliar even after statistics courses. Curiosity and initiative help a student learn how statistics and risk management are used while complementing academic study.
technical skills: LaTeX, design of practice questions and solutions, and statistical ideas used in the workshop, including probability, risk, and decision-making.
soft skills: Organisation, communication, teamwork, time management, and presentation.
courses mentioned: SDST2602.
tools and software: LaTeX.

company: The Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation Limited (HKMC)
job description: The Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation Limited operates through asset purchase and securitisation, the Mortgage Insurance Programme, retirement solutions including the Reverse Mortgage Programme and the HKMC Annuity Scheme, and policy loan guarantees such as the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The report describes it as a government-supported stabiliser rather than a profit-seeking commercial bank, taking on mortgage and SME credit risk so banks can keep lending. The intern worked in the SFGS and AI Team on credit-risk documents and on testing an internal AI system for risk due diligence.
job duties: Sorted lending-institution binders, including bank statements, corporate financial statements, credit evaluation reports, land searches, and writs of summons, as the document base for mortgage credit-risk review; redacted confidential information from large sets of risk documents to create test datasets; tested an in-house AI summarisation model used for requests for further information and due-diligence questionnaires, and logged deviation and error information in risk-scenario simulations; wrote a standard operating manual for the AI due-diligence process; compared versions of internal bank risk-management policies for new risk criteria, compliance requirements, and assessment criteria; classified summarisation mistakes and omission mistakes on financial statements and credit reports, related document type to the model's error probability, and wrote an optimisation suggestion that the technical team used to adjust text extraction and the weights of financial-risk indexes.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation was organised around risk management studies. HKMC's main businesses were reviewed first: the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme, the Mortgage Insurance Programme, the mortgage purchase programme, debt and asset securitisation, and retirement-planning solutions. Core topics from the major were also reviewed, including financial-risk identification, credit-risk evaluation, data analytics, and modelling, plus how AI is used in HKMC's business. Selection had a resume screen, a Zoom interview with the manager and vice president of the risk management department, and a final face-to-face interview with HR. The panel covered technical competence and situational judgment. Questions started with motivation, then went through the CV, with emphasis on earlier artificial-intelligence experience and how it could help this project.
what have I learned: The most enjoyable part was seeing statistics and AI change manual risk-management processes. Testing the summarisation model on credit-assessment reports, and comparing its output with professional manual assessment, showed strengths and weaknesses of AI risk models. Sorting policy updates helped match model logic to current industry practice. Classifying error types and relating them to document type produced a suggestion that led the technical team to change text extraction and financial-risk index weights, which increased the precision of the system's summaries. A glossary of mortgage risk terms was built to speed up later document and policy work.
what do I need to improve: At the beginning, professional terminology in financial documents and bank policies was unfamiliar, so classifying documents and comparing policies was very inefficient. The gap was addressed by asking senior staff, compiling a glossary of mortgage risk-management terms, and studying HKMC risk policies and industry due-diligence practice.
post-internship reflections: The goal of becoming a risk analyst in quantitative risk management and intelligent financial decision-making became clearer. Future study will concentrate on financial statistics, risk modelling, and financial compliance analysis, plus projects that apply quantitative analysis to real business situations. A return to HKMC after graduation is wanted because of its risk-management system and its digital risk-transformation strategy.
advice for future interns: Consolidate basic statistics and risk management so academic theory can be connected with practical business. Research the company's core businesses in depth. Understanding the company makes the interviews smoother.
technical skills: Organisation of credit-risk documents, redaction and test-data preparation, AI summarisation testing, classification of model errors, and comparison of risk-policy versions.

job description: EleBank is a Hong Kong-based digital bank focused on retail banking, including personal loans, secured loans, premium financing, and deposit products. It uses technology to simplify customer processes, strengthen risk management, and improve efficiency. In a competitive market shaped by interest rates, credit risk, and customer experience, the bank relies on data analytics for decisions, personalization, and risk monitoring. The internship supported market research and loan analysis, using statistical results in tables and reports so the team could compare scenarios and look for ways to improve profitability.
job duties: Entered and checked premium financing policy data for accuracy; collected and sorted market data; compared monthly loan interest-rate plans across banks using averages and medians; confirmed daily new loan cases and total amounts; analyzed each insurance company's share of business and use of loan amount; cleaned datasets that had missing values, inconsistent formats, or duplicates before analysis; supported new loan products by collecting and analyzing user needs; compiled a time-pressed meeting report around key discussion points rather than every detail; summarized competitor promotional-rate patterns together with daily loan volume and quota use so managers could review performance gaps and quota allocation.
pre-internship preparation: Banking was the target industry, so resumes and cover letters went to banks through the school CEDARS platform and online job sites. After an EleBank interview invitation, the company website was read and its main products were noted as personal loans and premium financing. Regression analysis, hypothesis testing, and multivariate analysis were reviewed, and Excel and Python were practiced because the role involved data analysis and market research. The interview was online with the department head and HR. One question asked how to judge a new loan product's competitiveness, and the answer covered market-share data, comparison with similar products, and methods such as cluster analysis. Another asked how traditional banks differ from virtual banks.
what have I learned: The placement showed how to turn statistical results into workplace reports that stress key findings rather than methods. Data preprocessing was used when source files had missing values, inconsistent formats, or duplicates, and simple averages and medians were enough to compare loan rates and see whether adjustment was possible. Market analysis added terms such as loan-to-value ratio and net interest margin. A further lesson was to prefer timely, sufficiently accurate insight over a perfectly optimized model, to ask the supervisor which factors matter for decisions, and to present key findings, business impact, and suggested actions. The intern also contributed to discussion of promotional timing and quota allocation.
what do I need to improve: At first it was hard to balance academic models with fast business needs, because managers wanted timely insight rather than a fully optimized method. Analysis was initially explained in technical terms, which reduced clarity. Short instructions were not always followed up, from a wish not to look inexperienced, and that sometimes caused misunderstandings about scope or report format. A meeting report was nearly over-written under time pressure until the supervisor advised focusing on the key discussion results. The stated remedies were to confirm each task immediately and to use visualization so results are easier to follow.
post-internship reflections: The career goal is data analysis or risk management in a bank or another private financial firm, and the internship strengthened that direction. After the summer, the plan is to study financial statistics and machine learning through online tutorials and to learn more programming methods. A return offer would be considered. Virtual banking is viewed as still having room to develop and as a possible starting point, and the team environment was described as harmonious.
advice for future interns: Students considering a similar role should improve statistical skills and also keep a positive attitude, pay attention to detail, and stay open to feedback, especially from supervisors and senior colleagues. Knowing the company before the interview, and linking statistical knowledge to business questions, makes interview answers stronger.
technical skills: Data preprocessing, averages and medians, regression analysis, hypothesis testing, multivariate analysis, cluster analysis as an interview example, market comparison, report writing, and data visualization.
soft skills: Communication, resilience under time pressure, seeking feedback, and confirming task understanding.
courses mentioned: NA

job description: Reinsurance Group of America (RGA) is a global business-to-business reinsurer that acts as a risk and capital partner for direct insurers, providing insurance for insurance companies and helping them pool financial, mortality, and morbidity risks. Its Traditional business includes yearly renewable term reinsurance for biometric risk. Global Financial Solutions offers asset-intensive reinsurance, longevity swaps, and financial reinsurance for capital efficiency and solvency. Hybrid solutions mix risk transfer with financial incentives. The six-month role was Internal Audit Intern, supporting compliance reviews, process reviews, and workflow automation in the third line of defense.
job duties: Reviewed regulations, including anti-money laundering rules in Hong Kong and Taiwan and Hong Kong risk-based capital rules, against internal manuals; reviewed process and responsibility charts across the pre-deal, pricing, and post-deal stages of Global Financial Solutions for control gaps; built a Microsoft Power Automate workflow for quality-assurance reviews and helped another intern test an AI agent; joined a Japan-branch solvency check by reviewing calculation spreadsheets, data sources, and accountability; replaced a long copied OneNote summary of Hong Kong risk-based capital rules with an interactive mind map organized by scope, business case, requirements, and risk type; prepared Power BI client data for the next audit plan, separating traditional business from Global Financial Solutions by business line and branch, which led to a priority list.
pre-internship preparation: Interview preparation covered a self-introduction, motivation, behavioural examples, technical industry knowledge, and questions for the interviewer. The introduction stressed a quantitative background in risk management, statistics, and accounting, and the motivation was to see how a Fortune 500 firm handles risk in internal audit. Behavioural answers used the STAR method, especially for conflict and deadlines. A mind map covered life and non-life reinsurance, accounting standards, and operational risks. Selection was a CV review, a panel interview on background and soft skills, and a one-hour interview with the department head, who recommended How to Win Friends and Influence People. A stress test asked for time series modelling to be explained so a child could understand it. A first textbook answer was rejected; a puzzle analogy was accepted.
what have I learned: The internship showed how regulations are applied in practice and how the third line of defense reviews compliance and business analytics. Coursework in investment maths, derivatives, and credit risk helped with Hong Kong risk-based capital topics such as yield curves, matching assets to long-term liabilities, and risk capital by risk type. Peak weeks with three simultaneous projects were handled by splitting work and setting priorities. A useful lesson from the department head was to tell a manager when there are too many tasks and let the leader set priority. Changing a useless text dump into a mind map, and separating business lines in a risk dashboard, showed that presentation can change what auditors see.
what do I need to improve: The first attempt to explain time series modelling was too textbook-like and had to be replaced with a simpler analogy. The first regulation summary, copied into OneNote, became a large block of text that senior auditors could not use. job description: Millennium is an investment management firm that runs a multi-strategy hedge fund. It allocates capital across many portfolio managers seeking returns that are less tied to broad markets. Strategies include fundamental long/short equities, event-driven work such as index rebalancing and merger arbitrage, systematic quantitative strategies such as statistical arbitrage and derivatives, and macro strategies in fixed income, currencies, and commodities. The internship was as a Quantitative Researcher in the Central Equities Risk Department. The project was a pipeline to diagnose the performance of an equity factor risk model and to find why that performance changed.
job duties: Built a pipeline to diagnose an equity factor risk model; defined one metric for whether volatility was under- or over-predicted and another for beta, used in hedge sizing; split the model into systematic and idiosyncratic risk and checked whether its specifications still held; tested linearity of returns against factor loadings with the Patton-Timmermann monotonicity test; examined loading stability and distribution drift with Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises tests; applied principal component analysis to the idiosyncratic volatility matrix to check diagonality and missing factors; tested heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and orthogonality between systematic and idiosyncratic parts; identified the assumptions that contributed most to deterioration and proposed specification changes; learned enough SQL to query a poorly documented internal database.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started early in the academic year. Material from earlier statistics courses was reviewed, especially linear regression, machine learning, probability, and hypothesis testing. Reading included research papers and books on quantitative research and equity factor models: Elements of Quantitative Investing by Giuseppe Paleologo, Active Portfolio Management by Grinold and Kahn, and the Barra Equity Factor Model Handbook. Past interns were asked about the process and their roles. Recruitment had two stages. A 24-hour coding and quantitative assessment moved from syntax to a market-making algorithm and then a statistical arbitrage strategy. Four team interviews followed: two on probability and statistics, and two on case studies and personal equity-factor projects.
what have I learned: The internship gave practice with industrial-scale data and with statistics coursework applied to risk-model diagnostics. Experienced teammates explained why models for different regions or time frames may need different hyperparameters, estimation methods, or factors. SQL had to be self-taught because documentation was thin and some original developers had left. Greater independence was learned by asking sharper questions about project objectives. The project linked periods of underpredicted volatility to a weaker idiosyncratic-independence assumption. The principal-component pipeline flagged clustering, and the Cramer-von Mises test showed factor loadings becoming skewed away from normal when the market trended, so the team did not have to inspect every distribution by eye.
what do I need to improve: There was no prior SQL knowledge, so several days were spent learning queries on a database with limited documentation. Early on, more structured instructions were expected, and the research direction felt uncertain until independent work and more critical questions became comfortable.
post-internship reflections: The plan is to stay in quantitative finance but move toward a more risk-taking role, such as trading or working under a portfolio manager. The internship showed a need for a stronger technical base through more advanced statistics and quantitative courses. Postgraduate study in Statistics or Financial Mathematics is being considered after several years of work. Rejoining Millennium would depend on the role and team. The firm's infrastructure is a reason to return, but the current team does not match the desired direction, and internal transfers appear uncommon.
advice for future interns: Build a strong statistics foundation and also study beyond the curriculum, because firms expect concepts that university courses cover only lightly. Personal projects or independent research help show curiosity, initiative, and interest in quantitative finance, which was valued in recruitment.
technical skills: Linear regression, machine learning, probability, hypothesis testing, equity factor risk models, volatility and beta diagnostics, the Patton-Timmermann monotonicity test, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises tests, principal component analysis, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and orthogonality tests, and SQL.
soft skills: Working independently and asking probing questions of experienced teammates.

advice for future interns: Ask supervisors when something is unclear, because a thoughtful question is usually answered and early clarification prevents wasted effort. job description: The Occupational Safety and Health Council is a statutory body that promotes safety and health in Hong Kong workplaces through research, training for construction workers, and public education. The summer role was Summer Intern (Research), from 8 June 2026 to 31 August 2026, applying experimental design, regression, and survey methods to heat stress among outdoor workers. The largest project was a controlled experiment on the rooftop of the Tsing Yi OSH Academy. A second strand was face-to-face questionnaires with workers in hot jobs about hydration and employer heat-prevention facilities.
job duties: Reviewed 2023-2025 field data and found some shading categories too rare for regression, then proposed limiting the trial to common shading and ventilation measures, which was approved as 43 scenarios of standalone shading, standalone ventilation, and combined interventions; conducted the literature review, wrote the protocol, selected a QT-44 WBGT monitor, a UVAB meter, and an anemometer, and collected rooftop data with a paired direct-sun control; recorded wind speed and direction, UVA, UVB, HKHI, and wet-bulb globe temperature for later multiple linear regression, with processing in Excel and controls for wind and ambient temperature; surveyed chefs, gardeners, and construction workers and summarized findings for the mentor; rescheduled days that missed the 30 degree Celsius and UV conditions and doubled the setups per slot; asked other interns and mentors to help erect large shade equipment.
pre-internship preparation: Undergraduate methods were reviewed before the internship. R was practiced through STAT3621. what have I learned: The internship covered a research cycle from conceptualization and design through execution and data management, including choices about methodology and equipment. Regression reasoning changed the study from sparse field categories to a controlled rooftop design with a usable sample for each measure, and the mentor approved moving off real field sites. Face-to-face surveys required guiding workers toward detailed answers and turning many comments into short reports. Unsuitable July weather and the physical limits of the setup forced rescheduling, more trials per slot, and help from others. The broader point was that a reliable statistical comparison can support advice on worker heat protection.
what do I need to improve: During the written test it was hard to present observations in concise professional English, so synonyms and a more structured write-up were used. More than ten days in July 2026 were too cloudy or rainy for the required temperature and UV conditions. post-internship reflections: The internship confirmed a wish to use statistics on long-standing social problems, not only for career advancement. Rejoining the Council after graduation is of strong interest because its mission matches a wish to contribute to society and colleagues encouraged ideas.
advice for future interns: Build a foundation in regression, experimental design, and R, and be able to explain statistical ideas in English and Chinese. Be active in spotting problems and proposing evidence-based changes, because a research team depends on cooperation. Interns are given real say over the project, so initiative and clear communication matter.

job description: This was a two-month Student Research Assistant project at the University of Hong Kong on statistical learning for prediction and classification of pulmonary nodules, using a public dataset. The setting is biostatistics and medical informatics, where records may combine numbers, clinical descriptions, and CT images. Decision Analytics coursework was the background for building statistical learning models.
job duties: Followed an eight-week plan: read papers and outline the report, write the literature review, select a dataset, fit models, and compare them; the planned models were logistic regression, random forest, SVM, and neural networks, compared with AUC, sensitivity, and specificity; built models on a new public pulmonary-nodule dataset in Python, using earlier experience with logistic regression, random forest, and SVM from a course project; when the file size was overwhelming, followed preprocessing pipelines from the papers and iterated by fitting, reading errors, and changing the pipeline; used SHAP and variable-importance plots when complex models were hard to interpret clinically; tested performance ideas from the literature, including a preprocessing step that improved results.
pre-internship preparation: There was no formal recruitment interview. A professor was approached because applied statistics was of more interest than theory alone, after a course group project that used statistical learning to classify brain tumors. Medical topics were explored and pulmonary nodule prediction was chosen because a large research base and an online database already existed. Choosing a topic was difficult because the range was wide, and the professor's encouragement helped narrow it. The project was then organized as a two-month timeline from literature review through model comparison.
what have I learned: Python work on real medical data improved, as did the speed of finding papers, summarizing findings, and pulling out relevant methods. Preprocessing and iterative model fitting became manageable after the literature pipelines were followed. Medical reading added knowledge of disease diagnosis and of clinical issues in pulmonary nodule detection. SHAP and variable-importance plots were used to make black-box output easier to discuss. Completing the project without teammates was new. The main gain described is broader research skill and resilience, not the score of any single model.
what do I need to improve: The topic search felt lost because too many subjects were available. Data preprocessing had not been done before, so the size and complexity of the first dataset were overwhelming and it was unclear where to start. Complex models were hard to interpret until model-agnostic tools were tried. Early paper reading was slow and frustrating. Working without teammates at first raised doubt about whether the project could be finished alone.
post-internship reflections: The project increased interest in biostatistics and in a possible career in healthcare or the pharmaceutical industry. More biostatistics and data-visualization courses are planned for the final undergraduate year, and a master's in that direction is being considered. Joining a lab and collaborating on a larger topic is now of interest. The quality of any one result came to seem less important than the knowledge, skills, and persistence gained from finishing a project independently.
advice for future interns: If a course topic is interesting, talk to the professor, because interested students are welcome and opportunities follow from being active. job description: The summer role was Student Research Assistant in SAAS at HKU, and the report also describes it as an undergraduate research assistantship in the CDS department. The project studied approximate MCMC algorithms for Gaussian processes. Exact MCMC for a Gaussian-process posterior inverts an n by n matrix in every iteration, which is costly, so practice uses approximate solvers such as conjugate gradient. The question was whether the chain from the approximation still has useful properties such as ergodicity and stationarity. The work mixed scientific programming with mathematical proof, and industry-style topics were said not to apply.
job duties: Programmed an approximate MCMC module that uses a conjugate-gradient solver, and used Multiprocess for speed and CPU parallelism; on the mathematical side, applied published results on ergodicity and Markov chains to prove stability of the chain without the approximate solver, checking assumptions and adjusting arguments to obtain the desired properties; when a Wasserstein-bound approach did not give the expected result, looked for the failing step, such as a weak bound or an unsuitable inequality, and switched to a random-mapping argument that builds a random variable inducing the transition kernel and studies the expectation of its derivative; read the technical papers provided after the interview and related them to probability and measure-theory ideas from earlier statistics and mathematics courses.
pre-internship preparation: Interest in computational statistics began when the MCMC algorithm was introduced in a Bayesian statistics course taken at the University of British Columbia during an exchange. In spring 2026 a professor was contacted about possible summer research. The conversation covered that interest and a suggested similarity between MCMC and deterministic optimization. The interview went well, and relevant papers were provided so reading could start.
what have I learned: The main gain was reading rigorous papers and writing proofs beyond ordinary exercises, including checking assumptions and adapting known theorems for properties that had not yet been established for this approximation. Scientific coding was practiced alongside the proofs, especially Multiprocess for parallel performance, which was a useful check when a proof stalled. The project sits between high-dimensional statistics and convergence arguments such as Lyapunov methods. A stated limit is that even a simple Bayesian random-effect model with only a variance parameter is hard to treat, and realistic algorithms add hyperparameters and difficult priors. The preferred kind of work is theoretical research with a practical implication, rather than routine queries or conventional machine learning.
what do I need to improve: NA
post-internship reflections: The career aim is scientific engineering in the age of AI, combining rigor that some computer-science and data-science papers lack with practical impact that pure theory sometimes misses. A more concrete plan is a PhD in optimization, especially nonconvex and stochastic optimization and their uses in machine learning, reinforcement learning, signal processing, and large language models, with industry possible later. Choices already follow that plan, including a mathematics minor, advanced operations-research courses, and research projects. Research is preferred to junior corporate data work because the approach to a problem is personally owned.
advice for future interns: Professors at HKU are generally glad to include undergraduates in research. Take important courses early, including 2000-level STAT and MATH courses and introductory COMP courses, where knowing the languages is enough. Do not be intimidated by papers. OpenReview comments, scores, and author rebuttals show that strong-looking work is still debated. Start from a problem that is interesting, and learn the rest along the way.
technical skills: MCMC, approximate matrix methods, conjugate gradient, Gaussian processes, ergodicity and stationarity arguments, Wasserstein bounds, random mappings, Lyapunov-style convergence ideas, scientific programming, Multiprocess, CPU parallelism, probability, and measure theory.
soft skills: NA

Faculty course requirements for the credit-bearing internship were noted because some of that knowledge would be used on the job.
what have I learned: Product monitoring used life-contingency ideas such as reserves and survival probabilities when reading submission documents. Discussions of investment strategy drew on the Black-Scholes model, hedging, and options from financial derivatives and financial economics. VBA, shortcuts, and formulas saved time, and seniors later asked for a better report inventory and format. Two expert learning sessions, an intern project on guideline changes and peer comparison, coffee chats with actuaries, and team events widened industry knowledge and contacts. The extra two weeks at the end were set aside to hand knowledge to the next intern.
what do I need to improve: The previous intern left early, so handover was short, and teammates were senior directors with little free time, which made it hard to ask for help while still finishing their tasks. The product-approval system was also mid-transition, and some data entered by the previous intern were wrong, so a lot of time went into understanding the files.
post-internship reflections: The half year set a first step into actuarial risk work in the regional office and shifted interest toward local valuation and pricing. The student has been looking for related roles, plans another full-time half year and a part-time internship if one is available, and rearranged the course timetable for that. On graduation the preference is another company rather than returning to Manulife: work-life balance, flexible hours, and facilities were positives, but internal competition looked high and other cultures are still untried.
advice for future interns: Learn software skills and related computer knowledge before starting, because daily laptop work goes faster with them. Keep a positive learning attitude, ask seniors even when the gap in seniority feels large, and do not be too shy. Dig further instead of stopping at the first answer, and show that you are prepared and interested in the work.
technical skills: Product pre-launch and post-launch monitoring, quarterly sales summaries, turnaround-time analysis, VBA macros for asset-mix and interest-rate data, benchmark-compliance checks, reserves and survival probabilities, and the Black-Scholes model, hedging, and options in investment-strategy discussions.
soft skills: Communication with busy seniors, networking, time management, teamwork on the intern project, and asking prepared questions.
courses mentioned: Life contingency course; financial derivatives course; financial economics course.
tools and software: VBA

job description: Manulife is an international insurer offering individual and group life and health insurance, Mandatory Provident Fund products, retirement plans, and wealth management. The internship was in the reporting team of the Hong Kong Corporate Actuarial department, a local valuation function covering financial reporting, regulatory submissions, and participating-business management. The student supported IFRS 17 reporting, Canadian LICAT submissions, and monthly internal reports on Group Life and Health products, and joined a group project on the global minimum tax.
job duties: Produce monthly internal reports on Group Life and Health products by gathering data, building the database, and sending the reports to users; monitor short-term measures such as loss ratio and incurred-but-not-reported amounts for a product that is fully valued once a year; assist seniors with IFRS 17 financial reporting, Canadian LICAT submissions, and other business reports; automate data processing and analysis in Python, VBA, and SQL; research the global minimum tax and its effects on multinational insurers' financial position, product attractiveness, and participating-business management in a cross-department intern project.
pre-internship preparation: The opportunity came from a company visit arranged by the Statistics and Actuarial Science Society. Before the visit the student researched the company and prepared questions for team leaders, mainly on actuaries' day-to-day work and on IFRS 17. The visit had a company overview, a game on actuarial functions, and a networking session. Team leaders later told the recruiter they were interested, and the offer followed from that conversation rather than from a separate interview round described in the report.
what have I learned: Financial reporting was new. IFRS 17 measurement approaches, the contractual service margin, and related reporting practice became a base for later work, supported by insurance-reserve and accounting ideas from the degree and by short-term actuarial mathematics for loss ratios and incurred-but-not-reported amounts. Python, VBA, and SQL were used to automate data handling. The global-minimum-tax project, done with interns from other departments, widened the view of tax, product attractiveness, and participating business, and the group received the Best Team Award. Excel shortcuts, functions, VBA, and reusable templates were learned on the job.
what do I need to improve: The first months were difficult because the duties, insurance reporting, and Excel were all unfamiliar, so work was slow and timelines felt tight. Quarter-end and month-end stayed heavy, especially after the intern project started. The student treated time management and clearer communication with colleagues as the way to improve further.
post-internship reflections: The career aim before graduation is to pass four or five SOA exams and to try another internship, preferably in pricing, so that reporting and pricing can be compared. Excel and programming need to be stronger for future modeling work, even if the next role is not a modeling seat, so more technical courses in actuarial modeling and programming are planned. Rejoining the company on graduation would be considered seriously because of the colleagues and the half year there.
advice for future interns: Learn a little about the field first, and ask peers or teachers for specifics so the application is better prepared. On the job, explore without waiting for seniors to teach everything: self-study and small work tools speed the workflow. Stay occupied, either learning or doing the work.
technical skills: IFRS 17 financial reporting, contractual service margin, LICAT, loss ratios, incurred but not reported reserves, database building, and automation with Python, VBA, and SQL.
soft skills: Collaboration with teammates, communication during quarter-end reporting, and time management with a task list and regular check-ins.
courses mentioned: Short-term actuarial mathematics; actuarial program courses covering Python, VBA, and SQL; insurance reserves and accounting principles from the actuarial program; SOA exams, with a plan to pass four or five.
tools and software: Excel, Python, VBA, SQL, and a task management tool.

job description: The internship was in Manulife's Valuation Shared Service Centre under Regional Actuarial Services, a team that supports business units across Asia. This assignment covered Vietnam, Malaysia, and Cambodia and centered on quarterly valuation reporting with the actuarial system AXIS. The student extracted policy data, joined user acceptance testing, and helped correct model assumptions. A group project designed AI-assisted workflows for the Hong Kong local Corporate Actuarial team and received a best-performing team award.
job duties: Extract policy data with SQL and place it in a template for later follow-up; join user acceptance testing that rehearses quarter-end reporting and scans for unusual results; inspect how products are structured in AXIS and change model assumptions to fix critical errors found in testing, including a detailed Excel check for the Vietnam business unit; on the group project, try prompt designs and AI-assisted workflows for the Hong Kong Corporate Actuarial team, read a Power BI dashboard, smooth steps with Power Automate, add visuals, and tie the ideas to regulatory standards; explain the proposal to colleagues and seniors.
pre-internship preparation: The offer came from a company visit in first year rather than from a normal interview. Before the visit the student researched the industry and the company and identified pricing and valuation as two actuarial streams, then talked with company seniors and current students because the overall picture was still unclear. Regional Actuarial Services was chosen for work with colleagues in other Asian regions and for exposure beyond Hong Kong.
what have I learned: AXIS, SQL extracts, user acceptance testing, and assumption changes showed that models have to be refitted when results look unreasonable, not simply reused each quarter. STAT3901 helped locate premiums and reserves, but company jargon and stacked product types went further. The group project added prompt engineering, Power BI, Power Automate, and visualisation aimed at the Hong Kong Corporate Actuarial team's valuation process. Lunch-and-learn sessions linked daily tasks to the concepts behind them. Self-study from past-task documentation was a necessary workplace skill.
what do I need to improve: Early on, many terms beyond premiums and reserves were unclear, and colleagues were often too busy to explain, so past documentation had to be decoded alone. AXIS had a steep learning curve. Most teammates were in the Philippines and met on Teams, which left a gap in in-person contact that the student tried to fill by talking with people in the office.
post-internship reflections: After the internship the plan is to strengthen a personal portfolio, join more actuarial activities, work harder on actuarial exams, and study in a broader way. Manulife's culture, people, and structured internship were viewed positively, and working later in other firms, including reinsurers and consultancies, was also seen as a way to see the industry more fully.
advice for future interns: Do not stop at theory that appears on actuarial exams; learn how the ideas show up in real modeling and reporting. Read actuarial news, for example from the ASHK, and talk with seniors even as a junior. Get comfortable with Excel or Python. Stay curious, but know when to ask and when to deliver.
technical skills: AXIS model use and assumption changes, SQL data extraction, user acceptance testing, Excel investigation of product structures, prompt engineering, Power BI, Power Automate, data visualisation, and regulatory checks on an AI valuation workflow.
soft skills: Self-learning from documentation, curiosity about other teams' work, and explaining a project so colleagues and seniors could follow it.
courses mentioned: STAT3901; actuarial exams.
tools and software: AXIS, SQL, Excel, Microsoft Teams, Power BI, Power Automate, and AI tools.

job description: RGA (Reinsurance Group of America) is a global life and health reinsurer. At the Hong Kong local office, the student was a pricing intern on the Inforce Management team, which helps client insurers transfer part of their portfolio risk. The work supported critical-illness experience studies for four Hong Kong client companies described as leading direct insurers. Results, including actual-to-expected analysis, were delivered to management and used in pricing decisions, including for a client that accounted for about 90 percent of RGA Hong Kong's business.
job duties: For critical-illness experience studies, use SQL to extract, clean, and validate raw data and use Redi to build exposure; calculate expected claim count, incurred but not reported claims, and gross sum assured, then compute actual-to-expected ratios; when setting expected incidence rates, add half a year to the pricing year to reflect a mid-year average date; build age-standardized incidence rates by benefit, cancer site, and cause for 2019 to 2025, split by age, gender, and residency, and flag abnormal trends; deliver a lapse study comparing the 2022 and 2024 pricing bases, including demographic shifts and updated residency assumptions; trace an unusual thyroid actual-to-expected gap to a benefit change that moved thyroid and prostate conditions between covers; write Excel VBA macros for study templates.
pre-internship preparation: In a first-year Corporate Mentorship Program, a mentor discussed direct insurance, reinsurance, and consulting, the roles of pricing and valuation, intern expectations such as a proactive attitude, and typical selection points: at least two SOA exams (P and FM), basic Excel and Python plus any other actuarial software, a sound grasp of actuarial ideas, and willingness to learn. The RGA offer came after five mentoring sessions with no interview. For an earlier Fubon Life interview, behavioral and technical answers were prepared from STAT2901 and STAT3901, including premiums and reserves. A hard question on select-and-ultimate tables was answered, after a hint, that select mortality is lower than ultimate mortality at the same age.
what have I learned: The internship showed how reinsurance treaties, experience studies, actual-to-expected review, and incidence-rate monitoring feed pricing decisions. STAT3901 mortality models, STAT3906 short-term ratemaking, and STAT3903 multi-state models helped with expected incidence rates, the half-year timing adjustment, and a multi-pay critical-illness monitoring tool. SQL for large files, Redi exposure runs, and VBA templates became working skills. Findings included heart and stroke spikes in the COVID years, higher thyroid cancer claims linked to policy changes in Mainland China, and a lapse study that supported residency-based assumption updates. SOA Exam FAM ideas were visible in the same work. Communication improved when results were taken to management.
what do I need to improve: Excel VBA was unfamiliar at the start, so manager-provided learning material and similar templates were used to write new macros. On the earlier Fubon interview, select-and-ultimate theory had been memorized as formulas rather than understood, and it was not clear at first whether select or ultimate mortality was lower.
post-internship reflections: The experience pointed toward actuarial pricing or a close field such as risk management, with a preference for data analysis. Valuation work at Fubon Life had felt repetitive, while RGA pricing allowed experience, mortality, lapse, and population-health studies and a wider view of Hong Kong demographics across insurers. The preference after graduation is a reinsurer, including RGA. The plan is at least four or five SOA exams plus other modules or VEE courses before graduation in 2026, and more data-analysis courses to support programming and number sense.
advice for future interns: Strengthen SQL, Excel, VBA, and Python before an internship so large experience-study files can be cleaned and checked. Prophet or Axis is less urgent, because a license is required and tutorials are not freely available. Learn what actual-to-expected ratios, loss ratios, lapse rates, and mortality trends mean so the numbers can support a recommendation. When speaking to decision makers, be concise, highlight outliers and the reason, and use tables and graphs.
technical skills: SQL extraction and validation, Redi exposure generation, incurred but not reported claims, gross sum assured, actual-to-expected and loss ratios, age-standardized incidence rates, lapse studies, residency-based pricing assumptions, multi-state and multi-pay critical-illness monitoring, half-year timing adjustments, and Excel VBA.
soft skills: Communication when presenting analysis to management, including a clear statement of findings, outliers, and reasons.
courses mentioned: STAT2901; STAT3901; STAT3906; STAT3903; SOA Exam FAM; SOA Exams P and FM; VEE courses and further SOA exams planned before graduation.
tools and software: SQL, Redi, Excel, and VBA.

job description: Prudential Hong Kong Limited, a major subsidiary of Prudential plc, offers life insurance, health insurance, and retirement planning. The internship was in the Local European Embedded Value team, whose metric adds net asset value to the present value of future profits and which is implementing IFRS 17. The student generated Model Point Files for embedded-value reporting, joined user acceptance testing of new actuarial systems, and learned the extract-transform-load pipeline that feeds IFRS 17 models.
job duties: Gather policy, claims, and ledger data for Model Point Files and look for inconsistencies and missing values; in the Data Conversion System, group similar policies into model points, derive items such as duration in force and attained age, clean missing values and outliers, and format output for Prophet; reconcile model-point counts, policy counts, total sum assured, and total premiums with the source systems, and log discrepancies until the cause is fixed; take part in user acceptance testing of new actuarial systems; follow how this data work sits inside the wider IFRS 17 extract, transform, and load process, including contract groups and contractual-service-margin fields.
pre-internship preparation: NA
what have I learned: The main lesson was the path from a single policy's data through cleansing, model points, and projection models to a figure used by executives and regulators. Imperfect source data, Data Conversion System rules, and reconciliation of counts and financial totals made accuracy and auditability concrete. IFRS 17 was learned from the manager: it replaces IFRS 4, measures contracts at current value, and splits the liability into future cash flows, discounting, a risk adjustment, and a contractual service margin. Seeing model-point work as a small version of the larger extract-transform-load pipeline made the same skills usable on wider data problems. The report also links this chain to finance, data, and newer technology such as AI.
what do I need to improve: NA
post-internship reflections: The six months are described as a base for becoming an actuary and for the final year of study. The role showed the profession sitting between finance, data, and new technology such as AI, and the student credits the manager and colleagues for guidance on the IFRS 17 program.
advice for future interns: NA
technical skills: Model Point File generation, data collection and cleansing, Data Conversion System rules, reconciliation of policy counts and financial totals, user acceptance testing, and IFRS 17 concepts including the building block approach, risk adjustment, contractual service margin, and extract-transform-load processing.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Data Conversion System (DCS) and Prophet.

job description: Deloitte's advisory business helps clients pursue long-term goals by improving day-to-day operations, combining strategic financial planning with practical advice. This six-month actuarial consulting internship was described as applied problem-solving across changing projects and regulations such as risk-based capital and IFRS 17. The student supported a Macau risk-based capital engagement, prepared matching-adjustment figures for a client, built an internal Hong Kong risk-based capital briefing, and later modeled and tested cash flows on an IFRS 17 project.
job duties: On the Macau risk-based capital project, summarize documents, inspect Excel templates, and clean figures from raw data; build discounted cash-flow models and matching-adjustment calculations in Excel and VBA; prepare matching-adjustment figures for the client Tahoe and write PowerPoint slides on Hong Kong risk-based capital for an internal knowledge base; on the IFRS 17 project, model and test estimated cash flows and compare them with actual results; check figures against source files and document the steps so consultants could rely on them in client reports; where client materials were unclear, email the client for confirmation instead of guessing.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started weeks ahead: research on target companies' values and business lines, a list of questions to ask, seniors' internship reports and tips, practice of a self-introduction, review of economics and life-contingency models, and a line-by-line pass through the CV. Most firms used one interview and replied within a day or two, with about 48 hours to accept. An HSBC interviewer asked an economics question beyond the textbook; the student said the exact answer was not known, then shared a first approach based on courses already taken, and the interviewer added guidance. Looking back, a practice session with a CEDARS career coach would have helped with speaking under pressure.
what have I learned: Practical knowledge covered the structure of risk-based capital and IFRS 17 and the detail of cash-flow modeling. Office skills moved to advanced Excel functions and basic VBA, with logic carried over from a Python course. A useful method was to treat client files as linked, to look in another section when stuck, and to email the client rather than guess if a change was needed. Work was broken into smaller parts with short breaks. The student contributed checked, documented analytics that consultants used in client reports, and was told by a senior that the work matched a full-time analyst. Team overtime, including a weekend, was a memorable part of meeting a deadline.
what do I need to improve: A CEDARS practice interview was a missed preparation step. Corporate routine, eight-hour focus, and fatigue before deadlines were difficult at first, and problem-solving method was weak until large tasks were split up and exercise was added for energy. Coursework was often not advanced enough for a direct technical contribution, though it sped up the terminology and the logic of the models. There was also early self-doubt.
post-internship reflections: The goal is now actuarial consulting with an emphasis on technical model-building. A postgraduate finance program, suggested by the manager in late December, is under consideration, as are data-science internships. The study plan was changed to add finance and computer science courses while keeping core actuarial requirements. Rejoining Deloitte on graduation would be considered because of the teamwork and the support for professional development.
advice for future interns: Bring a real willingness to learn; interviewers do not expect a beginner to know everything, and enthusiasm matters more than a single fact. Practice thinking logically under pressure, because consulting deadlines are tighter than routine work. Actuarial knowledge helps, and a strong statistics or data-science background is also valued. The job is solving puzzles with the information on hand.
technical skills: Document review, Excel templates and advanced formulas, discounted cash-flow models, matching-adjustment calculations, VBA, risk-based capital, IFRS 17 cash-flow modeling and testing, and checking results against source files.
soft skills: Communication with clients and internal teams, teamwork under a shared deadline, and breaking work into manageable parts.
courses mentioned: Economics; life contingency models; a Python course; further finance and computer science courses, and a possible postgraduate program in finance.
tools and software: Excel, VBA, PowerPoint, and Python.

job description: Manulife offers individual finance products, group life and health cover, and MPF. The student completed an eight-month internship in the Corporate Actuarial Department under the Chief Actuary Office, a consolidation team that prepares regulatory submissions to the Hong Kong Insurance Authority and the Macau AMCM and handles group life and health treaty reviews and daily settlement approvals. The role was to turn raw data from other teams into submission templates, check group settlements, and build a claim dashboard that the group life and health team uses when repricing group medical insurance.
job duties: Consolidate raw data files, more than twenty a month, and complete templates for monthly and quarterly new-business statistics on QDAP, participating, and non-participating products for the Insurance Authority; verify and calculate group life and health settlements for Insurope and IGP before the manager's approval; build a claim dashboard from scratch by importing data, creating relationships, writing SQL, and showing movements within the policy year; compare premium and claims to judge whether renewal premiums should rise; flag possible abuse, such as an employee visiting doctors more than thirty times a year, and report details to the claim team; trace IHIP claims with hospitalization days but no surgical fee back to the claim number and share unexplained cases; summarize inconsistencies briefly in Teams meetings so other teams can correct them.
pre-internship preparation: From Year 1 the student followed department sharing sessions and the online recruitment system, then attended the department career fair in Year 2 and received an offer from Manulife. The interview included an approximately one-minute self-introduction and actuarial questions. Beforehand, the student researched the core work of pricing and valuation, which the interviewer did ask about, and planned to give an opinion even when a question was unfamiliar rather than stay silent.
what have I learned: STAT3901, especially the product nature of a deferred annuity, helped explain terminated benefits and the many transactions on paid-up QDAP policies in regulatory templates. The group life and health dashboard project taught how to import data, create relationships, write SQL, and present results, plus the basic logic of group medical pricing and of spotting unusually frequent claims. The dashboard is now used daily and supports pricing decisions. Communication and problem-solving improved through cross-team work, and learning the internal systems made independent data analysis possible. The team atmosphere, including quarter-end overtime, strengthened a wish to stay in the actuarial industry. A return offer was received, with a plan to rejoin in 2027.
what do I need to improve: At the start of the internship, the student did not know how to analyze data quickly and had to ask the team how to use the company system to find the needed information.
post-internship reflections: After eight months the student wants to work in the actuarial industry, seeing it as a fit with personal interests and strengths, and also treats company culture as important when choosing an employer. The Manulife atmosphere was a good match, and the return offer will be taken up in 2027. Before then the plan is to pass as many SOA exams as possible, follow industry developments, and use university sharing sessions to learn more about the field.
advice for future interns: Students applying for actuarial roles should pass Exam P and Exam FM before the interview, as a sign of commitment, and should become proficient in Python, Excel, and Power BI, because many companies use them daily and less training time can improve the chance of being hired.
technical skills: Regulatory submission templates; QDAP, participating, and non-participating new-business statistics; group life and health settlement checks; dashboard building; SQL; group medical pricing, including premium versus claims and high-frequency claim review; tracing claim-level data inconsistencies.
soft skills: Communication, problem-solving, and cross-team coordination, including raising data issues clearly in meetings; a positive and active approach in interviews.
courses mentioned: STAT3901; Exam P; Exam FM; SOA exams.
tools and software: SQL; Microsoft Teams; Python, Excel, and Power BI, which are recommended for applicants because companies use them in daily work.

job description: AIA International Limited is a long-established direct insurer serving individual and corporate customers in Hong Kong and Macau, with an aim of helping people live healthier, longer, and better lives. The student spent a half-year internship in the local office IFRS 17 reporting team. The role was to assist monthly closing and workflow enhancement, mainly in Excel and VBA, including a large share of ad-hoc work and a project to rebuild reporting templates so the process was cleaner and easier to maintain.
job duties: Assist the monthly close and enhance workflows, with most tasks done in Excel and VBA; take ad-hoc assignments from colleagues, which occupied the majority of the time; read, understand, and revamp about twenty Excel templates for one task, reducing them to four, with the design and functionality approved by seniors and managers; when work was quiet, ask to rejoin a project a senior was finishing and use the Bloomberg terminal, contributing insights that helped solve part of the problem; later rebuild existing Excel templates after a short briefing whose goal was to make the files clean and tidy, reviewing the work from the manager's perspective.
pre-internship preparation: This was a second half-year internship, so the student reviewed curriculum knowledge and expected interviews to test personality and logical thinking more than technical detail. Formats differed: some were group interviews with simple questions, such as naming an insurance product, and some were one-to-one, including a phone conversation with a department head. On a technical question the student did not know, a reasoned answer was derived and that interview led to an offer. After the IFRS 17 reporting role was known, basic VBA was learned and IFRS 17 material was read before the start date.
what have I learned: Programme knowledge of premiums, reserves, and time value gave a basic picture of insurance that classroom study alone had not matched to practice. The main gain was understanding Excel work instead of only clicking through it, solving problems independently, and thinking logically. Proactiveness led to extra project work and use of the Bloomberg terminal. The template rebuild also developed the habit of reviewing work from a manager's point of view. Confidence mattered when the work was unclear, and questions to seniors were used as a way to learn. Unlike an earlier internship, the student made a deliberate effort to connect with teammates and with interns from other universities.
what do I need to improve: Basic VBA study before the start was not enough: when about twenty templates and a VBA task were assigned, the student at first had no idea how to begin. An earlier internship had also left a habit of using Excel without understanding it, which this placement was meant to correct.
post-internship reflections: With no courses left except this capstone, there is no long-term career goal yet. The near-term aim is a permanent actuarial analyst role, preferring direct insurers and consulting firms over reinsurers because direct insurance is more prominent in Hong Kong and consulting fits a preference for challenge. The study plan is to gain as many SOA qualifications as possible before the first job in order to negotiate a higher salary. Rejoining AIA after graduation would be considered because the people and culture were comfortable.
advice for future interns: Be confident, know what you are doing, and be conscious of every act.
technical skills: IFRS 17 reporting, monthly closing, Excel template design and VBA, independent troubleshooting of spreadsheet processes, and use of the Bloomberg terminal.
soft skills: Proactiveness, logical thinking, independent problem-solving, confidence, reviewing work from a manager's perspective, and building relationships despite being introverted.
courses mentioned: SOA qualifications; IFRS 17 material read before the internship; curriculum knowledge reviewed for interviews, with no course code named.
tools and software: Excel, VBA, and the Bloomberg terminal.

job description: Prudential is one of the largest financial services groups, operating in Asia, the United States, and Africa and serving about nineteen million customers. Its products range from life and health insurance to retirement savings, asset management, and banking. The internship was in Capital Management, which differs from pricing or reserving: the team checks that the group holds enough capital for regulators and for growth, and it links market movements, new rules, and business strategy. The student monitored risk limits, forecast solvency, and supported several operational processes.
job duties: Run weekly risk monitoring of interest rates, equity markets, and credit spreads against breakpoints that require management action if broken; each quarter, retune those breakpoints from new shock profiles in complicated Excel models, derive implied break levels, and cross-check them against regulator stress tests such as one-in-two-hundred-year events; prepare a monthly solvency forecast of the next month's capital position under scenarios such as equities falling ten percent or interest rates rising fifty basis points; assist with IFRS 16 lease calculations, service-tax documentation for the Malaysian subsidiary PCA Re, cash reconciliations, payment processing, and invoice summaries; document recurring tasks, timelines, Excel templates, and default emails for the next intern; build Excel formulas that write report commentaries on unusual movements, which the supervisor later rolled out to other projects.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation included the business model, market valuations, recent financial reports, corporate culture, annual reports, and news articles, plus Capital Management terms: solvency ratios, Group Minimum Capital Requirement, Group Prescribed Capital Requirement, one hundred percent Required Capital, and an overview of newer insurance regulation. The student also rehearsed questions alone, wrote study examples meant to show analysis and attention to detail, and prepared questions to ask. The interview was with two or three staff and covered actuarial concepts, problem-solving, and case scenarios. The hardest question was how to handle conflicting deadlines; the answer was communication and prioritization.
what have I learned: The internship showed how capital management uses market moves and regulation in practice, and it strengthened Excel modeling well beyond smaller workbooks. Soft skills included explaining technical language, ranking work when several deadlines overlapped, and working in a professional setting where questions were welcomed. A personal method of tracing prior-year workings, and of trying for a while before asking, made large multi-sheet files manageable. Automated commentary formulas saved time, reduced inconsistent wording, and were adopted by the supervisor. Step-by-step notes were also left so the next intern would not face the same first weeks.
what do I need to improve: Workbooks with more than twenty dependent sheets were far harder than expected, and the first week was spent tracing a single calculation. The student was at first too reluctant to ask for help and lost hours; the later rule was to try for about thirty minutes and then ask a colleague.
post-internship reflections: The internship made a career in capital management more likely, with a long-term hope of a senior role that influences major decisions. The study plan is to keep high grades in final courses, prepare for professional actuarial exams, and learn programs such as VBA. Further internships in pricing or valuation are also planned. Returning to Prudential after graduation would be seriously considered because of the team and culture, while other employers would still be compared.
advice for future interns: Be proactive and ask for help after making a genuine attempt, without fearing to look inexperienced. Take an interest in why the team's work matters and where it sits in the wider business. Prepare for interviews with both company knowledge and the technical content of the role, and show real interest rather than memorized facts, because teams also look for someone who will fit and contribute.
technical skills: Weekly market-risk monitoring, breakpoint calibration against regulator stress tests, monthly solvency forecasting, Excel modeling, IFRS 16 lease calculations, cash reconciliation, and automated report commentaries. Solvency ratios, Group Minimum Capital Requirement, Group Prescribed Capital Requirement, and Required Capital were studied for the role.
soft skills: Explaining technical jargon, prioritizing several deadlines, asking for help after a real attempt, and working in a professional team.
courses mentioned: Professional actuarial exams; financial markets and risk analysis studied at school, with no course code named.
