tools and software: Excel; VBA, which the student plans to learn because it is described as important in this career.

job description: AIA Group is a leading pan-Asian life insurer headquartered in Hong Kong, with eighteen branch offices in Asia and a stated culture of healthier, longer, better lives. In the first half of 2025 the student spent six months on an actuarial audit internship at the AIA Group Office, in the General Insurance Audit division. Actuarial audit checks reserve calculations, regulatory compliance, and policyholder protection. The role began with quarterly management reports and grew into VBA and Power BI work, data-lineage tracking, reinsurance communication, and comparisons of external audit reports.
job duties: Review and sort quarterly management reports across business units and update figures with Excel VBA and Power BI; draft sections of actuarial audit summaries, including issue analysis, trend analysis, and issue lists; edit and troubleshoot nested VBA macros in legacy audit templates; support data-lineage tracking by cross-referencing sources in quarterly reports; learn Alteryx as a way to streamline repetitive audit work; prepare a reinsurance presentation for another team; find and correct a serious calculation error in historical data; when external AI tools were prohibited, design semi-automated Excel macro checks that reduced manual review effort by about thirty percent; build a Power BI view of quarterly revenue and claims by insurance type for branch decisions; compare audit reports from different firms with AIA inspection terms to help a branch choose a consulting firm.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation had three parts: reviewing course material on life insurance types, risk theory, and reserve calculation, plus industry reports on how actuarial work meets audit and risk management; practicing Excel functions such as VLOOKUP and pivot tables, and Power BI; and researching culture, history, employee views, and what the General Insurance Audit division expects of interns. Selection was a resume screen, a panel interview, and one-to-one interviews with leaders, covering the company, the work, and actuarial principles. The hardest question was how to stay motivated in repetitive calculation and data review. The answer was that careful detail protects policyholders, supports compliance, and is how hidden risks are found.
what have I learned: The internship deepened VBA, Power BI, Alteryx, and data-lineage work, and showed how reserve and risk-management knowledge changes the way audit figures are read. Supervisors explained quarterly data, the risk process, and reinsurance, and reviewed code after the student first tried alone. Trend charts were used in division meetings, a reinsurance presentation was well received, and updated audit summary tabs were praised for clearer stakeholder communication. Finding and fixing a historical calculation error was recognized as the kind of care the job needs. A conversation about using AI software also made information-security rules concrete.
what do I need to improve: At the start, the meaning of particular actuarial data points and their place in risk management was hard to follow, and compliance requirements were unclear. Using AI software led to a discussion of information security, because the audit team bans external AI tools and requires manual or controlled checks. Large repetitive reviews remained difficult until semi-automated Excel checks were designed with a supervisor's advice.
post-internship reflections: The career goal is to become a comprehensive actuary who combines traditional work with data science and artificial intelligence that still meets audit rules, including tools for actuarial auditing and, longer term, a supervised insurance platform. The plan is to study machine learning and regulatory technology while keeping an actuarial foundation. Quarterly figures in which electronic policies were under five percent of purchases were one reason for that interest. Rejoining AIA after graduation would be considered, in order to work on compliant semi-automated audit with the same supportive leaders.
advice for future interns: First, master foundational actuarial knowledge so data and the job itself can be interpreted correctly. Second, master Excel, including VBA, and explore tools such as Alteryx for efficiency and automation. Third, ask senior colleagues for guidance rather than relying only on self-study, and accept early repetitive work as the base for later tasks.
technical skills: Excel, including VLOOKUP, pivot tables, and VBA macros; Power BI visualization; Alteryx; data-lineage tracking; interpretation of reserve calculations and risk-management figures; audit issue and trend analysis; semi-automated validation checks.
soft skills: Asking for guidance, trying a problem independently before review, explaining reinsurance and audit results to other teams, and the meticulous checking the role requires.
courses mentioned: Actuarial courses covering life insurance types, risk theory, and reserve calculation, with no course code named.
tools and software: Excel, VBA, VLOOKUP, pivot tables, Power BI, Alteryx, and AI software, which the audit team did not allow.

job description: RGA is a reinsurer that shares risk with ceding companies. It responds to requests for proposal with price and coverage terms, invests premiums, holds reserves, and pays claims, which can reduce the cedent's required capital. From July to December 2024 the student was an Actuarial Intern on the local valuation team. The main assignment was the Hong Kong Valuation Process Innovation project, which changes assumption, data, governance, and modeling practice so valuation is faster, less complex, and less open to human error.
job duties: Build a SQL assumption model in Rate Management Services so users can enter an old assumption name, retrieve the linked treaties with business attributes mapped, and change a few terms instead of re-entering every condition for mortality, interest, lapse, and related assumptions; trace treaties that were tied to the target assumption but the wrong attribute, including Hong Kong Mass Market treaties classified as Hong Kong High Net Worth, back to source files and correct them; test the model on the previous quarter's update procedure and reach one hundred percent accuracy; on the data side, test every cession script set on both Alteryx and Toad, compare outputs, and edit benefit and reserve logic when results differed, as part of a redesign that cut runtime to one-eighth and lines of code by about ninety percent.
pre-internship preparation: The offer came through the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science Corporate Mentorship Programme: an on-site company visit and eight one-to-one meetings with an experienced actuary who later became the direct manager and recommended the student to human resources as an Actuarial Intern. Those meetings covered what actuaries do, how academic knowledge is used, how SOA exams help, and RGA's culture. On the mentor's advice, before joining, the student learned common Excel functions, Excel VBA, and SQL from YouTube tutorials and public exercises.
what have I learned: The placement showed how reinsurance works and how actuarial attributes such as underwriting method and plan type can be combined with programming to update valuation assumptions. Correcting misclassified treaties and matching the prior quarter's results gave a concrete check on accuracy. Working with seniors developed a cooperative way of using other people's expertise and of communicating without causing offence. The company also emphasized work-life balance, including exercise and team activities, which made the six months memorable. Management support for the project was tied to measured gains in accuracy and runtime.
what do I need to improve: NA
post-internship reflections: Nearing graduation in actuarial science, the student wants a first formal industry role, then broader experience before specializing. The immediate plan is to keep working on SOA exams; all six ASA exams had already been passed. Rejoining RGA would be considered because of the culture, familiarity with the reinsurance business, and a wish to contribute more after further study.
advice for future interns: Study the requirements of the role and learn the related knowledge and skills in advance, both for interviews and for a faster start. When working with seniors, stay open: learn practical actuarial points and their professional attitude, not only the assigned steps.
technical skills: SQL assumption modeling, Excel and Excel VBA, Rate Management Services, mapping treaties to mortality, interest, and lapse assumptions, and parallel testing of cession scripts in Alteryx and Toad, including benefit and reserve logic.
soft skills: Collaboration, communicating without offending others, and combining colleagues' expertise on a shared problem.
courses mentioned: SOA exams; all six ASA exams, which had been passed. Actuarial and programming knowledge from school was used, with no course code named.
tools and software: Excel, Excel VBA, SQL, YouTube, Rate Management Services, Alteryx, and Toad.

job description: Manulife is a direct insurer selling life protection, savings products, and MPF. Its actuarial departments include Marketing Actuarial, Corporate Actuarial, Regional Actuarial Service, and Actuarial Risk Management, covering product pricing, reporting to the Insurance Authority and the public, and risk monitoring. The student joined the pricing team, the Hong Kong Marketing Actuarial Department, after a society company visit. The work mixed special quotations required of all interns with product projects and a cross-team intern project on valuation reporting.
job duties: Prepare special quotations for death benefit, special premium discount memos, reinstating premium, and cost-of-insurance and cost-of-rider illustrations for investment-linked assurance schemes; carry out user acceptance testing and AXIS model checking for the Apollo Protection Linked Plan, comparing assumptions in AXIS with the base source; enhance cost-of-insurance and cost-of-rider illustration tools; support Future Assure rate submission, illustration samples, and user acceptance testing, including adding that product's logic to a shared illustration workbook; assist a short-term endowment proposal for DBS; prepare anniversary statements and in-force illustrations for a special policy loan; complete dividend-scale-change and Genesis user acceptance testing; join an intern project with other teams on using ChatMFC, Manulife's AI chatbot, for financial and value reporting with Corporate Actuarial.
pre-internship preparation: The offer followed a Statistics and Actuarial Science Society company visit to Manulife on 1 March 2023. As an executive committee member, the student had already visited once to discuss the agenda. Human resources showed the working floors in Manulife Financial Centre and Manulife Tower, and groups then spoke with department heads, who were FSAs, about actuarial work and how to prepare for actuarial exams. The next day human resources phoned with an internship offer and asked for a team preference. The student chose the pricing team, the Hong Kong Marketing Actuarial Department. Little Excel preparation was done before the job itself.
what have I learned: STAT3901 supplied a basic picture of how an insurance product works, which the daily tasks otherwise used only lightly. The largest gain was Excel. At the start only SUM and AVERAGE were familiar. Product specifications, copying formulas out to study them, Apollo Protection Linked Plan model checking, and two months on Future Assure user acceptance testing led to INDEX MATCH, XLOOKUP, SUMIF, and the ability to trace formulas. A task manager praised organization, communication, and the proposal-checking method. The student also learned to explain a suggested fix under time pressure and to set expectations about timeline and personal capacity.
what do I need to improve: Excel was a major gap: before the internship the student knew almost nothing beyond SUM and AVERAGE, and the first user acceptance test was confusing because product items, functions, and formula tracing were all unfamiliar. That first test did not feel like a large improvement; the later model-checking and Future Assure work is where the skill actually grew.
post-internship reflections: A return offer changed the plan. More time will go to SOA exams than to school exams, because the job is secured and further passes can raise salary. Rejoining is likely, including a scholarship of 30000 dollars for returning for more than one year. The department is busy, which may be a faster way to learn the industry, and the staff were described as friendly and willing to help.
advice for future interns: It is acceptable to start this department with little technical preparation, because the tasks teach the Excel functions that matter and pre-learning the wrong ones can waste time. Be willing to ask and to figure answers out. Manage task managers' expectations, and when already at capacity ask the intern manager to discuss workload with them rather than silently taking on more.
technical skills: Excel functions including SUM, AVERAGE, INDEX MATCH, XLOOKUP, and SUMIF; formula tracing; AXIS model checking; user acceptance testing; special quotations and illustration logic for investment-linked and other products.
soft skills: Organization, communication, asking for help and raising problems quickly, and managing managers' expectations about timeline and capacity.
courses mentioned: STAT3901; actuarial exams discussed with qualified actuaries during the company visit; SOA exams, which the student plans to prioritize after the return offer.
tools and software: Excel, AXIS, Microsoft Word, Google, and ChatMFC.

job description: HSBC is described as a leading financial institution. Its global insurance division mainly provides direct insurance to clients, with a smaller reinsurance activity. In the second half of 2024 the student completed a six-month full-time internship in the Global Insurance department on a special project team that rotated across roles. The work covered participating-fund management, variable-fee-approach eligibility testing for life treasury products, user acceptance testing, and support for the actuarial information-technology manager.
job duties: On participating-fund management, learn participating and investment-related products and the RBC and IFRS 17 frameworks, use Prophet Enterprise and Prophet Professional, and build macros to automate data extraction while working with the manager and the investment team; for variable-fee-approach eligibility testing, select model points such as age, sex, monthly premium, and smoking status for basic life treasury, par rider, and non-par rider products, set interest and mortality assumptions in Prophet, and check results in Excel through weighted internal rate of return and long-term investment return; replicate Prophet calculations in Excel for user acceptance testing of five products, independently finish the product Accelerate, help run ten model-point validation tests per product, and write generalized formulas; with actuarial information technology, monitor storage usage and Policy Management and Control System performance and help move data-system code from Python scripts to BigQuery.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started with a curriculum vitae and cover letter, then review for academic and behavioral interviews. Academic topics included types of insurance products, the different kinds of insurance companies, roles of actuaries, bonds, annuities, discount rates, probability distributions, and reserve calculations, plus a clear account of any earlier experience. A memorable behavioral question was how to describe the color purple to a blind person; the student treated it as a test of critical thinking. The intended personal points were teamwork, critical thinking, responsibility, and communication.
what have I learned: The internship introduced Prophet Enterprise and Prophet Professional, regulatory ideas such as RBC and IFRS 17, model-point selection, assumption setting, and analysis of weighted internal rate of return and long-term investment return. Programming studied at school helped turn unfamiliar Prophet code into Excel checks. Independently completing user acceptance testing for Accelerate, and generalizing formulas across five products, was described as the main milestone. Communication improved through meetings with the manager and the investment team. Information-technology tasks added macros, BigQuery, and a broader view of how data systems support actuarial work. The stated gains were transferring study into practice, adaptability, collaboration, and more confident problem-solving.
what do I need to improve: The specialized tools and online platforms were entirely new at the start. Prophet code looked very long, its language was unfamiliar, and rebuilding those calculations in a spreadsheet was the hardest part of the internship until the logic was peeled back step by step with help from managers.
post-internship reflections: The goal is to start as an actuarial analyst in insurance and eventually become a fully qualified actuary. The plan is to take more advanced courses in actuarial mathematics, statistics, and risk management, and to prepare for Society of Actuaries exams, while also looking for further internships or part-time work and continuing technical study. Rejoining the company after graduation would be considered because the environment and teamwork were motivating.
advice for future interns: Strengthen both academic knowledge and practical skills, look for internships early, stay humble, and show a willingness to learn. Stay confident and interested in the work. Early hands-on experience can improve understanding of the profession and help in a competitive career fair.
technical skills: Prophet Enterprise and Prophet Professional, Excel replication of model calculations, macros, model-point validation, internal rate of return and long-term investment return analysis, user acceptance testing, Python, and BigQuery.
soft skills: Communication with managers and other departments, collaboration, adaptability, problem-solving confidence, and interpersonal skills. Teamwork, critical thinking, responsibility, and communication were also the traits prepared for interviews.
courses mentioned: Society of Actuaries (SOA) exams; planned advanced courses in actuarial mathematics, statistics, and risk management. Programming knowledge from school was used, with no course code named.
tools and software: Prophet Enterprise, Prophet Professional, Excel, Python, BigQuery, and the Policy Management and Control System (PMCS).

job description: AIA Group Limited is the largest independent publicly listed pan-Asian life insurance group, headquartered in Hong Kong, listed as 1299.HK, and active in eighteen Asia-Pacific markets. Products include life, health, and accident cover and savings and retirement plans. In 2025 the student was an actuarial intern for six months in the Actuarial Solution Architect department, which was integrated with the Financial Data Solution Architect team in July 2025. The role built and ran data-checking tools, especially a summarization tool for the Australia office ahead of IFRS 17.
job duties: Complete digital induction on IFRS 17 and the Statistical Analysis System; each day, run an Excel file and a SAS script used to audit insurance contract groups, report inconsistencies, and learn the logic; develop a SAS and Microsoft Excel data summarization tool for the Australia office to replace outdated tools and keep outputs in line with group policy for IFRS 17; write VBA macros to automate repetitive data entry and organization, and code SAS routines for large datasets and summarized outputs; request operation manuals, reverse-engineer older files, and search the internet or use programming AI when formulas were unfamiliar; pass the Alteryx Designer Core Micro-Credential; compile pointed questions for the supervisor and financial-data experts; join virtual meetings with the Australian team to resolve a field-definition difference between the Hong Kong and Australian offices.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation was treated as starting with the actuarial programme itself: a substantive curriculum vitae and cover letter, then ranking listed companies from public information against personal interests. Course notes on financial concepts and calculation methods were reviewed for technical interviews. Applications went through the actuarial department system on 10 April 2024, and AIA Group replied within eight minutes. Many interviews, including phone and Zoom calls of at least fifteen minutes, had to be scheduled without clashes. They covered a self-introduction, the resume, qualitative links between economic factors and security prices, and features of existing insurance products. When offers required a decision within hours, the student kept the original first choice and accepted the AIA Group Office.
what have I learned: Academic knowledge of insurance terms, product structures, reserves, and premiums explained what the data meant, while SAS, VBA, and Excel were needed to build the tools. IFRS 17 and internal SAS procedures were new and came first from e-learning. Owning the Australia-office tool, later used in the daily workflow, was the most satisfying part. Efficient questions and meetings with Hong Kong and Australian colleagues kept the work aligned with group data policy. A random phishing email, disguised as a LinkedIn message, was clicked despite cybercrime training, which left a lasting reminder about cybersecurity. The Alteryx Designer Core Micro-Credential was passed on a supervisor's suggestion.
what do I need to improve: Training materials were not enough for the project, and the other intern's departure left the full workload with the student while the supervisor was also unfamiliar with the Australia office process. Separately, the student clicked a phishing link during an information-technology cybersecurity test and treated that as a mistake to remember.
post-internship reflections: The primary goal is still the Associate and then the Fellow of the Society of Actuaries, but the internship suggested that a modern actuarial career should not stop at traditional calculation. Several computer science courses have been added in the final year at the University of Hong Kong, and a postgraduate degree in financial engineering or computational finance is planned to strengthen programming. Rejoining AIA would be welcome because of its digitalization work and newer areas such as premium trust products.
advice for future interns: Learn core financial principles, not only actuarial textbook material, because interviews and daily work both use them. Look for internships early so the resume and interview answers are concrete. Take the role with confident curiosity and humble diligence: ask questions and offer ideas, while remembering that performance and attitude shape a professional reputation.
technical skills: SAS programming, Excel and VBA automation, IFRS 17 data summarization and contract-group audit checks, Alteryx, and translating actuarial calculation methods into data tools.
soft skills: Professional communication with supervisors and overseas teams, asking clear questions, independent ownership of a project, and alertness to cybersecurity.
courses mentioned: Financial concepts and calculation methods reviewed from course notes; computer science courses in the final year at the University of Hong Kong; Associate of the Society of Actuaries (ASA) and Fellow of the Society of Actuaries (FSA); a planned postgraduate degree in financial engineering or computational finance.
tools and software: Statistical Analysis System (SAS), Microsoft Excel, VBA, Alteryx, Zoom, and programming AI used to interpret unfamiliar code and formulas.

job description: Prudential HK Limited is a leading life insurer with a global presence, working in risk management, product development, and regulatory compliance. From December 2024 to June 2025 the student interned in the actuarial reporting team. The placement focused on solvency, data validation, and financial reporting under IFRS 17 and Solvency II. Day-to-day work managed Prophet workspaces for more than one country, covering deterministic and stochastic models, sensitivity testing, and reasonableness checks on reported figures.
job duties: Maintain Prophet workspaces for multiple countries; fill Prophet Automation Input Templates with interest rates, discount rates, and shock levels, and classify models as deterministic or stochastic, including asset-liability stochastic types; assign risk drivers and shocks for base and stressed scenarios with yield-curve details; for stochastic runs, select economic scenario generator files with interest rates, inflation, and zero-coupon bond prices over a one-hundred-year horizon; build Prophet tables in Excel, match template variables to the models, upload Prophet Enterprise results to a SQL Server database, and query SQL for calibration and consistency checks; debug failed runs from mismatched variables, wrong shock levels, date formats, or a VBA failure when the template held too much data; find undetected calculation and input errors from a local business unit and coordinate fixes with the international team.
pre-internship preparation: About one month was spent reviewing STAT3901 Life Contingency, STAT3903 Stochastic Model, and STAT3907 Linear Models and Forecasting, chosen for their link to internship work. Seniors advised that Excel matters, so VLOOKUP, IF, SUMIF, and similar functions were practiced. Invitations also came from AIA, Chubb Life, and AXA, but Prudential's offer was accepted on the first day because of a twenty-four-hour deadline. The three interviews each had a self-introduction, technical questions, and a discussion of the company. Technical topics included annuities, stochastic models, and actuarial departments. Prudential asked about the Prophet model, which the student had not learned; the gap was admitted and the offer still followed.
what have I learned: Daily use of Prophet Enterprise, Prophet Professional, SQL, Excel, and VBA built practical reporting skill and a way to debug failed runs. IFRS 17 and Solvency II, including best-estimate liabilities, discounting, the minimum capital requirement, and the solvency capital requirement, became concrete. Life contingencies and financial mathematics from university helped when model outputs and discounting were checked. Catching local-business-unit input and calculation errors before a reporting deadline showed why validation matters. The student also learned when to ask a senior and when to continue alone, and gained communication practice and a sense of workplace etiquette.
what do I need to improve: Prophet had never been studied before the interview or the job, so model structure had to be learned at work. A VBA automation failure caused by too much data in the input template could not be fixed independently before the deadline, and a senior had to walk through the manual steps. Many failed runs also came from small mistakes such as mismatched variables, wrong shock levels, or unexpected date formats.
post-internship reflections: The student wants experience in other actuarial areas, such as pricing or modeling, to broaden an industry view. If Prudential HK offers a role after graduation, joining full time would be welcome because of the collaborative culture and because the systems and environment are already familiar.
advice for future interns: Improve Excel proficiency and review STAT2902 and STAT3901. Students with more time should also learn the basics of Prophet software before applying for a similar reporting role.
technical skills: Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise, Prophet Automation Input Templates, economic scenario generator files, deterministic and stochastic model runs, SQL database checks, Excel and VBA, sensitivity testing, and IFRS 17 and Solvency II reporting controls.
soft skills: Communication with colleagues, workplace etiquette, and judging when to ask for help versus continue alone.
courses mentioned: STAT3901 Life Contingency; STAT3903 Stochastic Model; STAT3907 Linear Models and Forecasting; STAT2902, recommended with STAT3901 for future applicants. Stochastic modeling and financial mathematics courses were also applied on the job.
tools and software: Prophet Professional, Prophet Enterprise, Excel, VBA, SQL, and SQL Server.

job description: FWD Life Insurance Company (Bermuda) focuses on savings products and medical products. The student joined through the department internship application system for a first full-time actuarial internship, from mid-December to early July, on the pricing team inside Product Data Management, a team of about thirty people. Interns were grouped in batches of four. The role supported actual-versus-expected claim analysis, user acceptance testing of new products, updates so illustrated customer returns met a regulatory cap, and checks of illustrations after a policy was sold.
job duties: Each month, prepare actual-versus-expected files for major claims in Hong Kong and claims in Macau: import valuation data through Microsoft Access into Excel, filter and edit formulas, and add new products when a filter error appears; pass graphs to a senior who reports to the Chief Product Officer; at year-end, build 2025 tabs and check formulas cell by cell; design user-acceptance-test cases for a Bermuda indexed universal life product, covering fixed and indexed accounts, flexible premiums, current, guaranteed, and alternative bases, and maximum, minimum, and premium-to-endowment approaches; reproject products so illustrated returns stay within the Insurance Authority cap of 6.0 percent per annum for Hong Kong dollar products, and compare pricing-tool figures with the system across channels; check post-sale illustrations for new savings and medical policies; write VBA macros, including one for the premium to endowment.
pre-internship preparation: The internship was obtained through the Internship Online application system of the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science. The student started in mid-December immediately after finals, so there was little time to prepare before the first day. On onboarding, a senior introduced the office, explained the intern work, and provided guides.
what have I learned: Actual-versus-expected work showed how products contribute to profit and how formulas link large sets of tables. Year-end template updates forced a closer reading of those relationships, and the senior later explained more of the theory once the monthly process was familiar. User acceptance testing and post-sale checks built familiarity with illustration tools and with indexed universal life features such as flexible premiums, account weightings, caps, and crediting rates. The internal-rate-of-return task showed how pessimistic and optimistic illustrations are kept inside a regulatory cap. VBA and advanced Excel formulas were learned on the job, including macros for testing tasks.
what do I need to improve: The student wrote that more eagerness and passion could have been shown, and that help or background should have been requested earlier when a task was new or a difficulty appeared.
post-internship reflections: Seven months produced a clearer personal picture of what an actuarial analyst does. The range of products and challenging tasks made the student more eager to learn related knowledge and to take on a wider variety of actuarial work.
advice for future interns: NA
technical skills: Excel formulas, Microsoft Access data extracts, VBA macros, actual-versus-expected analysis, user-acceptance-test design, internal-rate-of-return reprojection, and insurance illustration tools.
soft skills: Working with the other interns in the batch, who helped one another, and gaining enough trust that a senior explained more of the formula theory.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Excel, Microsoft Access, and VBA.

job description: Prudential is a global insurance and financial services group whose core business is long-term life insurance and retirement products. The student joined the asset-liability management team, which aligns assets such as bonds and equities with long-term obligations to policyholders. The internship supported the real-world economic scenario generator used to test interest rates and market returns, judge solvency, and plan investment strategy. Production work was coordinated with the economic capital team and the strategic asset allocation team.
job duties: Help develop, calibrate, and validate the company's real-world economic scenario generator; prepare and analyze historical interest rates, credit spreads, and equity returns; run stochastic simulations that generate hundreds of future economic scenarios; check outputs against historical periods and stylized facts; at month-end, quarter-end, and the half-year reporting point, extract the latest Bloomberg data, update the yield curve and other assumptions, run the generator under different scenarios, and organize deliverables for local business units, often within the first working day; on model development, use the Vietnam long-term deposit model as an entry to the wider system, collect data, and code tools so the deposit could be treated, with adjustments, as an alternative to corporate bonds; suggest, from the analysis, placing that deposit between government and corporate bonds for capital allocation and reserving.
pre-internship preparation: Applications began in year two, with a cover letter and resume sent to insurance, reinsurance, and consulting firms. Interview invitations included Deloitte, AIA, and Prudential. Preparation was a review of life contingency, financial mathematics, and derivatives, especially material used in SOA exams, plus company research and practice on common questions. Follow-up questions were a weakness: duration could be defined, but the effect of a parallel yield-curve shift or a coupon change was answered slowly. Later interviews were used as practice. The final choice was between the Sun Life pricing team and the Prudential group asset-liability management team; Prudential was chosen for platform size, geographic location, and interest in a broad strategic view.
what have I learned: The work connected duration matching and the Black-Scholes model to industrial spreadsheets and code, and it gave a wider view of bond portfolios and of risk-neutral versus real-world scenario uses. Closing the gap took three steps: reading Society of Actuaries practical guides on economic scenario generators and internal procedure notes, regular questions to a mentor about why calibrations were chosen, and learning one component at a time, starting with the long-term deposit model. Month-end production tested organization and stress tolerance. Coding, with Copilot and colleagues, was the main gain on the Vietnam deposit work, and the resulting risk-return analysis was used in a suggestion about where that asset should sit for capital and reserving.
what do I need to improve: Interview follow-ups exposed a gap between knowing a definition, such as duration, and applying it under pressure. On the job, complicated Excel workbooks and the link between abstract code and financial ideas were hard to read at first. Data collection and coding were the main obstacles on the Vietnam long-term deposit model.
post-internship reflections: The career goal is still open. The student is more willing to try different kinds of experience than to commit now to non-life work in general insurance pricing, reserving, or valuation. The plan is to apply for internships in other roles, choose final-year electives on different insurance topics, and sit professional actuarial exams. Rejoining this team would still be appreciated because of the modeling exposure and the supportive environment.
advice for future interns: Treat programming as a core skill alongside Excel: automating repetitive work, handling large datasets, and building more robust models can distinguish an applicant. Ask questions with care and genuine interest. Practice curiosity, communication, and resilience as deliberately as the technical work.
technical skills: Economic scenario generator development, calibration, and validation; stochastic simulation; Bloomberg yield-curve updates; duration matching; the Black-Scholes model; Excel; coding for model tools; analysis of a long-term deposit portfolio.
soft skills: Curiosity, communication, resilience, and stress tolerance during reporting production, together with coordination with the economic capital and strategic asset allocation teams.
courses mentioned: Life contingency, financial mathematics, and derivatives, especially SOA exam content; risk theory; life contingencies; statistical and data analysis from the core curriculum; an introductory coding course; Society of Actuaries practical guides on economic scenario generators; professional actuarial exams; planned final-year electives on insurance topics.
tools and software: Excel, Bloomberg, Copilot, and the economic scenario generator.

job description: AIA Group is the largest publicly listed life and health insurance group in Asia. It offers life, accident, and health insurance, savings plans, retirement schemes, and wealth management, and says it aims to help people live healthier, longer, and better lives through many local business units. The student accepted an actuarial reporting internship in the Actuarial Solutions Architecture Department, on the Project Window team in the reporting subledger stream. The work supported IFRS 17 tools, communication with local business units, and an artificial-intelligence document platform.
job duties: Support enhancements to IFRS 17 reporting tools and communication with local business units; contribute to a custom script-tracing tool so those units can visualize important IFRS 17 calculations and read the data more easily; help improve the contractual service margin control report so mistakes are easier to find; test a retrieval-augmented generation platform that searches AIA SharePoint for IFRS 17 policy documents, give feedback on usability and functionality, and help tune settings, including capacity for more complicated reasoning and coding tasks; record practical difficulties users faced and recommend a team of information-technology staff, Group Office actuaries, and local business unit users to manage the platform; present the platform work and a summary of the six-month internship at an internal competition, as one of six interns chosen from more than twenty.
pre-internship preparation: In Year 1 the student attended internship presentations and began a resume and cover letters. In Year 2, applications went through the Internship/Job Online-Application System. Interview requests arrived the same day from AIA HK, AIA Group, Sun Life, Prudential, and Deloitte, by email, phone, or WhatsApp, and without much notice. Formats included phone, one-to-one Zoom, and group interviews. Before each one, the student read the company's mission, slogan, goals, and competitive advantages, and prepared answers on why that company, what they hoped to learn, life insurance, and financial mathematics. AIA's session lasted about an hour with five candidates and with human resources and actuaries from AIA HK and AIA Group. Questions included assumptions needed to launch a product, the most important characteristic of a financial model, and risks of an insurance company. Offers came from AIA HK, AIA Group, Prudential, and Deloitte. The AIA Group reporting internship was accepted after comparing company size and employee benefits.
what have I learned: The internship showed actuarial work meeting data architecture, IFRS 17, and digital tools, not only pricing and reserving. Financial mathematics, risk modelling, and insurance principles made the reporting requirements easier to follow, and prior statistical software and programming made Prophet, SAS SQL, and Excel usable. The most rewarding project was testing an artificial-intelligence retrieval platform and seeing later versions adopt suggestions. A finalist place in the internship competition, without a return offer, was still described as motivating. Adapting to SAS SQL and to the data flow between the reporting subledger and Prophet took tutorials and colleagues' help. Meetings with international units taught clearer questions and closer listening. Proposed control-report changes were adopted, and comments on user needs were taken into later design discussions.
what do I need to improve: The student felt underprepared when interview notices arrived suddenly, and group interviews were especially difficult. On the job, new programming languages were a major challenge: SAS SQL and the full data flow between the reporting subledger and Prophet models were not mastered at the start. Coordinating with international local business units also exposed communication barriers and unfamiliar regional requirements.
post-internship reflections: After this first actuarial internship the student is open to technical research and modeling and also to client-facing work such as insurance consulting or financial advice. Interests to explore include pet insurance product design, virtual-economy analysis in gaming, and prediction of an ACGI cultural-content lifecycle, alongside actuarial and statistical skills. Further study, possibly a master's degree in data science, finance, or applied statistics, is being considered, with more programming and artificial-intelligence study. Returning to AIA would be considered if a future role matched those abilities and aims. No return offer was received from this internship.
advice for future interns: Build technical range and be proactive. SQL, R, Python, or SAS is increasingly important, and so is curiosity and the ability to explain complicated models to non-technical people. Be ready to work carefully with large datasets, keep a sustainable pace, and stay open to study across disciplines because artificial intelligence and actuarial work are converging. Apply for internships and look at more than one area of insurance and finance.
technical skills: IFRS 17 reporting tools, Prophet, SAS SQL, Excel, script tracing, contractual service margin control reporting, and testing of a retrieval-augmented generation document platform.
soft skills: Clear and structured questions, active listening, and explaining solutions to technical and non-technical stakeholders. Curiosity and communication are also what the student advises future interns to develop.
courses mentioned: School study of insurance, annuities, financial mathematics, derivatives, and linear regression models; courses in financial mathematics, risk modelling, and insurance principles. A master's degree in data science, finance, or applied statistics is being considered. No course code is named.
tools and software: Prophet, SAS SQL, Excel, and AIA SharePoint. SQL, R, Python, and SAS are also named as languages future interns should know.

job description: Ernst & Young Advisory Limited is a Big Four professional services firm covering assurance, tax, consulting, and strategy. Its actuarial team, in Financial Services Consulting, advises insurers, pension funds, and financial institutions on pricing, reserving, capital modeling, regulatory compliance, and risk analytics. In the first half of 2025 the student interned on the life insurance consulting team. The projects were Hong Kong risk-based capital audits for a pan-Asian life and health group and a Hong Kong-based reinsurer, plus product rationalization for a leading life insurer.
job duties: For two Hong Kong risk-based capital audits, help with sample checks, unmodelled reserve checks, and incurred-but-not-reserved checks, and assist the actuarial summary review memorandum, including analysis of year-over-year balance-sheet changes; in Excel, project monthly policy counts, premium, commission, and renewal expense from mortality, morbidity, and lapse assumptions, discount the cash flows with Insurance Authority rates to a best-estimate liability, and compare that result month by month with client cash flows; investigate mismatches, including an extra face amount used as a ratio in a premium tab and a case where mortality and morbidity rates had been swapped, then attend the client meeting and document the product-based explanation in the memorandum; for product rationalization, read product specifications, identify features, and help colleagues group hundreds of products so the client could move them onto a newly developed system.
pre-internship preparation: Before applying, the student researched Ernst & Young, the difference between its General Insurance and Life teams, how it compares with other Big Four firms, and what its actuarial team does in the Hong Kong insurance market. Technical practice covered probability, financial mathematics, and insurance modeling, and Excel and Python were reviewed because data work was expected. The application and resume were submitted on the firm's website, followed by an individual interview with a manager. One question asked for the expected value of a six-sided die, answered as 3.5. Another asked whether one dollar is worth more today or next year, answered with time value of money from Year 1 actuarial courses. Behavioral questions covered teamwork, adaptability, and communication, illustrated with group projects and committee work in a university society.
what have I learned: The internship showed how audit work examines actuarial assumptions and how risk-based capital feeds into client decisions. Building Excel projection engines made the components of the Hong Kong regime more familiar, and reading many product specifications showed how direct insurers design benefits. A memorable check found that a small extra face amount was the ratio needed to match a sample cash flow. Another check found mortality and morbidity rates used on the wrong decrement; the client meeting established that product nature can require those rates to be switched, and that method was written into the summary memorandum. Asking colleagues to connect each task step with the firm's study notes gradually made the risk modules understandable. Both technical and interpersonal skills were described as sharper by the end.
what do I need to improve: Hong Kong risk-based capital templates and the way risk modules interact were hard to understand by reading the firm's learning materials alone. The gap closed only by interpreting each step during the work and by asking staff assistants and managers.
post-internship reflections: The student is more committed to becoming a professional actuary, with a clearer view of how capital frameworks affect insurer behavior. Discussions with seniors led to a revised plan to pass as many SOA exams as possible during university, because competition is increasing and the syllabus changes, and preparation has started. Returning to Ernst & Young after graduation would be seriously considered because of its regulatory consulting reputation, mentorship, and collaborative culture.
advice for future interns: Build an early understanding of regulatory frameworks and risk modeling. Familiarity with Insurance Authority guidelines and the ability to read financial statements are advantages, and Excel proficiency is essential. In interviews, show genuine curiosity and a willingness to learn. Approach the internship with an open mind and a wish to contribute, not only as technical training.
technical skills: Excel cash-flow projection, Hong Kong risk-based capital sample and reserve checking, including unmodelled reserves and incurred-but-not-reserved amounts, best-estimate liability discounting, mortality, morbidity, and lapse assumptions, balance-sheet movement analysis, and product-feature grouping. Python was reviewed before the internship for data work.
soft skills: Teamwork, adaptability, communication, explaining technical points to non-specialists, and interpersonal work with seniors, managers, and clients.
courses mentioned: Year 1 actuarial courses, including time value of money; probability and financial mathematics practiced for the interview; SOA exams.
tools and software: Excel and Python.

job description: AIA Group is a life insurance and financial services company that offers products such as life and health insurance. Actuaries forecast claims, design products, and set premiums using statistical models, with a direct effect on policyholders' financial security. After a department recruitment exercise, the internship was accepted at AIA and placed in the Actuarial Solutions Architecture Department at the Group Office, on the Asset Liability Management team rather than Financial Data Analytics Solution. The role supported local business units in developing Prophet models for needs such as statutory reporting and pricing, and covered models from business units including China, Singapore, Korea, and Thailand.
job duties: Watched lecture videos on the functions and applications of Prophet; read and observed models such as Par Dynamic Bonus, UL Dynamic Lapse, and Liability Linkage, including their formulas and VBA; compared variables and calculations across Excel files generated from master models; refreshed unit tests so data were updated for different business units and periods, including 2025 H1 HKRBC and 2024 H2 HK IFRS17; changed run parameters such as run numbers, run methods, and variable groups; continued unit-test refreshes and some administration tasks over the following months; completed a final assessment that refreshed a unit test on a previously unseen model, with help from Copilot.
pre-internship preparation: The opening was found through HKU-SASS Recruitment News for the Actuarial Internship Programme in the first half of 2025. Job preferences were ranked and submitted online. Interview invitations came from AIA Group, Transamerica Life, and Sun Life; the first two were attended, both as Zoom group interviews. Preparation was reading each company's background, specialisms, and leadership. The AIA interview, with one HR interviewer, two managers, and seven or eight candidates, asked for a self-introduction and motivation, an explanation of an insurance product, for which travel insurance was chosen, and an explanation of an actuary to friends or family. An AIA offer arrived about one hour later and was accepted. A Transamerica Life offer was also received and declined. Friends were consulted before the Asset Liability Management team was chosen.
what have I learned: The main technical gain was practical use of Prophet, Excel shortcuts, and VBA macros, which the report says cannot be learned from books. Python from the Actuarial Science programme helped because the models used VBA macros and Python in VS Code. Copilot was used to study macros and other code. The internship also gave a first view of how an insurance company operates, and showed that building or debugging models depends on programming.
what do I need to improve: Software and programming were a stated weakness, so macros and coding were studied with Copilot and online material rather than from existing skill. The report says programming was still not strong enough to develop a new model or debug an existing programme without self-study or artificial intelligence, and that higher programming skill was needed to be competitive.
post-internship reflections: The plan after the internship is to focus on SOA exams and to look for further internships, because many practical skills come only from the workplace. Modelling work made programming look essential. Rejoining AIA after graduation is of interest because of staff welfare, facilities, and a reported one to two work-from-home days a week for contracted staff. Other companies are also of interest, because the skills and experience would differ.
advice for future interns: Learn the field briefly before applying, and ask peers or teachers for insight before the interview or the job. Acquire basic software and programming skills, especially Excel, because seniors often assume those skills and may not teach them. Ask questions instead of staying quiet, and use a short half-year internship to learn.
technical skills: Prophet model runs and unit-test refreshing, Excel shortcuts, formulas, and functions, VBA macros, Python in VS Code, and use of Copilot to read macros and code.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: Python studied in the Actuarial Science programme is cited as useful on the models. Further SOA exams are planned.
tools and software: Prophet, Excel, VBA, Python, VS Code, and Copilot.

job description: Blue Cross is a general insurance company. General insurance was unfamiliar apart from travel insurance bought before trips. The actuarial team is small, so the internship covered both pricing and valuation rather than one specialty. Pricing work used monthly in-force and claim data to monitor products, compare experience with pricing assumptions, and support campaigns and the next-year strategic plan. Valuation work monitored group and individual medical business and summarized company expenses across departments.
job duties: Downloaded monthly in-force and claim files in Microsoft Access and extracted the needed fields with SQL into Excel; calculated IBNR, IBNP, loss ratio, earned ratio, and profit margin; compared loss ratios by age group and by channel, including online purchase and agents, and selected lower-loss combinations for sales campaigns; compared real premiums under the pricing loss ratio with real claims to see how assumptions differed from experience, and used that gap in the strategic plan of target sales, loss ratio, and operating profit by product and channel; each month monitored policy and member counts for group and individual medical policies, persistency, and solvency; on an ad hoc expense task, consolidated headcount, GWP, salary, and underwriting profit by department and calculated profit efficiency.
pre-internship preparation: Two interviews were required, one with AIA and one with Blue Cross. Preparation included a self-introduction script about a previous internship, research on general insurance after asking friends who had studied STAT4903, and a refresh of Excel, Python, and basic life-insurance knowledge from school and that earlier internship. The AIA interview was a group interview on self-introduction and challenges in school or a previous internship. The Blue Cross manager asked about life-insurance terms from that internship, including surrender value and lapse rate, and about wanting a second internship in a different actuarial field before graduation.
what have I learned: General-insurance pricing became clearer, including how loss ratios by age and channel guide campaigns and how actual claims can differ from the pricing assumption. A STAT3953 product-design project had given only a simple start. Valuation was new and was described as a view of the whole company rather than one product, covering persistency, solvency, and expenses such as salaries, benefits, IT, advertising, and rent. The difference between earned premium and written premium was explained by seniors. Communication improved so that questions and requested tasks could be stated clearly, and confidence with computer skills grew after comments on simpler Excel formulas. Seniors also discussed SOA exams and career paths.
what do I need to improve: There was a fear that simple questions would bother busy seniors. SQL and some Excel formulas that would make the work easier were also unfamiliar. The response was to search online first and ask only if the concept was still unclear, to study coding in free time, and to use colleagues' advice, past models, and comments on submitted work.
post-internship reflections: The six months made a continued path toward becoming an actuary feel almost certain. More SOA exams are planned before graduation. Rejoining Blue Cross is under consideration because general insurance still includes many lines that were not learned in depth, including travel, motor, house, employee compensation, and housewives insurance.
advice for future interns: Be a proactive learner and ask a mentor about anything that is not understood. Keep studying in free time, including VBA, Python, SQL, and Excel, because those skills are needed in the internship and later. Seniors will also give advice on work and career if asked.
technical skills: SQL extraction from Microsoft Access into Excel; calculation of IBNR, IBNP, loss ratio, earned ratio, profit margin, persistency, and solvency; expense consolidation and profit efficiency; simpler Excel formulas after senior review.
soft skills: Communication improved so that questions could be expressed clearly and seniors' instructions could be understood.
courses mentioned: STAT4903 was discussed with friends and had not been taken. STAT3953 was used through a group project on designing a product. SOA exams were discussed with seniors and further exams are planned.
tools and software: Microsoft Access, SQL, Excel, VBA, and Python.

company: AXA General Insurance Hong Kong Limited
job description: AXA General Insurance Hong Kong Limited is a general insurance company offering products such as auto, employee, and house insurance. The report describes general insurance as a smaller part of the Hong Kong market than life insurance, with different pricing, and as a field that has to adapt to a changing external environment. The six-month role was an actuarial internship in the pricing team of the Employee Benefits Department, with work also done for the data team. The role centered on reporting and data retrieval for other teams, colleagues, and brokers, and later on making that reporting process less manual.
job duties: Handled claim-data requests and loss-ratio reports, applying IBNR by incurred and payment period; discussed plan performance using loss ratios; used AS400 to pull data and Tableau to analyse claim and premium data; edited SAS code so raw data matched broker formats; imported data with Microsoft Access, used DBeaver to merge tables, and wrote Cisco SQL to retrieve, filter, sort, and group data; used Excel shortcuts, PivotTables, and Power Pivot, including a breakdown of one policy's weak claim experience for seniors; with a senior, streamlined data exchange, updated Excel files, and wrote VBA to automate report generation; prepared a Policy Year End Report involving reinsurers; completed simple pricing-template tasks.
pre-internship preparation: Before a phone interview, actuarial knowledge and concepts studied earlier were revised, the company background was researched, and the kind of employee the firm might need was considered. The interview was a long call focused on tasks and experience from a previous actuarial internship. Scenario questions covered cooperation and communication with colleagues, urgent situations, and work ethics.
what have I learned: Reporting practice became familiar, including why IBNR is applied to a loss ratio and how non-standard requests differ from template reports. Tools learned on the job included AS400, Tableau, SAS, Microsoft Access, DBeaver, Cisco SQL, Excel shortcuts, PivotTables, Power Pivot, and VBA. Time management, priority setting, and problem-solving improved. A Policy Year End Report introduced the role of reinsurers and how data are exchanged with them. Seasonality and the steps toward a quotation were learned, while advanced pricing methods were not.
what do I need to improve: Company systems, tools, and the many report formats were unfamiliar at the start and were hard to absorb quickly. Non-standard requests from colleagues, clients, or brokers could not be met with existing templates. Pricing knowledge stayed shallow because only simple template tasks were assigned and advanced pricing methods were not required.
post-internship reflections: The tasks differed from a previous internship because the company and team were different. The experience shifted the study plan toward practical work rather than theory, including coding beyond the Actuarial Science programme. Rejoining the company after graduation is under consideration because colleagues were willing to teach people who were new.
advice for future interns: Train fundamental coding and analytical skills before applying for a similar role. Do not be afraid to ask for help. Asking and listening are described as the fastest way to learn during an internship.
technical skills: IBNR and loss-ratio reporting, AS400 retrieval, Tableau analysis, SAS formatting, Microsoft Access, DBeaver, Cisco SQL, Excel PivotTables and Power Pivot, and VBA automation of report generation.
soft skills: Communication and presentation skills improved in STAT3953 were used in discussion with colleagues. Time management, arranging priorities, and problem-solving are also described as improved.
courses mentioned: STAT3953 is named as the source of communication and presentation skills used in discussions. Concepts from the Actuarial Science programme were applied to the tasks, and further coding outside that programme is planned.
tools and software: AS400, Tableau, SAS, Microsoft Access, DBeaver, Cisco SQL, Excel, PivotTable, Power Pivot, and VBA.

job description: The internship lasted about 6.5 months at Manulife in the Regional Actuarial Service Department, under the Hong Kong and Philippines Valuation Shared Service Centre, with work assigned across two teams. Valuation had been expected to be dull and repetitive. Month-end and quarter-end production was repetitive, but model changes required analyzing a problem and translating a real situation into a model. The role covered local production, user acceptance testing, model change management, model promotion, spot-checking, and ad hoc tasks, including Hong Kong IFRS17 reporting and Macau local production.
job duties: Handled month-end and quarter-end local production for the Philippines and Hong Kong; carried out user acceptance testing, model change management, model promotion, spot-checking, and ad hoc tasks; assisted a Contract Boundary model change and learned how moving contractual service margin measurement from the premium allocation approach to the general measurement model can release CSM; spot-checked a basis change for a manager in another country's office, covering contract boundary, lapse studies, and premium adjustments in AXIS, and completed the checks required by auditors; at the last quarter-end, when a model change filtered Macau and Hong Kong policies and made BD1 inconsistent with BD-5 on reserves, dropped policies, and system errors, proposed a change to the checking template, updated the SQL used for extraction, and delivered the revised process to the business units on time.
pre-internship preparation: In second year, a corporate mentorship programme led to monthly lunches with a senior director at Manulife. Those meetings covered academic life, career paths, hobbies, and cultural differences between Hong Kong and Indonesia, and later the mentor referred the application to HR. There was one interview with a director. Preparation included research on the company's reputation, analysis of the job description against personal skills, review of relevant course materials, and practice of behavioural questions. The interview focused on personality, social problem-solving, and relevant strengths.
what have I learned: Excel VBA, SQL, and AXIS were new. VBA was used for data validation and processing, SQL for storage and extraction, and AXIS for modelling. Life contingency knowledge, including life and annuity models, benefit premiums, and reserves, helped interpret automated templates. Communication, time management, and balancing two teams improved. A difficult spot-check taught a different communication approach: propose options instead of asking for detailed instructions. Contract boundary, lapse studies, and modelling of premium adjustments were learned while completing auditor checks.
what do I need to improve: In the first two months, deadlines for month-end production for the Philippines and Hong Kong were missed or difficult to meet until the workflow was familiar. A later spot-check was hard because a manager in another office had an unfamiliar communication style, and asking for detailed instructions did not match what he expected.
post-internship reflections: Before the internship, actuarial work had been compared unfavorably with visual communication design, and a career as an actuary was uncertain. Coffee chats near the end, especially about valuation, shifted that view. The plan is to complete SOA exams P, FM, and FAM by graduation and to obtain ASA within the first three years of work. A longer aim is roles that combine actuarial work with design through data visualization and presentation. Returning to Manulife is of interest, while other employers that fit that aim remain open.
advice for future interns: In interviews, be yourself and show why you fit the role. During the internship, take each task with curiosity and understand its purpose and business contribution rather than only meeting deadlines. Build communication, collaboration, and adaptability, which matter in regional offices, through student organizations, volunteering, or leadership roles. Seek feedback and keep learning because the field changes.
technical skills: Excel VBA for data validation and processing, SQL for extraction, AXIS modelling, contract boundary and contractual service margin under the premium allocation approach and the general measurement model, lapse studies, premium adjustments, and user acceptance testing.
soft skills: Effective communication, time management, prioritization across two teams, collaboration, and adapting communication style to different senior colleagues.
courses mentioned: The Life Contingency course is named as preparation for interpreting life insurance and annuity models, benefit premiums, and reserves. Planned exams are SOA P, FM, and FAM, with ASA as a credential goal.
tools and software: Excel VBA, SQL, and AXIS.

job description: Manulife International Limited offers individual financial products and group life and health quotations to companies, and the report says its health business has grown through Voluntary Health Insurance Scheme products and critical illness products. The 6.5-month role was an actuarial internship in the Pricing Team, focused on product development and pricing. Two main projects were post-launch system checking for critical illness products and pre-launch support for new savings products. Daily work also included special quotations, and a separate intern project looked at artificial intelligence in financial risk management for the Asia segment.
job duties: Wrote test scopes and plans for product features; sent plans to IT for system runs and discussed modifications with the pricing team; cross-checked IT results against internal calculations and built checking tools; completed post-launch checking for Income Guard Critical Illness Protector and Income Shield Critical Illness Protector, including an early-stage claim at 20 percent of the notional amount followed by a major illness; supported pre-launch work for Prestige Achiever and Gensis Centurion, including policy rates and system checks used for HKRBC and IFRS17; prepared special quotations for extra premium cuts, reinstatements, death benefits, and policy values; built an Excel VBA tool that cut month-on-month asset-allocation comparisons for Asia business units from about two hours to under ten minutes.
pre-internship preparation: There was no job interview before the internship started. Preparation was a company visit to Manulife organized for the Statistics and Actuarial Science Society, including logistics with campus recruitment staff, who said offers might go to students who showed interest in actuarial work. Two 15-minute networking sessions paired a small group with a Pricing Team director and a Regional Actuarial Service director, and one of them later became the supervisor. An interview was arranged only near the end of the internship and included a question on the components of a reserve calculation.
what have I learned: The projects gave exposure to product features, comparisons with similar products, and the checks required before launch, including policy rates and system calculations so that HKRBC and IFRS17 cash flows use the right data. Product manuals were used to resolve claim rules, including that a major critical illness benefit is reduced by earlier claims. Clear communication with seniors was harder than expected when calculations and errors needed investigation. Excel and VBA improved through an AI-assisted tool that shortened asset-allocation comparisons for the Asia financial risk management team.
what do I need to improve: Articulating complex findings to senior colleagues was more difficult than expected. Holding several tasks at once was also difficult. One memorable case combined a critical-illness user acceptance test that needed sign-off on the day the cases arrived with several urgent special quotations due the same day, which exposed a need to organize time and set priorities before starting.
post-internship reflections: Pricing work is described as interesting because it can move across areas such as quarter campaign offers, forecasting, and dividend scale changes. The hope is to continue a career in product pricing and, in parallel, to take further courses and study on product pricing, including regulator changes that affect how a product is priced.
advice for future interns: Join company visits when they are offered, and use them to learn what staff actually do and to build connections. Those connections may later give advice on career paths or referrals for jobs and internships, and keeping them is described as a way to understand how the actuarial industry is developing.
technical skills: Product test planning, cross-checking system results, building checking tools, special quotations, Excel, VBA, and AI-assisted automation of month-on-month asset-allocation comparisons.
soft skills: Clear communication with senior colleagues, collaboration with IT and the pricing team, multitasking, time management, flexibility, and resilience under same-day deadlines.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Excel, VBA, and AI tools used to write VBA.

job description: SunLife (Hong Kong) Limited is described as a leading international financial services organization that provides wealth, insurance, and health solutions to individual and institutional clients. The internship, from July to December 2025, sat under the group reporting team and assisted two sub-teams. Profitability management oversees value of new business and monitors items such as new business contractual service margin. Planning management sets operational and strategic plans and looks after expense categories. The role prepared model output and business-plan files so that pricing and production results could be used for planning.
job duties: Ran a time value of options and guarantees tool through Coherent Spark and checked the results; organized policy listings and converted year-to-date data into monthly data; set up AXIS pricing models so cash flows included expense categories missing from the original model, loaded results into a workbook by pay term, and changed the file so pay terms could be typed instead of copied; split acquisition and maintenance expenses in AXIS and ran expense studies; recorded adjustments in traditional, non-traditional, and amount-on-deposit projection models, sent a fix list to production, and wrote a run manual; generated business-plan files in an Excel BP tool after checking asset-share, portfolio, and new-business inputs; reran sensitivities for client incentives, immediate annuity or indexed universal life, and extra agency or broker sales; updated the HKD-CAD rate and recorded equity indexes and treasury rates on Bloomberg.
pre-internship preparation: The department Corporate Mentorship Program led to regular coffee chats with a mentor at SunLife, a look at that mentor's past CV, and a briefing on technical skills and qualities employers treat as important. There was one virtual interview with the line manager. Preparation included a review of probability and actuarial concepts from coursework and research on products that are particular to SunLife. The interview asked for a brief introduction, questions based on the CV, and basic probability and insurance questions, including how a life insurance policy works.
what have I learned: Excel functions and shortcuts made large datasets easier to handle. AXIS, which had no prior background and was used for a large share of the work, became familiar enough to set up model runs and check outputs, after a new-joiner pack and questions to the team. The internship also showed differences between industry cash-flow, expense, and planning work and what had been learned in class, including value of new business, contractual service margin, and business-plan sensitivities.
what do I need to improve: AXIS was the main difficulty. Nearly 40 percent of the job used it, and at first a simple model run was hard and the reason for each step was unclear. The welcome-pack documentation was studied and questions were asked before model runs became manageable.
post-internship reflections: The career goal is to become an FSA within three years after graduation and to work as an actuary in a valuation team. The internship clarified what actuaries do day to day. SOA exams are the study plan, with preliminary exams to be finished before graduation. Rejoining SunLife Hong Kong is of strong interest because of the supportive atmosphere and rotation programmes across insurance and financial work.
advice for future interns: Ask senior students or people with experience for a current picture of the actuarial sector, and read industry news such as IFRS17 and risk-based capital. Strengthen technical skills and academic foundations before applying, even if an internship interview stays basic. During the internship, try to fix an error before going to a supervisor, and ask once it is clear the problem cannot be solved alone.
technical skills: Excel functions and shortcuts, AXIS model setup and output checks, Coherent Spark runs from a time value of options and guarantees tool, business-plan file generation and sensitivity cases, and Bloomberg updates of exchange rates, equity indexes, and treasury rates.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: Probability and actuarial concepts from coursework were reviewed before the interview, with no course code given. Planned credentials are SOA preliminary exams and FSA. IFRS17 and risk-based capital are named as industry topics to follow.
tools and software: Coherent Spark, TVOG tool, AXIS, Excel, BP tool, and Bloomberg Terminal.

job description: From June to December 2025 the internship was in the capital management team at AIA International Limited, described as the AIA local office in the Wan Chai district. The team was established in late 2024 with people from Hong Kong risk-based capital reporting and from asset and liability management. Its goal is to monitor and optimize the capital position of the Hong Kong and Macau offices, including remittances and capital planning. The actuarial intern ran and optimized Prophet and Excel models for sensitivity risk analysis that was passed to a manager, and tried to simplify reporting and data collection through coding.
job duties: Ran and optimized Prophet and Excel models for sensitivity risk analysis and submitted the results to the manager for further analysis and decisions; tried to simplify reporting and data collection through coding so the team had better support; applied classroom material such as a best-estimate liability model in regression analysis; learned manual modelling techniques with help from a mentor, usually a senior analyst or assistant manager, and from other teammates; for the half-year intern competition, refined a key project with the supervisor, built PowerPoint slides, rehearsed through mock presentations, and presented to senior managers after being selected as one of six finalists from more than 30 interns.
pre-internship preparation: The opportunity came through the SAAS internship portal. The process was a phone call, a Zoom interview, and an offer, with only about half a day to one day between the invitation and the interview. A one- to two-minute self-introduction was written and practiced. Behavioural and skills answers were prepared from technical material learned in class and from extracurricular activities, including how challenges in past internships were handled. The offer letter from AIA HR arrived in December 2024. Before the first day, HR email was checked for personal information, onboarding documents, and visa matters, and the administrative contact for day one was obtained.
what have I learned: Daily work applied actuarial study to capital monitoring for the Hong Kong and Macau offices, including Prophet and Excel sensitivity analysis and a best-estimate liability idea from regression analysis. A mentor arrangement made onboarding and manual modelling faster. The competition showed that project content can be missed if it is not presented calmly, because the judges had only about 10 to 15 minutes.
what do I need to improve: Programming and computer-language skills were not proficient enough. In the final presentation the delivery broke down: the voice trembled, lines were stumbled over, and the fluent rehearsal was lost, so the intern was not one of the two winners. The report treats hesitation in a short presentation as a reason judges might doubt composure under pressure.
post-internship reflections: After the competition, the stated goals are a more resilient mindset, more chances to speak in public, and rehearsal that includes difficult questions and different audience reactions, with the focus on stating key points rather than seeking immediate approval. Further study is planned in Prophet and R Studio to address the programming gap. The report does not say whether a return to AIA is intended.
advice for future interns: Start interview preparation as soon as an application is sent, because the gap before a Zoom interview can be only half a day to one day. Prepare a one- to two-minute self-introduction and practice it. Also prepare common behavioural questions, such as how challenges in past internships were handled, using technical knowledge from university and soft skills from extracurricular activities.
technical skills: Prophet and Excel model runs, sensitivity risk analysis, coding to simplify reporting and data collection, best-estimate liability modelling linked to regression analysis, and PowerPoint for a project presentation.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Prophet, Excel, and PowerPoint.

job description: FWD is a life insurance company. A mentorship match led to a half-year internship in the pricing team of the product department, after the interview answer that product work was more interesting than repetitive quarterly reporting. The tasks were tied directly to products.
