They covered monthly monitoring of premium payment on flexible-payment products, customized quotations, death and critical illness claim quotations, and user acceptance testing so that pricing spreadsheets, the company system, and IT illustrations stayed consistent before launches and feature changes.
job duties: Each month, monitored premium persistency on flexible-payment products and explained rates that were not 100 percent, including pay-mode changes, extra premiums, and a reduced sum insured found in the system, statements, and letters; prepared special quotations for reduced sum insured, premium holiday, withdrawals, booster payments, and regular contribution, using templates such as Maxfocus, i Ulife, Wealth ICON, and Basic Plus, and back-solved amounts so a policy could last to pay-to-endow; downloaded history with SQL for death and critical illness claim quotations, checking dividends, coupons, and automatic premium loans, and adding fund units and prices when investment-linked; spent about half the internship on user acceptance testing, including medical renewal with no-claim discount and loading, and Imperial Fortune, an S&P 500-linked universal life product, covering illustration bases, quit-smoking cost-of-insurance transitions, and HKIA commission checks; wrote notes and taught the next interns.
pre-internship preparation: In first year, a mentorship match was with FWD. The mentor described the company structure and team responsibilities and later asked HR to arrange an interview, which led to the offer. Lecture notes were reviewed on financial mathematics, including nominal and effective interest, present values, and annuities, and on probability, including Bayes theorem, conditional probability, and conditional expectation and variance. Industry reading covered IFRS17, universal life, endowment, critical illness, and medical products, and terms such as grace period, automatic premium loan, lapse year, and cash value. The interview asked for a self-introduction, how company reserves are calculated, what investments are made with premiums, and which team was of interest. The reserve answer, present value of premium minus present value of death benefit, was given without life contingencies and is described as not correct. Government bonds and corporate bonds were the investment answer. The product team was requested.
what have I learned: Pricing work covered how flexible-payment persistency can be distorted by mode changes and extra premiums, how special quotations use product-specific templates, and how claim amounts depend on dividends, coupons, loans, and investment funds. User acceptance testing showed how pricing Excel, the company system, and IT illustrations are checked together, including medical repricing and a quit-smoking cost-of-insurance transition. Teaching the next interns consolidated those tasks. Reporting and reinsurance, including the detail of IFRS17, were not part of the experience.
what do I need to improve: The interview answer on reserves was incorrect because the life contingency course had not yet been taken. On the job, unusual persistency percentages were hard to trace, especially a case that combined a pay-mode change with a reduced sum insured. The report also says knowledge of the reporting world and the reinsurance world is still blank, including the details of IFRS17.
post-internship reflections: Another internship, in a valuation team or a reinsurance team, is the aim, in order to learn other parts of the industry, including IFRS17 and other actuarial programmes and software. SOA exams will continue, and UEC credit from courses is part of the plan. A return to the FWD pricing team would be accepted because the colleagues and the working atmosphere were good.

job description: FWD Life Insurance Company (Bermuda) Limited is a life insurer operating in Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, Thailand, and Vietnam. The report says it was founded in 2013, grew quickly with the help of acquisitions, and has a vision of changing how people think about insurance. The internship ran from June 2025 to January 2026. The work was actual-to-expected analysis of mortality and morbidity assumptions, user acceptance testing when the valuation team updated models for new products, revised assumptions, or regulatory changes, and construction of product illustration files in Excel.
job duties: Retrieved claims data, entered it in Excel, and computed actual-to-projected claim ratios for regular tests of mortality and morbidity assumptions; designed and implemented test cases when models were updated, checked that outputs matched expected results, and reported anomalies; learned INDEX-MATCH, XLOOKUP, and SUMIFS, and wrote a VBA macro in an illustration file for a new product so a manual step was no longer needed; debugged a complex IF statement that gave different results by premium-payment mode and traced the error to a wrong relative reference; built a new illustration from scratch for a product with annual reversionary bonuses, a terminal bonus based on investment performance, and new premium rates, using OFFSET and CHOOSE after studying three existing illustration files, and fixed a bonus that had been linked to the premium input cell by mistake.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started about two weeks before a 30-minute interview with a manager in the HR team. Course materials from STAT2902 and STAT3901 were studied, including reserve calculation, life contingencies, interest, survival models, and present values. FWD annual reports and recent media announcements were read, including regional expansion such as Cambodia. Situational answers were prepared on teamwork, dealing with pressure, and learning from failure. The hardest question was the most challenging episode in a previous wealth-management internship at AIA, which was preparing a client portfolio and recommending a product after the client also brought price quotes from other companies.
what have I learned: Excel moved to intermediate and advanced use, including lookup and conditional sum functions, pivot-style summary needs, and a VBA macro that saved time on an illustration. Building a file from scratch, rather than copying a template, showed how premium inputs, benefit schedules, and discounting fit together. Debugging a relative reference and a wrong bonus link made independent problem-solving feel more reliable. The earlier view of actuarial work as only technical changed: the report describes judgment, business context, and behaviour as part of the job, and testing as an active check that a model behaves as expected.
what do I need to improve: The greatest difficulty was creating an illustration for a new product whose bonus structure and premium rates meant a template could not be reused. Functions such as OFFSET and CHOOSE were unfamiliar. One error came from accidentally connecting the bonus to the premium input cell, and another IF formula failed because of a wrong relative reference. Both were found by comparing files and testing formulas before asking a manager.
post-internship reflections: The aim is now to qualify as an actuary working in life insurance. Electives planned next are SDST3951, Topics on Advanced Actuarial Modelling, and SDST3956, Advanced Life Contingencies, and a Finance minor is under consideration for investment management and derivative pricing. SOA Exam SRM was enrolled for September, Exam PA is planned later in the year, and at least four SOA exams are hoped for before graduation. Rejoining FWD after graduation is under consideration because of the culture and continued contact with a mentor.
advice for future interns: Train Excel before applying, including INDEX-MATCH, XLOOKUP, pivot tables, and simple VBA, so formulas can be used in the first week. Also question why a calculation is performed, which business decision it informs, and how it might be improved, rather than treating the job as only technical.
technical skills: Actual-to-expected analysis of mortality and morbidity, user acceptance testing of model updates, Excel functions including INDEX-MATCH, XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, OFFSET, and CHOOSE, VBA macros, and construction and debugging of product illustration files.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: STAT2902 and STAT3901 were studied before the interview. Planned courses are SDST3951 and SDST3956, with a Finance minor under consideration. Professional exams named are SOA Exam SRM and Exam PA.
tools and software: Excel and VBA.

job description: The internship, from June to December 2025, was in the Prudential group Asset Liability Management team, which supports local business units. The team maintains and develops an economic scenario generator and produces economic scenario sets split into real world and risk neutral. Real-world scenarios are used mainly to evaluate returns on assets held, and risk-neutral scenarios are used for pricing. As a real-world intern, the focus was simulations of interest rates and asset returns, plus tools the team was moving from Excel VBA to Python so that generator run time would be shorter.
job duties: Transformed VBA into Python and ran user acceptance testing so new tools could return to production; debugged generator runs that failed from wrong inputs or bugs; each half year, took bond-portfolio data request forms from local offices and downloaded Bloomberg data for interest-rate estimation; updated the real-world Fixed Income Return Tool Summary of Assumptions from 2025 half year to 2025 year end for every currency; checked results for abnormal returns, including an interest-rate minus 1 percent case against the base, and looked for false positives; with other interns, checked more than 70 virtual desktops after a scheduler failed because of Excel updates; handed concepts and tricks to the next intern group.
pre-internship preparation: The offer came at a career fair organized by the department, which had first been treated as a scouting visit rather than a planned interview. Preparation was mainly a self-introduction on what had been learned at university and how it could be applied at work, plus communication practice such as eye contact and sitting, with time to relax in Chi Wah Learning Commons before the fair opened. The recruiter wanted interns with Python and Excel VBA for tool development. COMP1117 and STAT1018 were used as examples of Python and basic Excel, although VBA had not been used often.
what have I learned: Economic scenario generator work had not been taught in university, but the real-world flow became familiar: half-year data requests, Bloomberg interest-rate inputs, tool runs, and checks against a base scenario. Excel VBA and Python were used while the team tried to shorten run time, and user acceptance testing and debugging were part of putting tools back into production. Automatic warnings were not treated as final because false positives can appear. Working with other interns and handing over to the next group improved interpersonal skills. The G2++ distribution and the return formula were not learned in depth.
what do I need to improve: A stated disappointment is that there was not enough time to go beyond the surface of the tools. Formulas such as the underlying G2++ model and the return formula were not fully investigated. The report says the next internship needs to leave room to understand the methodology, not only to finish the assigned tasks. At the start, unfamiliarity with the economic scenario generator and a worry about working independently are also named.
post-internship reflections: The internship was not focused on traditional actuarial work, but it still built data-checking skills and a clearer view of the job market. Interpersonal skills improved through daily work and handover with other interns. The stated change for the next internship is to be more deliberate about the methods behind the tools, including distributions such as G2++, rather than only completing runs.
advice for future interns: NA
technical skills: Excel VBA, translation of VBA tools into Python, economic scenario generator runs, Bloomberg data for interest rates, user acceptance testing, debugging of failed runs, and checking of scenario results including false positives.
soft skills: Interpersonal skills, communication while handing work to the next intern group, and teamwork with other interns on shared checks and daily tasks.
courses mentioned: COMP1117 and STAT1018 are named as courses in which Python and basic Excel were used and then cited in the career-fair interview.
tools and software: Excel VBA, Python, Bloomberg, and VDI.

job description: Sun Life Hong Kong Limited operates in insurance and financial services. Its business includes life insurance, health insurance, and wealth-management solutions aimed at risk management, retirement planning, and financial goals for clients in Hong Kong. From 2 July 2025 to 31 December 2025 the role was an actuarial internship in the Assets and Liabilities Management department. The report describes that department as matching asset and liability cash flows and managing risks such as interest rates and exchange rates, with links to pricing, reserves, capital, and solvency. The intern's own work was running economic scenario generator programmes, checking outputs, and occasional ad hoc tasks.
job duties: Ran economic scenario generator programmes and verified the outputs; used Excel models to double-check that figures were accurate; completed occasional ad hoc tasks; in mid-July calculated figures in the statement of financial position with Excel functions, using the statement format from ACCT1101 so the task could be finished more efficiently; at the beginning of July calculated financial figures that had been studied in STAT2902 and identified an error in the calculations independently; extracted data from Bloomberg; when an exchange-rate input error forced every earlier economic scenario generator output to be rerun, worked with a colleague for one day until 3:00 a.m. and met the deadline.
pre-internship preparation: A senior advised preparing a self-introduction and Society of Actuaries Exam FM knowledge, because those might be asked. A 30-second to one-minute introduction on education and personal interests was written, and key concepts for Exam P and Exam FM were reviewed. IFRS17 and the features of various insurance products were researched online and later came up in interviews. Four Zoom interviews with three companies ran between November 2024 and January 2025, and offers came from two companies. Questions covered actuarial science, finance, and economics. The interviewer for the asset and liability management offer asked whether every risk in an insurance product can be diversified or eliminated. The answer was no: some risk can be transferred by reinsurance, while risks linked to age, gender, or health cannot be removed.
what have I learned: Interpersonal communication improved through day-to-day contact with colleagues. Technical skills that had not been taught in lectures included extracting data from Bloomberg and using Excel shortcuts across many workbooks. ACCT1101 made the format of a statement of financial position familiar, and STAT2902 helped both the calculation of financial figures and the independent spotting of an error. Rerunning a full set of economic scenario generator outputs in one day showed what a tight deadline and a heavy workload feel like. New financial abbreviations were memorized so that repeated searches took less time.
what do I need to improve: Excel shortcut knowledge was too thin for work that regularly used many workbooks, so the economic scenario generator tasks were inefficient at first. Shortcuts were then self-taught online, with colleagues pointing out which ones mattered most. Unfamiliar abbreviations of financial terms were a second gap: each new abbreviation had to be looked up online until it was memorized.
post-internship reflections: The career goal remains to become an actuary, to pursue Fellowship of the Society of Actuaries, and to keep working in insurance. Associate of the Society of Actuaries is aimed for within two years after graduation. Exam FAM and Exam SRM are planned for 2026 because they are requirements for that associate credential and are the current priority. Rejoining Sun Life after graduation is described as a definite interest, partly because about half of the internship could be worked from home.
advice for future interns: Learn as many Excel shortcuts as possible before the internship starts, because Excel is unavoidable and shortcuts change efficiency. Also review the content of university courses already taken, so tasks are easier to understand and finish. Being prepared is described as a way to show professionalism and leave a better impression on supervisors and colleagues.
technical skills: Economic scenario generator runs and output verification, Excel models and shortcuts, Bloomberg data extraction, and calculation of statement-of-financial-position and other financial figures.
soft skills: Interpersonal communication with colleagues, and working under pressure on a same-day rerun with a large workload.
courses mentioned: SOA Exam P and Exam FM were reviewed before interviews. Exam FAM and Exam SRM are planned for 2026, with ASA and FSA as credential goals. IFRS17 was researched before the interviews. ACCT1101 and STAT2902 were used on the job.
tools and software: Excel and Bloomberg.

job description: Prudential Hong Kong Limited hired the intern for the IFRS17 Actuarial Solution Team from July 2025 to January 2026, about six and a half months. The central monthly deliverable was model point file generation. Those files were a core team output that other teams across the company used for reserves calculation, financial reporting, and experience analysis. The role also developed Python scripts to automate manual steps and carried out user acceptance testing on tools intended to improve the model point file process.
job duties: Produced model point files at each month-end, learning the procedure and rationale in the first month and then taking a large share with help from colleagues, using Microsoft Excel, Access, Python, DCS, and Brioquery; developed and enhanced Python code for specific projects so automation reduced manual workload, clarified requirements with teammates, and explained the scripts in non-technical terms; completed two user acceptance tests of tools for the model point file process by attending developer demonstrations, running the new tools, comparing and investigating unexpected discrepancies in data and tables, and reporting to the manager, including work with the tool developer and other testers; in the last two weeks, handed the routine process to a new intern with step-by-step demonstrations of model point file generation and notes on tricky steps.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation began in first year through the Prudential Corporate Mentorship Program. Monthly meetings with a mentor at Prudential Services Limited covered the actuarial profession, industry trends, career pathways, that team's responsibilities, actuarial examinations, and job interviews. At the start of second year, on the mentor's recommendation, the SAAS career fair was used to talk with actuarial employers about the working environment and the skills they value. The internship offer from Prudential Hong Kong Limited, one of the companies at the fair, came with no interview.
what have I learned: Model point file production, Python automation, and user acceptance testing built technical proficiency and a habit of investigating discrepancies. Weekly face-to-face meetings showed how the team exchanges ideas and negotiates solutions. Explaining scripts and aligning with a tool developer and other testers practiced professional communication and simplification of jargon. A two-week handover of model point file generation was the main leadership experience. Periods with user acceptance testing and Python development due together taught prioritization after deadlines were discussed with colleagues.
what do I need to improve: Balancing several tasks at once was a stated difficulty. In some periods, user acceptance testing and Python development both had tight deadlines. The response was to ask colleagues for help or to adjust deadlines. The report treats that episode as a gap in prioritizing tasks and managing time until the work still met the team's expectations.
post-internship reflections: The internship confirmed a plan to work in the actuarial field after graduation. More SOA exams are planned before graduation, both as a hiring credential and because many exam concepts matched processes seen at work. Rejoining Prudential Hong Kong Limited is a strong interest because the environment was supportive and the working arrangements were flexible.
advice for future interns: For a similar position, improve Microsoft Excel and Python before the internship. Those two applications were used most of the time, and learning them earlier helps a new intern adapt faster. The report groups this preparation with soft skills.
technical skills: Month-end model point file generation, Microsoft Excel, Access, Python scripting for automation, DCS, Brioquery, and user acceptance testing of new tools, including investigation of data and table discrepancies.
soft skills: Professional and effective communication, collaboration in weekly meetings and with other stakeholders, leadership during a handover to a new intern, and time management when several deadlines overlapped.
courses mentioned: SOA exams are named as exams to take before graduation. Python is described as programming knowledge from university, with no course code given.
tools and software: Microsoft Excel, Access, Python, DCS, and Brioquery.

job description: Prudential HK Limited, a subsidiary of Prudential plc, is an insurer established in Hong Kong in 1964. The report names teams such as IFRS 17, pricing, and risk-based capital, and business that includes pension and medical insurance. There was no prior actuarial work experience. The internship was in the reinsurance team rather than the valuation team that had been requested. That team analyzes data involving the insurer, clients, and reinsurers, and concentrates on critical illness products because benefits for conditions such as heart attack, stroke, and cancer are large. The role prepared administration files and predictive figures for other teams and for reinsurers.
job duties: Built monthly, quarterly, and yearly files for each product, including the calculations needed before processed data were reported to other teams and to reinsurers, and uploaded those files to the system website and to reinsurer folders; used Prophet to find and calculate variables such as predicted loss ratio, and in one case adjusted rates to see how that ratio changed under different scenarios; compared more than 15 critical illness products and wrote conclusions on disease coverage, additional benefits, and target customers, which a supervisor used to analyze why reinsurer premium-rate increases differed and which product features drove the gaps; created an AI agent to search reinsurance treaties for specific information; checked the credit ratings of reinsurance companies.
pre-internship preparation: There was no earlier actuarial work experience. The Actuarial Mentoring Program of the HKU Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science included Prudential HK Limited. The mentor covered what an actuary does day to day, changes in the industry, and useful Excel formulas and shortcuts. The internship was sought by messaging the Prudential HR manager met in that programme, not through the department website. The manager asked why the company was of interest and which team was preferred. The answer cited the firm's size and role in the industry, a visit to the office during mentoring, and a preference for valuation because it analyzes a company's financial position. The assignment was the reinsurance team.
what have I learned: The work applied Excel, Python, Access, and Prophet, and used present value, mortality rates, and financial ratios from statistics, accounting, and economics courses when comparing products and calculating figures. Professional communication was new: report progress even if a task is not finished, and keep a polite tone, including greetings and thanks, in Teams or Outlook. The critical illness comparison was used by a supervisor in further analysis, reports, and meeting material. Asking questions and keeping notes, rather than relying on colleagues each time, reduced mistakes after a difficult first month.
what do I need to improve: The first month was the hardest period. Reinsurance was unfamiliar, colleagues were not yet close, and the software was not proficient, so even uncomplicated tasks felt difficult. There was hesitation to ask for help, and mistakes were common. Accuracy improved after questions were asked actively and notes were applied on the next task instead of asking the same thing again.
post-internship reflections: Actuarial work seemed more dynamic than expected, because an actuary has to keep watching the market, including US interest rates and artificial intelligence, and AI tools may change how the work is done. The aim is to become an actuary, follow insurance and AI news, and pass more SOA exams, including UEC credit in HKU statistics courses, before work becomes busier after graduation. An offer to rejoin Prudential HK Limited at graduation would be accepted.
advice for future interns: For an internship in a reinsurance team, compare the details of different insurance products. Features such as disease coverage, interest-linked savings, and family protection can change premiums and how the company values the products. Mistakes are common for interns. Ask about anything that is not understood, and take on tasks actively in order to learn more.
technical skills: Excel, Python, Access, and Prophet, including predicted loss ratio and scenario changes; present value and mortality calculations; comparison of critical illness product features; an AI agent used to search reinsurance treaties; and checks of reinsurers' credit ratings.
soft skills: Professional communication with colleagues, including regular progress reporting and a polite tone in Teams and Outlook, and asking questions instead of working in isolation.
courses mentioned: Accounting and economics courses are credited for ratios used to judge financial health. Statistics courses are credited for present value and mortality. A programming course is credited for Python. The Actuarial Science programme is credited overall. Further SOA exams and UEC credit in HKU statistics courses are planned. No course code is given.
tools and software: Excel, Python, Access, Prophet, Teams, Outlook, and an AI agent.

job description: Manulife is a leading Canada-based insurance group. At the Hong Kong Regional Office, the business covers markets including Hong Kong, Malaysia, Vietnam, Singapore, and Indonesia, and offers insurance to customers of different ages and conditions. The student held a six-and-a-half-month full-time actuarial internship, from 2 July 2025 to 16 January 2026, in the Regional Actuarial Services department's Valuation Shared Services Center, supporting Malaysia and Vietnam. The role assisted quarterly valuation production and user acceptance testing so that model updates, assumption changes, and financial reporting stayed consistent.
job duties: Assisted quarterly production and user acceptance testing for Malaysia and Vietnam; extracted data with SQL and ran models in AXIS and Excel macros to calculate best-estimate reserves and liabilities; updated sensitivity validation files with the latest data and economic assumptions, including interest-rate shocks such as RF +50bps, lapse rates, volatility, and other scenarios; checked whether impacts matched the prior quarter in scale and sign, verified reasonableness, identified outliers, and explained differences; supported Model Change Management promotion of AXIS model changes, Gainwave Python runs that automate basis-change impacts, and Life Insurance Capital Adequacy Test work; reported expected and unexpected errors and impacts in sensitivity analyses and reserve summaries so managers could use the findings in later valuation steps.
pre-internship preparation: The application started from an interest in Manulife as a major Asian insurer and a search for a full-time actuarial internship. Preparation included company research, annual reports, and checking actuarial intern openings on the website. A university career fair visit to the Manulife booth led to a recommendation for a later firm visit. Before the visit to the Kwun Tong office, the student reviewed the company background again and prepared questions on day-to-day work, challenges, and skills valued in interns. Senior actuaries and managers discussed operations during the visit. HR then called with an offer for the six-and-a-half-month role, which was accepted.
what have I learned: The internship built a practical view of the end-to-end valuation process under IFRS 17 and gave cross-market exposure through Malaysia and Vietnam. Life contingencies and financial mathematics helped with cash-flow components and discounting, and probability and statistics helped with reasonableness checks. SQL and Excel improved, as did documentation, time management under quarter-end pressure, and communication. A quarter-end model-run error that forced validation files to be redone showed how much teamwork matters. Reporting differences in sensitivity and reserve outputs gave managers an organised view of model results. Relationships with senior actuaries became an important source of mentoring.
what do I need to improve: When unexpected results appeared in validation files, the first explanations were not convincing enough, and further reruns and explanations were needed with senior actuaries. The later study plan also treats Excel and Python as skills that still need to be strengthened.
post-internship reflections: The internship clarified a long-term goal of becoming a fully qualified actuary and deepened interest in valuation work. The study plan moved from a coursework focus toward scheduling professional actuarial exams and building Excel and Python skills. Rejoining Manulife after graduation is of strong interest because of the opportunities and the relationships formed with seniors.
advice for future interns: Read the websites of companies of interest in detail and join a firm visit if one is available, so the choice is based on genuine interest. Take the initiative and show a desire to learn.
technical skills: Technical work covered SQL data extraction, AXIS and Excel-macro model runs, best-estimate reserves and liabilities, sensitivity analysis, user acceptance testing, IFRS 17 valuation, Model Change Management, Gainwave Python runs, and the Life Insurance Capital Adequacy Test.
soft skills: The report names clear documentation, time management under quarter-end pressure, communication, teamwork, and problem-solving.
courses mentioned: Courses described as useful are life contingencies, financial mathematics, and probability and statistics. Professional actuarial exams are part of the later study plan.
tools and software: Named tools are SQL, AXIS, Excel, Excel macros, and Python.

job description: Manulife (International) Limited hosted a six-month full-time internship, from 2 July 2025 to 16 January 2026, with the IFRS17 team in the Hong Kong Corporate Actuarial department. The work sat in insurance financial reporting. The student analysed how the cost of guarantees responds to stochastic economic scenarios, built VBA automation for routine workflows, and worked with other teams on data inputs and valuation methods. A group project with interns from other departments looked at Regional Actuarial Service, which aligns local business units with the parent company and links the local office with headquarters.
job duties: Each quarter, modelled stochastic scenarios from the Economic Scenario Generator and examined their impact on the cost of guarantees; performed reasonableness checks and identified drivers such as interest rates, assumption changes, and policyholder behaviour; summarised results and sent them to seniors by email; built VBA tools that automate routine data processes, scenario runs, and email updates, including a tool that generates email text and pastes Excel tables into email; worked with the asset management team on analysis inputs, with the Python team on cost-of-guarantee Python runs, and with the regional department; joined an intern group project on the role of Regional Actuarial Service.

job description: RGA is described as the only global reinsurance company focused primarily on life and health reinsurance. It assumes risk from insurance companies, called cedents, in exchange for premiums, which helps those insurers manage risk exposure, capital requirements, and underwriting capacity. The student was an actuarial valuation intern on the regional valuation team from 2 July 2025 to 9 January 2026, after a one-week extension. The work focused on Long Duration Targeted Improvement, the US accounting update for long-duration contracts, including reserves, earnings, and the effect of assumption changes.
job duties: Studied LDTI terms used in the valuation files, including net premium ratio, gross premium, net premium, benefit margin, reserves as the present value of future benefits, and unlocking impact when gross premium or the net premium ratio changes; updated quarterly checking tools that review benefit margin and treaty expense margin for the business; supported SQL extraction of projected premiums, projected benefits, historical premiums, historical benefits, and other variables for the manager; built a value breakdown of benefit margin into gross-premium and net-premium-ratio effects from last quarter to the current quarter; created a template to track that change.
pre-internship preparation: The internship came through a mentorship programme. The interview lasted about 30 minutes and had two parts: basic insurance and reinsurance knowledge, and how to handle problems in a team. Preparation for the knowledge part was a review of STAT3904 and STAT3905 and a look through the RGA website for its main business.
what have I learned: SQL, Excel, communication, and LDTI actuarial knowledge were learned largely from scratch. Excel moved beyond copy and paste to formulas that link data, so colleagues can trace the work and keep it consistent, plus pivot tables and shortcut keys. During university, the student would rather intern at more companies and in other positions to see what kind of work fits. The actuarial capstone is credited with helping students find direction while still in college.
advice for future interns: Students applying for an actuarial valuation internship should practise Excel, learn programming, and be able to communicate efficiently, so they can adapt to the working environment and the intensity of the work.

soft skills: The report names communication, including asking for help proactively, and a shift toward a more structured way of explaining and tracing problems.
courses mentioned: STAT3904 and STAT3905 were reviewed before the interview.

job description: The report covers a year of full-time actuarial internship in two insurance teams during 2025. In the first half, the student worked on AIA Group's modelling team, providing modelling work and helping enhance models and test tools used to evaluate risk. In the second half, the student worked on Prudential Group Limited's economic capital team. That responsibility was to help with calculations and development for Group internal economic capital reporting across local business units in Asia and for projects on various reporting bases. The main focus was cash-flow projection of assets and liabilities, with Prophet and Excel as the main software.
job duties: On the AIA modelling team, ran the Prophet model, analysed cash-flow relationships between variables, checked and updated variable coding, and extracted data; learned Prophet inputs, amendments before a run, and how to select products and variables; used Excel VBA checking tools on inputs before and after Prophet runs; used SQL to query data after the model run; on the Prudential economic capital team, assisted calculations and development for group internal economic capital reporting and projects across reporting bases; performed cash-flow projections of assets and liabilities in Prophet and Excel; debugged mismatched Prophet output by checking policy data, interest tables, and discount tables, and used VLOOKUP after extracting file paths from Prophet Enterprise.
pre-internship preparation: NA

Excel VBA checking tools, SQL queries, and VLOOKUP for missing Prophet Enterprise file paths became part of daily modelling. Debugging error messages, remembering common errors, and checking tables independently strengthened problem-solving. job description: AIA is described as a leading international life insurance company operating across major Asian markets, with managed risk systems, balanced financial operations, and high regulatory compliance. The student spent six months as an intern on the Macau Team within the Integrated Reporting Team. That department provides shareholder reporting, regulatory reporting, business projections and forecasts, and other projects, split by valuation basis for internal management and external disclosure. The team was small, with three permanent members plus the intern, and the work included Macau regulatory reporting and AIA Re reinsurance documents, often in coordination with mainland offices.
job duties: Performed calculations and data extraction for financial reports and verified calculations in financial models under different reporting bases; handled reporting on Macau RBC and AMCM standards, processed AIA Re reinsurance documents, and coordinated timelines with mainland colleagues; rebuilt the Macau annual-report file on both the current AMCM basis and the RBC basis, including the QIS2 liability tab, after template changes, new items, a shift to Set B scenarios, and hardcoded values that were not linked to source files; traced formulas and reference files under a two-month window after a delayed government sample; transferred a slow data-processing workflow to Alteryx, mapped old commands into Alteryx steps, debugged outputs against prior results, wrote notes on each command, and held an Alteryx session for local and mainland colleagues.
pre-internship preparation: The interview call came about an hour after a STAT3902 midterm. There was time only to go home, change into a formal shirt, and prepare a self-introduction on the way. It was a first actuarial internship interview and a group interview with four candidates. Questions covered why AIA, hopes for the six-month internship, known insurance types, and preferred department. Most candidates wanted pricing. The pricing manager asked what VNB meant, and the student could not answer because of the lack of preparation. The lesson taken was to study the target department's workflow, operations, and professional knowledge early.
what have I learned: The Macau annual report showed how heavy a regulatory file is when documentation is incomplete and formulas cannot be reused. Patience, careful checking, and staying calm under overtime pressure were practical gains, including a late evening spent clearing the last error on the liability tab. Alteryx was learned without an internal expert, by reading the old workflow, the Alteryx site, and outside guidance, then proving the new output matched the old one. Communication improved by giving teammates full detail when asking for help and by considering their workload. The six months also made independent exploration and teamwork feel more natural.
what do I need to improve: Interview preparation was too thin, and the VNB question went unanswered. On the job, the annual-report handover lacked a full operating procedure, some data were hardcoded, and last year's formulas did not fit the new QIS2 template. Alteryx was new to the student and to the team, so functions had to be learned without specific guidance.
post-internship reflections: This was a first experience of professional work, and it settled a wish to rejoin AIA after graduation and keep developing there. Later work will start from other people's perspectives, and questions to teammates will include enough detail that they do not have to reconstruct the issue.
advice for future interns: For the same kind of role, use Excel more and learn shortcut keys so the work is faster. For professional software such as Alteryx, it is better to learn by doing the real tasks the company assigns.

job description: After several same-day interviews, the student joined the Group Economic Capital Team at Prudential Corporate Asia and worked in the Heavy Model Team on part of the year-end Group Internal Economic Capital Assessment. Local business units supplied models that were run in Prophet to produce calibration tools for groups of products. The Lite Model Team then used those tools to cover losses from unexpected catastrophic events, including mass lapses, bond defaults, and morbidity. The modelling supported capital assessment rather than product design. Inputs also came from the Asset Liability Management team and from checking templates meant to limit human error.
job duties: Ran local-business-unit models in Prophet to produce calibration tools for product groups in the year-end GIECA project; used Economic Scenario Generator files from the Asset Liability Management team for stochastic runs; applied template files from the Lite Model team and local business units to check results; studied Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise, including conventional and summary libraries, if-else variables, model point files, global tables prepared with VBA, run settings, variable groups, and accumulations; uploaded models from Prophet Professional to Prophet Enterprise and ran test and batch runs; investigated wrong-model submissions, VBA that failed, unused risk factors left on, missing bond data, and model-structure changes from local business units.
pre-internship preparation: The search began in September 2024 after the department advertised its half-yearly Actuarial Internship Program. A resume was submitted, and many interview calls arrived the same day, so preparation was mostly a self-introduction. The day included phone interviews, Microsoft Teams individual interviews, and group interviews, with technical and situational questions. Financial mathematics and stochastic processes came up, linked to STAT2902 and STAT3903, and knowledge of the efficient frontier from STAT3904 and Markov chains from STAT3903 was used. A question on growing-profits calculations went badly. Verbal offers still arrived the same day, and Prudential was chosen after comparison.
what have I learned: Classroom modelling had focused on training and testing simple models. The internship showed that a production run depends on inputs from several teams, checking files, and controls against human error. Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise became familiar, including how libraries, products, model point files, global tables, and run settings determine the calculation path. Limited machines and workers, plus many input tables and output variables, explained the long runtimes discussed in STAT4904. The work also showed that modelling is used for capital, not only for designing insurance products.
what do I need to improve: Some interview answers were weak, including a growing-profits calculation. In production, the wrong model inside a local-business-unit file blocked testing scenarios for a week. VBA failures took a long time to trace. One internship still felt like too little exposure to decide which area of modelling fits best.
post-internship reflections: Modelling had been thought of mainly as a product-development tool. Seeing it used for capital, inside an insurance company but not mainly about the insurance product itself, raised interest in how modelling is used across the industry. A single internship was not enough to choose an area, so other opportunities will be considered before a career goal is fixed. Rejoining the company is not ruled out.
advice for future interns: Treat the internship as a chance to learn, and be explorative rather than following guidelines without understanding them. Manuals studied in the first two months did not explain why steps were done and did not solve production problems. Once the logic of how Prophet produces results was clear, unexpected issues were easier to sort out than anything the manuals or books provided.
technical skills: Technical work covered Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise, calibration tools, stochastic runs using Economic Scenario Generator files, VBA global tables, model-point and run-setting structure, and debugging of model, bond, and risk-factor inputs.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: Courses named are STAT2902, STAT3903, STAT3904, and STAT4904.
tools and software: Named tools are Prophet, Prophet Professional, Prophet Enterprise, Excel, VBA, the Economic Scenario Generator, and Microsoft Teams.

job description: Manulife International Limited is described as a large life insurer in Hong Kong, with a local office in Kwun Tong and a regional office in Ngau Tau Kok. job duties: Handled special quotes, mainly cutting first-year commission so a client could receive a larger discount, special discount offers, reinstatement amounts, death benefit amounts, and proposals that the front end blocked because the return might hit the Insurance Authority cap; issued memos after director approval and sent reinstatement or death benefit figures to other teams after senior review; on the High-End Medical repricing, checked hash totals of rates returned by IT against issue age and duration; ran new-business and in-force user acceptance testing across issue age, riders, campaign discount, coverage class, and deductible, and compared front-end results with results from the new rates; checked pricing rates against AXIS and followed up differences caused by the repricing.

job description: The internship was in the modelling team of Prudential plc, also called Prudential Group, a leading international financial services group in insurance and asset management. The group is headquartered in London and listed in London, Hong Kong, Singapore, and New York, and operates across Asia and Africa. Distribution includes agents, bancassurance, and digital platforms, with products such as investment-linked plans and health insurance. The modelling role turned statistical and economic assumptions into analysis for financial reporting and risk management, including half-year management reports that support decisions under regulatory constraints.
job duties: Ran benchmark and stochastic scenarios to analyse how interest-rate moves, credit spreads, and changes in mortality or life expectancy affect the value of bonds and funds; built and updated cash-flow forecast models and summarised results for the half-year management report; turned detailed model output into written summaries and charts for strategic decisions; checked errors by reviewing VBA and Prophet code; applied present-value analysis of benefits and premiums using financial mathematics and statistical models.
pre-internship preparation: Actuarial internships were sought through job fairs, the college application system, and LinkedIn. Before the interview, the student researched the company's background, culture, business, and values, and compared the job description with personal fit and technical skills. In the interview, actuarial software experience and multi-tasking were presented, and the team was asked about daily duties and expectations of interns. Some technical questions could not be answered completely, so the reasoning was explained step by step.
what have I learned: The life cycle of insurance products, and the place of models in financial reporting and risk management, became much clearer. Statistical modelling improved, and Prophet and Excel VBA were used for data analysis and predictive modelling. Senior actuaries shared work habits, including leaving work marks and backing up files, and gave advice on job hunting and on balancing exams with work. The early difficulty of seeing how small production tasks fit the model led to reverse-tracking errors with mentors, which built a more systematic approach to debugging.
what do I need to improve: At the start, separate production tasks could be completed, but it was hard to see how they fitted the modelling framework, so a wrong model output had no obvious place to begin debugging. Some technical interview questions also could not be answered fully in the time allowed.
post-internship reflections: The internship confirmed a plan to become an actuary with a strong technical base and a wider business view. More computer science courses are planned because programming matters more in data analysis and predictive modelling, and further economics courses are considered for commercial knowledge. Other actuarial internships, such as asset-liability management or pricing, are of interest. Rejoining Prudential Group is a hope, given the modelling team's support and the group's position in Asia.
advice for future interns: Become familiar with Excel, Prophet, and SQL before a similar role, and show strong interest throughout the application. During the internship, stay curious, ask questions, volunteer for extra team work, and seek feedback from the mentor regularly.

job description: Prudential Hong Kong Limited placed the student in the pricing team, after an earlier indication that the reporting team was more likely because pricing demand was high. The pricing team sets insurance rates and balances risk, profit, and market conditions. Over six months, intern work centred on policy administration cases, special quotations that the main sales system could not price, and user acceptance testing when rates or products changed. Permanent staff, by contrast, design products, do market research, build Prophet models, and write department reports. More than 400 policy administration cases were handled.
job duties: On a weekly rotation, downloaded the latest credit ratings from the Bloomberg terminal for pricing and valuation models, and edited an Excel macro that emailed Outlook reminders for pending policy administration cases; prepared case replies on surrender, partial surrender, reduced paid-up, bonus encashment, and death benefit by updating product spreadsheets; used Brio Query to pull historical fund unit prices and allocations and to support loan and premium deposit account values; recalculated premiums after changes such as quitting smoking or a new payment frequency; built future value illustration PDF reports for encashment, combined withdrawal, and reduced paid-up; updated cost-of-insurance rate reviews; manually priced special quotations outside PruCompass limits; entered user-acceptance-test cases into pricing spreadsheets and compared them with IT system output and system-generated PDFs.
pre-internship preparation: Hiring for a second-half 2025 internship was expected to finish by the end of 2024, so the student attended a career fair in October 2024 that included insurers, reinsurers, and banks. Earlier work as a financial consultant in Prudential Group shaped the booth conversation, which covered actuarial study, an insurance career plan, and a plan to take the Society of Actuaries exam. A formal offer arrived later that night. Before the start date, HR was contacted by email and onboarding forms, a resume update, and the company account were completed.
what have I learned: University had not included a course on how insurance products operate, so terms such as bonus encashment, combined withdrawal, and reduced paid-up were new. The steep start produced practical knowledge of policy values, illustrations, and testing that books had not provided, together with communication skills from a team that explained mistakes. The contrast between intern tasks and permanent staff work, especially product design, market research, and Prophet models, prompted a more serious approach to actuarial modelling.
what do I need to improve: Many mistakes were made at the beginning because product operations and terms such as bonus encashment, combined withdrawal, and reduced paid-up were unfamiliar, and the learning curve was steep.
post-internship reflections: Six months made the internal work of an insurer more concrete and showed the gap between intern casework and the product, research, and modelling work of permanent staff. Actuarial modelling study began during this period. To test fit and see other departments, the student applied for an actuarial internship in another team in the second half of 2026.
advice for future interns: For a pricing internship, stay proactive, use spare time to practise Excel shortcuts, and learn the basics of insurance products so it is possible to contribute from the first day.
technical skills: Technical work covered Excel macros, policy-value and premium calculations, Brio Query extracts, future value illustrations, cost-of-insurance reviews, special quotations, and user acceptance testing against IT output.
soft skills: The report names communication skills gained from teammates who explained product operations and from the need to write clear case replies.

job description: AIAHK is described as focused on insurance and wealth management, mainly life and medical insurance for individuals and groups, plus long-term savings plans. The student was an actuarial intern on a project and reinsurance team during a half-year internship. The team was upgrading Project READ, an Alteryx system for analysing claims and premiums linked to reinsurance claim recovery. Regular work also covered monthly lapse experience and checks of reinsurance claim recovery, including reading treaties and confirming ceding ratios. The role was to test the new system against the old one and to support those recurring reinsurance tasks.
job duties: Compared Project READ results with the old system and summarised monthly booking trends for claims and premiums, including changes in ceded amount and possible errors in program logic; compiled an issue list and discussed it with colleagues; analysed monthly lapse guarantees from policy terminations over ten or more years, using an approach similar to discount-rate work from STAT2902; extracted claim-record fields such as policy number, event date, treaty code, and claim amount from large files with Foxpro and Python-related code; checked claim referral limits and treaty ceding ratios, including sum assured; read reinsurance treaties; for a reinsurance-aging task, built pivot tables and graphs of amounts owed by reinsurer, quarter, and treaty, split into aging bands, and presented the findings.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started about a week before the AIAHK interview email, with a self-introduction on reasons for actuarial work and related experience, plus research on the company's culture, mission, and history. There were two interviews. The first was a group interview with four candidates and four actuaries, who took turns asking actuarial and insurance questions. One question was how an insurance company earns profit. The student was unsure, let others answer first, added to their ideas, and tried to sound confident despite being the least experienced candidate.
what have I learned: Reinsurance was new because it had not appeared in school. Reading more than 40 treaties showed how ceded net amount at risk, new products, and retention ratios differ by treaty. Excel shortcuts sped up daily work. An Alteryx flow for recalculating ratings and flats, which the student had never used, was documented in a manual after a week of reading functions and asking other interns. Taking over a departing intern's tasks forced faster familiarisation. Pivot tables and graphs on reinsurance aging were used to show decision-makers where amounts were outstanding.
what do I need to improve: In the first month it was unclear how to finish both new tasks and the work of an intern who was leaving, and colleagues were too busy to ask easily. Alteryx had never been used, so explaining each step of a ratings-and-flats flow was difficult. The manual that resulted still felt less concrete than it could have been, although the team was satisfied.
post-internship reflections: The career aim is to become a broadly skilled actuary with strong risk management and critical thinking, first by earning actuarial credentials, and later by becoming a chief actuary. Weekly or monthly study milestones, plus rest, are the planned way to keep progress steady. Rejoining AIAHK is of definite interest, preferably on a different team so the exposure is wider.
advice for future interns: Practise Excel or Python before the internship, including pivot tables and VBA. Be active and willing to ask questions, and treat communication and presentation as part of the job, because actuarial interns often have to present their work to the team.
technical skills: Technical work covered Alteryx and Project READ reconciliations, Excel shortcuts and pivot tables, Foxpro extraction, Python-related coding, treaty-based ceding calculations, lapse analysis, and charting of reinsurance aging.
soft skills: The report names asking questions, communication, presenting findings to the team, confidence in interviews, and managing time when several tasks arrived together.
courses mentioned: STAT2902 is named as the source of discount-rate learning used on the monthly lapse-guarantee task.

job description: Chubb Life Hong Kong is described as a leading Hong Kong insurer offering property insurance, savings plans, risk-management programmes, and wealth preservation, with multiple 10Life 5-Star Insurance Awards. The student interned in the valuation team. job duties: Compiled sales and premiums collected for each insurance product and made manual adjustments for strange monthly cases; collected data on equities and bonds owned by the company; learned Microsoft Access coding to integrate data and turn it into tables; passed summarised figures to other departments for analysis of policy-number changes; supported figures released publicly, such as monthly interest rates for product OT18; later took on more advanced investigation tasks; used Access SQL to summarise datasets on product sales and reported data problems, including new criteria that made product compilation easier.
pre-internship preparation: Before the Chubb interview, several hours went into the company's history, aims, target customers, how it differs from other insurers, and its rough structure. After advice from colleagues, premium calculation, life annuity models, and survival distributions from STAT3901 were revised. job description: Prudential Plc. is an international financial services group, mainly in life insurance and asset management. The student was the actuarial intern in the Group Asset-Liability Management team at the Group Office, which oversees the global organisation rather than one local business. Unlike pricing, which designs products, or valuation, which calculates liabilities, this team aligns long-term assets with long-term liabilities. Work is split between Production, which projects asset cash flows for 100 years under scenarios such as inflation and interest rates, and Development, where the intern sat. Projects pass through a doer, a checker, and a reviewer. The intern was mainly the doer, and the central assignment was a Pythonisation project that rewrote slow Excel VBA tools in Python.
job duties: Translated Excel VBA tools for asset cash-flow calculations into Python so the process would run faster and could meet more regulations and calibrate more variables; worked between the Production and Development sectors so the tools matched what both sides needed; on day three, started an Excel VBA macro that reads a directory of four CSV files, exports them into a workbook, and applies Excel formulas; used Pandas, NumPy, OS, and Xlwings so Python could create files and work with Excel; used Beyond Compare 4 to compare text files, Python files, and folders when scripts changed; sent sign-off email to the reviewer after the checker had agreed the work.

The first fair produced no interviews after CVs were given to twenty companies. At the second fair, the Asset-Liability Management director held a short one-to-one that was mostly an introduction to the team and the intern role, plus a question on Excel and Python. COMP1117 had not been taken, but willingness to learn was emphasised, and an offer arrived the next day. Before day one, an actuarial analyst recommended Pandas, NumPy, Xlwings, and Excel functions such as VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, INDEX, and MATCH, which were practised in advance.
what have I learned: Excel formulas and shortcuts, Excel VBA macros, and Python libraries including Pandas, NumPy, OS, and Xlwings became working tools, along with Beyond Compare 4. Python from the actuarial programme was the knowledge that transferred most directly into the Pythonisation work. Sitting between Production and Development made technical tasks easier to see as part of long-term financial decisions, and required combining what both sides wanted. Life contingencies were not central to this team, but permanent staff said that material matters for pricing and valuation. Copilot and tutorial videos were used to get through the first VBA macro.
what do I need to improve: Excel VBA had never been used or taught, so the first macro was confusing, including coding terms such as dim, cells, and offset, even though two weeks were allowed and the Excel formulas had been studied beforehand.

Future courses will be studied for what the material means, not only for the calculations. Rejoining Prudential is of interest if the chance arises, because colleagues explained both the steps and the reason for them.
advice for future interns: Ask the team what to prepare before the start. Learning Excel formulas gave a faster start, and Excel VBA is worth learning beforehand because it is widely used in actuarial work.
technical skills: Technical work covered Python, Pandas, NumPy, OS, and Xlwings, Excel formulas and shortcuts, Excel VBA macros, file comparison in Beyond Compare 4, and rewriting VBA asset-cash-flow tools in Python.
soft skills: The report names communication between the Production and Development sectors and the ability to combine different requirements into one result.
courses mentioned: COMP1117 is named as a course not yet taken at the time of the interview. Life contingencies are named as knowledge that matters for pricing and valuation. STAT4767 is the internship course that prompted the job search.
tools and software: Named tools are Excel, Excel VBA, Python, Pandas, NumPy, Xlwings, OS, Beyond Compare 4, Copilot, Jobsdb, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp.

job description: Manulife operates a Regional division covering Asian markets including Japan, Singapore, and Malaysia, and a Local division focused on Hong Kong. The business includes life insurance, health insurance, retirement solutions, and wealth management, with actuarial work centred on valuation and pricing. Interns sit either at the Manulife Financial Centre in Kwun Tong or at the Manulife Tower in Ngau Tau Kok. The student spent six months in the second half of 2025 on the regional Japan valuation team. Japanese reporting follows a framework that differs from IFRS 17, and the supervisor was a modelling specialist, so the role centred on AXIS modelling, SQL extracts, and a reconciliation project called DIMT.
job duties: Compared model output before and after changes; summarised reserves under different model versions; checked that business specifications matched data extracted from AXIS; worked on regular life, annual, and universal life policies, in a Japanese framework illustrated by NWL and SPWL; wrote SQL in Spyder to extract and process data; on the DIMT project, reconciled model outputs with business-unit data, researched unfamiliar document terms, wrote extraction scripts, and built reconciliation templates and a visual comparison workflow that had not existed before; helped with monthly team events by ordering food, contacting vendors, and confirming attendance.
pre-internship preparation: The offer did not come from a formal interview. It followed a Firm Visit to Manulife organised by the HKU Statistics and Actuarial Science Society, assessed through conversations with management and actuarial staff. Preparation covered Manulife's history, business segments, and Asian footprint; the branches of valuation, pricing, reinsurance, and consultancy; the IFRS 17 framework, helped by an earlier university seminar; and Excel, Python, and basic accounting and commercial ideas. During the visit the student was asked about IFRS 17 and its effect on financial reporting. HR later said the discussion had stood out and invited the student to join.
what have I learned: AXIS was learned without official documentation, by trying functions and by asking the supervisor in person or by phone rather than only by email. SQL in Spyder differed from R or Python syntax used in coursework, but the programming logic transferred, and premium and reserving ideas from core actuarial courses applied directly. The DIMT reconciliation templates practised turning messy comparisons into something decision-makers could read. Monthly logistics and an escape-room outing showed a flat team culture. A group-project dispute with a Korean colleague, caused by cultural miscommunication and unilateral file changes, was resolved by talking through concerns and splitting the work again.
what do I need to improve: Early weeks were lost in AXIS menus because the software has no official documentation, which led to frequent overtime. DIMT began with unfamiliar abbreviations and business terms. A cross-cultural misunderstanding on a final group project strained the team and slowed the work until it was discussed openly.
post-internship reflections: The internship changed a fear that actuarial work only means constant overtime. Pace and culture differ between regional and local teams and across product lines, and working with colleagues from Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia, Korea, and elsewhere made cultural range a factor in later job choices. Actuarial examinations were reprioritised as a short-term goal because qualified actuaries described them as necessary for hiring and promotion. The student wants to return to Manulife and build a career in valuation on a regional team.
advice for future interns: Start actuarial examinations early, because credentials affect both hiring and promotion. Strengthen English, since regional teams use it as the working language and cross-cultural work depends on it. Become proficient in Excel and in programming languages such as SQL and Python, which are used for reconciliation, extraction, automation, and linking to models.
technical skills: Technical work covered AXIS modelling, SQL extraction in Spyder, dataset and reserve comparisons, assumption checks, reconciliation templates, and scripting for the DIMT project.
