job description: Prudential Corporation Asia, introduced through the Prudential Hong Kong company description, provides financial planning and products including individual life insurance, investment-linked insurance, retirement solutions, health and medical protection, general insurance, and employee benefits. The internship was based at IFC in the Group Internal Economic Capital Assessment Heavy Model team. That assessment is an Insurance Authority requirement for designated insurance holding companies in Hong Kong, so the firm holds enough capital for its risks. The Heavy Model team focuses on computation, especially best-estimate liabilities under risk-factor shocks, while the Light Model team focuses more on model building. The intern ran tools that apply those shocks to assets and liabilities for later investigation.
job duties: Ran Excel templates in Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise to apply risk-factor shocks to assets and liabilities and estimate future values; prepared inputs, including out-of-model mortality adjustments, before jobs were submitted; investigated unexpected Prophet Enterprise run-log errors, separating operational mistakes from source-data, bond, job, table, or model issues, and reported suspected source problems to the reviewer; updated workspaces from the latest source in time for submission; built an Excel VBA tool so morbidity adjustments could cover more than 1,000 jobs after a business unit simplified its groups, then used AI to cut a run from about five to ten minutes to under one minute; flagged a mismatch between changed bond credit ratings and applied interest rates, and proposed a fix that needed a model change.
pre-internship preparation: NA
what have I learned: University work had been mostly theoretical, including insurance pricing in STAT3901, while the internship stressed spotting problems in calculated results, solving a stated issue, and making the process faster. Practical gains were Excel shortcuts, Excel VBA, and how Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise run. A morbidity-adjustment workbook was built by asking AI for small functions and formulas and combining them, rather than asking it to write the whole tool, as a way to learn VBA, which is still widely used in insurance. Communication with colleagues and email writing were also practised. The placement showed how data and models are combined to support company decisions.
what do I need to improve: Excel VBA was unfamiliar before the internship, so the morbidity tool had to be learned while the work was underway. The assigned tasks also depended more on general problem-solving than on calculating the target variables, and a suggested interest-rate correction for bonds whose credit ratings had changed could not be finished because it needed a model adjustment.
post-internship reflections: The career goal remains becoming an actuary, with a wish to try other parts of insurance first, in the order of asset-liability management, then valuation, then pricing, before choosing a field, including reporting. Prudential's working environment is described as excellent, and rejoining after graduation would be welcome. The role also showed that not every insurer has a group economic-capital team.
advice for future interns: Students applying for a similar role should prepare soft skills, especially communication, and hard skills, mainly Excel, and should be able to work independently because colleagues are often too busy to give advice whenever it is needed.
technical skills: Excel templates, shortcuts, and VBA; Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise, including job runs and run-log checks; out-of-model input adjustments for mortality and morbidity; and using AI to assemble VBA functions while learning the language.
soft skills: Efficient and correct communication with colleagues, email writing, and working independently when teammates are busy are named as skills from the internship.
courses mentioned: STAT3901 is cited for insurance pricing learned at school. STAT4904 is named as the course closest to the work and as a course being taken while the report was written.
tools and software: Excel, Excel VBA, Prophet Professional, Prophet Enterprise, and AI used to draft VBA functions and formulas.

job description: Manulife Financial Asia Limited is described as a Canadian insurer that provides life and health insurance, the Mandatory Provident Fund in Hong Kong, and wealth and asset management. The internship, from 2 July 2025 to 16 January 2026, was in the Regional Actuarial Services Department on the Embedded Value Reporting team. It was a first job. The role supported group reporting of new business value and related capital measures. The first two weeks overlapped with the previous intern, and the last two weeks were spent teaching the next intern.
job duties: Consolidated financial data across Manulife business units for New Business Value reporting; analysed the acquisition expense gap; reconciled New Business Value with New Business Contractual Service Margin; built and revised spreadsheet templates for Organic Capital Generation, Free Surplus Generation, and 2026 capital planning; processed data for access-control management on the local drive and SharePoint; read IFRS 17, including why New Business Contractual Service Margin is used and how its assumptions differ from New Business Value; joined a group project on using AI in the Financial Risk Management team's daily work, noting that AI still failed at routine tasks such as reading PDF files; wrote a task manual and taught the next intern the steps and ideas such as Annualized Premium Equivalence.
pre-internship preparation: The department career-fair email was missed. Applications through the department Internship and Job Online-Application System drew no replies, so applications were sent through job websites. Manulife human resources replied about ten minutes after a CV was submitted. A first interview asked financial-mathematics questions, including how a bond price reacts to an interest-rate change, and ended in rejection because preparation was weak. For a second interview in another department, financial mathematics, probability, and life contingencies were revised, but the director only asked for an English self-introduction and then chatted in Cantonese. The offer was for Regional Actuarial Services. LinkedIn was later activated, and the career fair and mentorship programme were noted as routes through which friends had found internships.
what have I learned: Actuarial mathematics was less directly used than the intuition behind it, while ideas such as the statement of financial position helped on a reporting team. Excel efficiency and keyboard shortcuts improved. Reading IFRS 17 gave a basic view of New Business Contractual Service Margin and of how it differs from New Business Value. Teaching the next intern, with a written manual, tested whether the tasks were really understood. A group project showed both uses and limits of AI in financial risk work, including failure on routine PDF reading. The placement also widened a network of interns and managers.
what do I need to improve: The first interview was poorly prepared, and some financial-mathematics questions could not be answered. Teaching the next intern was also hard: even with a manual, it was difficult to remember and explain all of the concepts learned from the manager and the previous intern during the first two weeks.
post-internship reflections: Long hours among managers and directors, including a working email at 3 a.m., led to a rethink of whether an actuarial or insurance career was enjoyable, without fully giving up on becoming an actuary. Other ideas were secondary-school teaching in mathematics or Business, Accounting and Financial Studies, and further study in statistics or Chinese linguistics. The study plan was set toward Society of Actuaries University-Earned Credit for Advanced Short-Term Actuarial Mathematics, with MATH3911 Game Theory and Strategy in the current semester and, next semester, STAT4903 Actuarial Techniques for General Insurance, STAT3906 Risk Theory I, and STAT3910 Financial Economics I, plus possible Chinese courses. A return was unlikely: there was no return offer, the industry choice was still open, and a coffee chat described Manulife as known for long hours.
advice for future interns: Applicants for a similar role should have insurance knowledge and some financial sense. Business School courses, especially finance, were recommended as more useful for understanding the work than advanced mathematics or computer skills, which managers do not expect from an intern and which give only a small advantage.
technical skills: Microsoft Office, especially Excel and its keyboard shortcuts; spreadsheet templates for new-business, surplus, and capital reporting; and applied reading of IFRS 17, New Business Value, New Business Contractual Service Margin, Annualized Premium Equivalence, Organic Capital Generation, and Free Surplus Generation.
soft skills: Teaching a successor, including simplifying a manager's explanations, teamwork on a group presentation, and building relationships with other interns and managers are described.
courses mentioned: Interview revision covered financial mathematics, probability, and life contingencies. Later plans name MATH3911 Game Theory and Strategy, STAT4903 Actuarial Techniques for General Insurance, STAT3906 Risk Theory I, STAT3910 Financial Economics I, and Society of Actuaries Exam ASTAM through University-Earned Credit. Business School finance courses are recommended. IFRS 17 was assigned reading at work.
tools and software: Microsoft Office, Excel, SharePoint, a local drive, and LinkedIn.

job description: The internship at AIA Group, from July to December 2025, was in Group Corporate Solutions on the finance team's financial reporting work. That department coordinates local business units on employee benefits and provides life, medical, and credit insurance to corporate clients rather than individual policyholders. It helps subsidiaries design products, set premiums, and communicate with clients. The intern supported monthly business reports for Group executives, including IFRS 4 and IFRS 17, and arranged meetings with local business units. The Group office was chosen over a separate AIA Hong Kong offer in order to see more of how the insurer operates. The headquarters referred to is the AIA building at Stubbs Road.
job duties: Collected financial files from local business units and screened them in Excel for IFRS 4 and IFRS 17 monthly reporting; built basic Excel VBA to consolidate files from different local business units and prepare recurring reports, reducing manual errors and hours of work each month; arranged Microsoft Teams meetings by contacting managers and directors across nine local business units and keeping the schedule for those nine meetings; recorded data issues and project updates for managers to use in the monthly business reports; memorised calculations and meanings of reporting measures such as the combined ratio and persistency, using internal manuals and help from a senior associate; joined discussions of data discrepancies and saw finished reports reviewed by Group executives.
pre-internship preparation: Before the interview, preparation covered AIA's history, the motto Healthier, Longer, Better Lives, its position as a leading pan-Asian life insurer, and fundamental insurance concepts from the first two years of study. Selection was a group interview with four candidates and two interviewers, focused on background, commercial awareness, and knowledge of the company rather than on mathematics. Each person gave a self-introduction and a reason for choosing AIA. One task was to describe a product in detail; critical illness was chosen, including how its benefits differ from general medical insurance. Another was to justify a past project on attention to detail and on turning complex data into insights. Phone calls then came from the Group office and from AIA Hong Kong, and the Group office offer was accepted.
what have I learned: VBA showed how repetitive consolidation could be made faster and less error-prone. Monthly meetings showed how data-heavy discussions depend on clear communication and on PowerPoint and Excel. Watching incurred-but-not-reported amounts and expected claims move from month to month gave a practical view of claims development and reserves. The Group office was seen as turning local-business-unit information into group strategy, and the intern's data checks fed reports read by Group executives. A director's questions on key performance indicators, some of which were answered incompletely, added context on how the combined ratio and persistency are calculated and how they affect the company.
what do I need to improve: The first two months, under a director known for high standards, were the hardest period. Memorising the calculations and meanings of reporting indicators was overwhelming at first, and not every question could be answered correctly when tested, so the mistakes had to be corrected from the director's explanations and from extra reading of internal manuals.
post-internship reflections: The internship clarified a career aim. Society of Actuaries certifications were seen as necessary for technical credibility, while financial markets and macroeconomic trends were seen as important for reporting roles. Because of artificial intelligence and a crowded traditional actuarial market, the plan is a double major in Finance and possibly CFA exams alongside the actuarial path, so as to move between actuarial work and the wider financial industry. Rejoining AIA after graduation would definitely be considered. The Stubbs Road headquarters, free sports sessions, and leaving at 3 p.m. on the second Friday of each month were cited as support for balance in a high-pressure job.
advice for future interns: Accuracy should come first, because one spreadsheet mistake can affect reporting for several countries and group-level disclosures. Excel, VBA, and Python matter, because efficient analysis and automation free time for actuarial work such as interpreting trends and advising on capital management.
technical skills: Excel data screening and consolidation, Excel VBA automation, IFRS 4 and IFRS 17 reporting files, measures including the combined ratio and persistency, and a practical view of incurred but not reported claims, expected claim experience, claims development, and reserves. PowerPoint was used for presentations.
soft skills: Clear communication in fast data-oriented meetings, presentations in PowerPoint and Excel, contacting managers and directors across local business units, and taking part in discussions of data discrepancies are described.
courses mentioned: Society of Actuaries certifications are described as essential, and CFA exams are a possible addition to the actuarial path. Fundamental insurance concepts from the first two years of study were reviewed before the interview. No HKU course code is named.
tools and software: Excel, Excel VBA, Microsoft Teams, and PowerPoint. Python is named as important for similar roles.

job description: The internship was at Sunlife HK Limited as an Actuarial Intern in the Valuation Group Reporting Team, and it lasted half a year. Unlike classroom calculation of premiums and reserves, the work used policy extracts, listings, and models. Information technology produced policy extracts; those extracts were turned into tables and queries for valuation and were also run through AXIS to obtain reserves and fund movements. Results were then reconciled and explained. The duties were grouped as month-end reporting, valuation-extract user acceptance testing when a new product was launched, and ad hoc tasks assigned by colleagues.
job duties: For month-end reporting, converted IT policy extracts into Access tables and wrote SQL queries for later valuation; ran extracts in AXIS for reserves and fund movements; reconciled AXIS output with the IT extract and traced differences; prepared reserve and fund movement analyses, using Ingenium to compare expected and actual values by policy for traditional and non-traditional blocks such as participating and universal life, then compiled a valuation summary; for valuation-extract user acceptance testing, checked that Ingenium captured the new product and sent defects to IT until the extract was clean; ad hoc work included AXIS dataset backup and download, lapse-study and AAR report updates, and remote laptop maintenance; at a first quarter-end, found a senior teammate had missed a data feed into AXIS, which would have left files short of thousands of policies.
pre-internship preparation: Knowledge of actuarial work was limited beforehand. Preparation included a corporate mentorship programme organised by the HKU SAAS Department, with a senior general-insurance consultant manager at PWC HK. Scheduled meetings covered interview tips, career suggestions, prospects at different actuarial employers, differences among direct insurance, reinsurance, and insurance consulting, how Society of Actuaries exams affect promotion, how pricing differs from valuation, and how to balance work, exams, and life. Those points were used to prepare for interviews and for the internship.
what have I learned: The first two weeks felt overwhelming, and Excel was less familiar than expected. Teammates taught shortcuts such as Alt+Tab, Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y, Ctrl+F, Ctrl+H, and Ctrl+Shift+L, and functions such as SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, INDEX, VLOOKUP, and HLOOKUP. Tracing formulas made it possible to see why a check was not zero and to correct it. Problem-solving, logical thinking, and comfort with the systems improved. Communication, in-person interaction, time management, and teamwork were practised, including the manager's example of running a model on a remote laptop while doing other work on a local one. Finding a missed data feed showed that the reconciliation work mattered to the quarter-end close.
what do I need to improve: Early on the pace was slow, it was hard to follow what others taught, and asking colleagues for help felt difficult, so each task took longer. Excel was also weaker than expected. A non-zero checking total in Excel was frightening until formula tracing showed how to find and fix the discrepancy.
post-internship reflections: The half year is described as a step toward an actuarial career and as a move from student to employee. Becoming an FSA, balancing work, life, and exams, and securing a permanent actuarial job are treated as difficult, but the plan is to keep studying and working toward that path. No course list and no decision about returning to the company are stated.
advice for future interns: NA
technical skills: Excel shortcuts and functions, including SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, INDEX, VLOOKUP, and HLOOKUP, plus formula tracing; Microsoft Access tables; SQL queries on policy listings; the AXIS model for reserves and fund movements; Ingenium investigations of differences; and reconciliation and movement analysis for traditional and non-traditional products.
soft skills: Communication, in-person interaction, time management, teamwork, and team-building activities are named, together with becoming more willing to ask colleagues for help.
courses mentioned: Society of Actuaries exams are discussed, in the mentorship, as a factor in actuaries' promotion. The FSA designation is the stated longer-term aim. No HKU course code is named.
tools and software: Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Access, SQL, AXIS, Ingenium, and remote and local laptops.

job description: The host organisation is not named. The internship was in a bank and included contact with customers who had different needs. A credit analysis report of more than 70 pages had to be prepared, including retrieval of stock-market information, with weekly group meetings on risk assessment and on revisions to the credit-analysis documents.
job duties: Gathered and evaluated information used to measure a company's credibility; interpreted financial statements and computed key metrics, including EBITDA; prepared and finalised a credit analysis report of more than 70 pages; retrieved stock-market information needed for that report; joined weekly group meetings on risk assessment and discussed revisions to the credit-analysis documents with teammates; spoke with customers, checked that their needs were understood, and confirmed key points; wrote client emails in a formal style and internal emails in a plainer style, and used blind copy so extra recipients' addresses stayed hidden.

what have I learned: Customer conversations showed the need to grasp needs and to confirm key information. Email practice covered a formal close for clients, a simpler tone inside the team, and blind copy for privacy. First-year accounting was applied to financial statements and to EBITDA. Weekly meetings improved the credit-analysis draft through teammate feedback. Conversations with a mentor added career advice and practice speaking with people older than typical classmates. Time management became concrete: Society of Actuaries study was kept to about one to two hours a day outside work over three months, and tasks were listed with time blocks so overtime could be avoided.

Combining the internship with Society of Actuaries study was another gap, because most work hours could not be used for study and preparation had to be planned outside work.
post-internship reflections: Talks with a mentor raised whether taking a course at a higher level than previous study would be a good use of time, and those talks shaped thinking about a future career. The stated direction is to keep building on what was learned in the internship and to pursue work as an actuary. No host name is given, so no return decision is stated.

job description: The internship was in the Investment Banking Division at CICC from 1 July 2025 to 30 December 2025, with the position stated as intern in investment banking. Two months of corporate orientation and industry-research training introduced due diligence. From 10 September the work was on site with a tutor from Department 13 at Gloryview Technology Co., Ltd., performing due diligence on a private placement of shares and taking part in the due diligence report. The role covered shareholder and financial analysis, a compliance review of contract substance, and substantive testing of the client's records.
job duties: Mapped Huijing Investment's 33 partners in Excel and drew an equity diagram in Visio, noting that nine were current senior executives; traced a computing-power statistic to its original chart via IDC, white papers, and brokerage research, and explained EFLOPS; analysed Gloryview Technology's shift toward computing-power revenue and refined customer concentration after related subsidiaries proved to be one client group; reviewed an issuance floor at 80 percent of the prior 20-day average price and the book-building step; tested whether a split equipment and maintenance contract was a service rather than quasi-financial leasing, using cash-flow matching and a coverage ratio; did voucher sampling, an R&D walk-through, and cut-off tests; tracked confirmations and compiled working papers on deposits and intercompany balances; checked property, land rights, and patents for mortgages or seizures; shortened data-request emails so the ask, reason, and deadline were clear.

job description: The internship was on the pricing team at SunLife Hong Kong. The report describes pricing work as using financial theory and statistical methods to evaluate risk and to support decisions in a changing insurance market. The role centred on non-standard special quotes, user acceptance testing of a new pricing tool, and comparison of savings products with competitors. Findings from the market comparison were later discussed by the team and affected features of a new product. The team mixed experienced actuaries and recent graduates.
job duties: Handled special quotes, meaning non-standard pricing requests, and calculated the value-of-new-business impact and the related commissions after discounts; conducted user acceptance testing of a new pricing tool by checking calculations, designing test cases for new features, and working with IT developers so the software met underwriters' needs; later managed the team's whole user acceptance test when a supervisor made that an urgent responsibility; compared the savings-product range with competitors on projected returns, including guaranteed internal rate of return and total internal rate of return, by reading brochures, setting assumptions about product features, and presenting a comparison; during talks on a new savings product, set out how those competitor returns compared with the firm's own projections and the trade-off between a higher return, lower profit, and weaker competitiveness.
pre-internship preparation: Interview preparation linked each part of the job description to degree modules, such as survival models for risk assessment and financial economics for pricing, and built a narrative from academic work to the company's goals. Evenings were spent on the annual reports, the product line, and industry news so the strategic setting was familiar. The interview asked for a weakness and, on the technical side, for the difference between Macaulay duration and modified duration, as taught and examined in STAT2902 and Exam FM. Behavioural practice covered adaptability and teamwork, using past group projects and how collaboration and presentation had been shown in them.
what have I learned: The market comparison gave a sense of ownership: after it was presented, the team discussed the findings and they eventually affected a new product's features. User acceptance testing showed the gap between model design and day-to-day use, and the need for clear communication between technical and non-technical people. When IT was slow to provide results or to fix issues, comments were reframed as ways to improve the test rather than as criticism. Informal talks with experienced actuaries and recent graduates added industry practice, exam tips, confidence, and a wider network.
what do I need to improve: During the urgent user acceptance test there was panic and hesitation about pointing out lapses by more experienced colleagues, from a worry that this would look like overstepping. Comfort with sharing those observations grew only as it became clear that the comments helped the team finish the test accurately.
post-internship reflections: The wish to become an actuary grew because technical work was seen to connect with commercial strategy. The plan is to pass the next three actuarial examinations within the year and to add case-study learning, because workplace problems do not follow a syllabus boundary. A return to the company after graduation would be welcome, with the hope of growing into a full-time analyst in a supportive team.
advice for future interns: Prepare thoroughly, including the job requirements and actuarial ideas, especially Life Contingency I and II, STAT3901 and STAT3909. Use chances to work with others and learn from them, because trusting relationships improve the experience. Take criticism, treat obstacles as lessons, and do not be afraid of mistakes if they are used to improve. A supervisor's point was that experience comes from having made many mistakes.
technical skills: Special-quote pricing, value of new business and the commission effect of discounts, user acceptance testing and test-case design, market comparison of savings products, and guaranteed and total internal rates of return. Preparation also used survival models, financial economics, and duration measures.
soft skills: Adaptability, teamwork, presentation, communication between technical and non-technical teams, and giving constructive comments to more senior colleagues are described, along with growing professional confidence.
courses mentioned: STAT2902 and Exam FM were used for the difference between Macaulay and modified duration. Life Contingency I and II are recommended as STAT3901 and STAT3909. Survival models and financial economics are named as interview-preparation topics. The next three actuarial examinations are planned but not named.

job description: The internship was in the pricing team of Prudential Hong Kong Limited, described as one of the major life insurers in Hong Kong, during the second half of 2025. The team sits under Product Management and Development and focuses on launching new products, repricing existing products, and administering existing policies. Other actuarial areas named in the firm include risk assessment, financial reporting, risk management, regulatory compliance, business strategy, actuarial modelling, and asset-liability management. The intern worked on existing-policy cases and assisted with new-product work.
job duties: Handled more than 350 policy-administration cases, about three a working day, in a doer-reviewer-approver flow. Requests included quotes of cash value, sum assured, cost of insurance, and premium; future-value illustrations after reduced sum assured, reduced paid-up, or withdrawals; claim checks; patching; and late fees. For an old product with no spreadsheet rate table, premium rates and histories were extracted from the database and rebuilt by year and pay mode against product specifications. Claim quotes used guidelines in the Prudential Information Library and were matched to the claims team. No-claim bonus on a medical plan was calculated from premium history when the system could not do it. Other work was monthly anniversary-statement checking, special quotations, user acceptance testing, fund credit-rating extracts, weekly progress emails, and a 15-minute presentation.
pre-internship preparation: About one and a half years before the internship, an HKU one-to-one corporate mentorship with a senior manager used monthly meetings to discuss the actuarial industry and career plans, including advice on finding an internship. After online applications, individual interviews were held with managers in actuarial departments. Those managers said that useful preparation, if an offer came, was Excel shortcuts, simple formulas, and VBA if possible. After the Prudential offer was accepted, those Excel tips were practised before the start date.
what have I learned: Daily work on life products used Life Contingency I, STAT3901, for product features, and Financial Mathematics, STAT2902, for present and future values in illustrations. Case work on premiums, claims, and no-claim bonuses showed how product rules are applied when no standard tool exists. The doer-reviewer-approver flow was a check on accuracy. Reviewers and approvers explained mistakes instead of only overriding them, which sharpened both the calculations and interpersonal skill. The placement strengthened the aim of working in life insurance.
what do I need to improve: Mistakes in the workings are acknowledged. Reviewers and approvers pointed them out and explained the knowledge behind them, even when it would have been easier to override the errors. No separate list of remaining weaknesses is given.
post-internship reflections: The half year strengthened the aim of becoming a professional actuary in life insurance, after seeing how life products are developed and managed. Following discussions with seniors, the study plan was changed to clear as many Society of Actuaries preliminary exams as possible during university, because competition is increasing and the exam syllabus keeps changing, and to take Life Contingency II and III rather than general insurance. A return to Prudential after graduation would seriously be considered, because colleagues were willing to teach through corrections.
advice for future interns: Build a solid Excel foundation and a brief understanding of different life-product features before starting. In interviews, show curiosity and a willingness to learn. Approach the internship with an open mind and a wish to contribute, because it offers both technical training and personal growth.
technical skills: Excel workings for policy-administration quotes; database extracts of premium rates and premium histories; present and future values; claim-amount and no-claim-bonus calculations; product-specification checks; fund credit-rating extracts; and user acceptance testing.
soft skills: Interpersonal skill is described as having been sharpened when reviewers explained mistakes in detail. Curiosity and willingness to learn are recommended for interviews. A short end-of-internship presentation is also part of the experience.
courses mentioned: Life Contingency I (STAT3901) and Financial Mathematics (STAT2902) were used on the job. The later study plan names Life Contingency II and III instead of general insurance, and as many Society of Actuaries preliminary exams as possible.
tools and software: Excel, spreadsheets, a policy and rate database, and the Prudential Information Library. VBA was suggested as preparation before the start; the report does not describe using it on the job.

job description: The host company is not named. Its business is insurance, and the internship was in a pricing team for about 6.5 months. The team supports product pricing, experience studies, and analysis of business strategy against market conditions and customer behaviour, in order to produce pricing models. Daily work was special quotations, sometimes with manual Excel changes when the quotation tool's logic did not fit the case. Project work covered an illustration cap on terminal dividend rates and a dividend-scale change, including user acceptance testing against the company IT system.
job duties: Prepared special quotations such as death benefits, reinstatements, surrender values, premium cuts, and cases over the product limit, using a quotation tool and manual Excel changes when its logic failed; adjusted interest on an automatic premium loan between dividend withdrawals with STAT2902 financial mathematics; on the illustration rate-cap project, prepared rates for all plans and changed logic for coupon and savings plans after a 6.5 percent cap on the illustrated terminal dividend rate; on the dividend-scale project, updated rates from seniors, checked them with XLOOKUP, INDEX-MATCH, and hash totals, sent them to IT, and ran user acceptance testing to explain differences between the tool and the IT system; in project meetings, reported the case type, how a difference was found, what was done, and how many similar cases were cleared.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation included reading the company website for mission, values, and culture, reviewing the intern-role requirements, and practising actuarial questions found on the internet and with AI. Human resources reviewed the CV first, and the hiring manager then interviewed. The interview included a self-introduction and questions. Explaining reserves was difficult; the first answer used a banking meaning of reserves until the interviewer asked leading questions about the use of reserves in an insurance company. The preparation was treated as meeting the role, and an offer followed.
what have I learned: Excel formulas were unknown at the start and were learned over a few weeks with Copilot, colleagues, and other interns. The rate-cap and dividend projects added actuarial concepts and a view of how insurers update plan rates each year for economic conditions, mortality, mobility, and lapse. Communication improved because reviewers were assigned randomly in a large team, so a quotation problem had to be stated in a few clear sentences. Project meetings required progress to be explained so decision-makers could follow the evidence. Asking seniors when stuck became easier, and successfully solving hard tasks supported an interest in actuarial work.
what do I need to improve: No Excel formulas were known when the first task arrived, and that task was confusing. It took a few weeks, with Copilot and questions to colleagues and other interns, to become comfortable with Excel. Mistakes and unclear points on later tasks were corrected by seniors who explained the detail.
post-internship reflections: After 6.5 months, the career goal of becoming a qualified actuary felt more certain. The study plan was adjusted toward actuarial courses for a clearer theoretical base, with more time on Society of Actuaries exams before graduation, and one or two further internships before full-time work. Rejoining this company after graduation would be considered because of the environment and the range of new tasks.
advice for future interns: Develop technical skills before joining, because they matter in actuarial work. When a task is confusing, set a time limit and then ask, rather than trying to solve everything alone. Keep an interest in learning, because new tasks keep introducing concepts that have not been seen before.
technical skills: Excel formulas, including XLOOKUP, INDEX-MATCH, and hash-total checks; manual adjustment of quotation interest logic using financial mathematics; illustration-rate and dividend-scale updates; and user acceptance testing against an IT system.
soft skills: Communication with many reviewers, stating a problem in a few sentences, reporting progress in project meetings, asking questions, and discussing methods with colleagues are described.
courses mentioned: STAT2902 Financial Mathematics was applied when adjusting interest calculations on quotations. Further actuarial courses and Society of Actuaries exams are in the post-internship study plan. The Actuarial Science programme is named as the source of the classroom material that was used at work.
tools and software: Excel, Copilot, a quotation tool, and the IT system used in user acceptance testing. The quotation tool and the IT system are not given product names.

job description: The internship was in Prudential's Asset and Liability Management team and lasted six months. It was obtained after the HKU career fair and a phone interview for an asset-liability management position. Daily production work collected shock specifications from local business units, prepared shock, assumption, and simulation files, debugged failed runs, and sent the files back. About half of the time went to debugging. A separate development task automated a daily interest-rate email that interns had previously built by hand from Bloomberg downloads of rates and of swap and option prices.
job duties: Collected shock specifications from local business units; prepared shock files in a usable format; prepared assumption files for both IFRS 17 and HKRBC; set up simulation files to run and debugged them when errors occurred; prepared a sign-off checklist for the manager after each run; drafted emails to the local business units and staged and shared the simulation files; automated the daily interest-rate email in Python, replacing a manual routine of about 20 to 30 minutes that downloaded interest rates and swap and option prices from Bloomberg, processed them in Excel, and pasted the table into Outlook; because Python could not reliably find and reply to the previous day's message, stored dated emails in a folder and used the datetime package to open, edit, send, and save the next file.
pre-internship preparation: The opportunity came from the HKU career fair, where CVs were given to employers and a direct conversation with staff at one booth led to a phone interview a few days later. Because the application was for asset and liability management, STAT2902, STAT3904, and STAT3905 were reviewed, including bond duration and the Black-Scholes formula, on the expectation of questions about financial assets and pricing. The interview did not test that material. It asked about habits, and the conversation turned to experience of trading stocks and bonds, including losing money. The offer arrived the day after the interview.
what have I learned: Debugging could not be fully taught in advance because each error differed, so it was learned from colleagues' demonstrations and from treating the workflow as a web of upstream steps rather than a single line. Written notes on each procedure were needed, because many processes had to be learned at once and files were often wanted urgently. The Python email project took repeated trials on finding the prior message, editing the format, and setting function arguments. Society of Actuaries exams were understood as something that can change pay, with a raise often attached to each pass. Breaks with colleagues helped concentration through a long office day.
what do I need to improve: Adapting to a 9-to-6 day was difficult. Focus dropped in the late afternoon, and waking early for the next day was tiring, compared with a university timetable. On the automation, many attempts still could not make Python reliably reply to the previous email or keep the proper format, until a dated-folder workaround was used.
post-internship reflections: After the internship, the plan is to work in an insurance company and to obtain the Fellow of the Society of Actuaries designation as soon as possible. Passing exams can raise salary, and many companies reimburse exam costs, which adds to that aim. After the designation, other roles are of interest so as not to stay only inside the actuarial industry. No decision about returning to Prudential is stated.
advice for future interns: For an insurer's asset-liability management team, book knowledge matters less than being willing to learn on the job. Be humble, accept advice, and build good relationships with colleagues, who are working toward the same goal. Ask questions, and try hard whether or not the work is enjoyable, because the internship is a single chance to be there. Taking breaks with colleagues is also suggested as a way to stay focused through the day.
technical skills: Shock files, IFRS 17 and HKRBC assumption files, and simulation setup and debugging; Python automation of an Outlook email, including the datetime package; Bloomberg downloads of interest rates and of swap and option prices; and Excel processing of those market data.
soft skills: Asking colleagues questions, accepting advice, and keeping good working relationships are stressed. Lunch conversations with colleagues are described as a way to stay focused, and drafting emails to local business units was part of the daily production work.
courses mentioned: STAT2902, STAT3904, and STAT3905 were reviewed before the interview, including bond duration and the Black-Scholes formula. Society of Actuaries exams and the FSA designation are discussed as plans after graduation.
tools and software: Python, the Python datetime package, Excel, Bloomberg, and Outlook.

job description: AIA is described as a leading life and health insurer in Asia-Pacific, offering life insurance, health coverage, savings plans, retirement solutions, and wealth management for individuals and businesses. The six-month internship was in Product Pricing. The main brief was to support new-product launches through background and market research, checks of premium and dividend rates, and user acceptance testing. Daily work also included special quotations for other departments and help setting up a new pricing model. The tasks showed how pricing connects with underwriting, reinsurance, and distribution channels.
job duties: Did background and market research for new products and organised features and specifications; checked premium and dividend calculations, using mortality assumptions and material from STAT3904 and STAT3909; supported user acceptance testing by reconciling illustration figures and checking system performance before launch; handled special quotations, including policy values after a partial withdrawal, value-of-new-business margin for brokers and agents, and facultative referrals to underwriting or a reinsurer for large cases or special medical conditions; on a new pricing-model project, adjusted simulation parameters, compared output with the existing model, and investigated inconsistencies with Risk-Based Capital and IFRS 17 ideas; wrote macros and Python scripts to automate repetitive tasks; used Prophet, Python, SQL, and VBA in daily work.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started with the job description, the company website for products, strategy, background, and core values, practice with software that might be used, and a review of lecture notes so actuarial topics could be discussed. Selection was a group interview with managers from several departments, including Pricing, asset-liability management, and Valuation, who first outlined those roles. Questions were practical rather than highly theoretical: a short self-introduction, prior coding, problem-solving on projects, willingness to learn new tools quickly, and how several tasks would be scheduled together. The coding example given was Python and VBA scripts that automated repetitive data processing and reconciliation.
what have I learned: The placement added the structure of an insurance company and Risk-Based Capital and IFRS 17 ideas that lectures had not covered. STAT3904, STAT3909, and earlier lectures on asset shares and liability valuation were used in rate checks and in understanding the new model. SQL, VBA, Python scripts, and macros cut manual effort and errors, and COMP1117 made the coding logic easier to follow. CSCI and CAES language courses supported emails, presentations, and discussion in team meetings. Independence, critical thinking, time management, and working to several deadlines improved. Model checks and special quotes were used to suggest adjustments and to balance client requests with profitability.
what do I need to improve: Workload overload and projects with no prior pattern were recurring difficulties. The response was to list tasks by priority, keep the supervisor updated, and sometimes decline extra requests so that quality was not sacrificed. For unfamiliar problems, the gap was closed by reading online, trying approaches, and asking whether a proposed method was acceptable instead of asking for the answer outright.
post-internship reflections: The six months set a path toward becoming a qualified actuary. The next focus is Society of Actuaries exams, together with keeping up with actuarial news and industry developments. Rejoining AIA would definitely be considered. The environment is described as friendly, with patient colleagues and support for learning across many kinds of projects. No further course codes are added to that plan.
advice for future interns: Be a proactive learner. Ask appropriate questions instead of investigating every new topic alone, because seniors are usually willing to teach. Asking also shows willingness to learn and helps build a healthy relationship with the team, and it saves time.
technical skills: Prophet, Python, SQL, and VBA, including macros and scripts for repetitive work; premium and dividend rate checks; illustration reconciliation and user acceptance testing; simulation setup under Risk-Based Capital and IFRS 17; and value-of-new-business and facultative quotation support. COMP1117 is cited as the programming base.
soft skills: Communication by email, presentation, and spoken discussion in team meetings, linked to CSCI and CAES language courses; independent work on complex tasks; critical thinking; time management; working under pressure; and asking questions of colleagues from new graduates through to directors.
courses mentioned: STAT3904 and STAT3909 were used when checking rates. COMP1117 is named for programming logic. CSCI and CAES language courses are credited for workplace communication. Lectures on asset shares and liability valuation are mentioned without a course code. Society of Actuaries exams are the priority after the internship.
tools and software: Prophet, Python, SQL, and VBA, including customised macros and Python scripts.

job description: RGA Reinsurance Company is described as an American reinsurer focused on life and health insurance. It offers risk products to direct insurers and takes a portion of a very large policy or a large group policy by temporary or treaty reinsurance, so that one major event is less likely to destabilise the direct writer. The internship was in the Quotation Team of the pricing department, which assesses, designs, and quotes reinsurance plans. The work covered group quotations and the different treatments of facultative, catastrophe, and high-net-worth cases, together with profit summaries, a test of an artificial-intelligence classification tool, a premium library, and a quarterly business summary.
job duties: Used Excel for risk analysis and preliminary pricing from industry, age, gender, historical claims, and quote volume, applying empirical rates, credibility theory, and group heterogeneity; distinguished facultative pricing for one high-risk life, catastrophe pricing by scenario analysis, group schemes, and high-net-worth cases; built profit summaries in AXIS and Excel for net amount at risk, sum assured, profit margin, and new-business embedded value; tested an AI disease-classification tool by classifying sample data manually, comparing it with the tool, and telling Product Development that formats and instructions were unclear and that manual edits were needed; helped build a Premium Library of direct insurers' transaction records so figures stayed traceable; updated the quarterly business summary; on a quote for mid-size technology firms, noted that a young and healthy group could be accepted within the risk limit, and the decision-maker agreed.
pre-internship preparation: Before the interview with RGA Reinsurance Company, preparation covered how reinsurance operates, RGA's global business and market position, and its strategic position in Hong Kong. Coursework on principles of life insurance pricing and risk models was revised, with notes on how those ideas are used in pricing and in evaluating risk. Mock interviews practised describing personal abilities, teamwork, and ways to handle complex problems. The interviewer asked about the actuarial market in Hong Kong, the company, and the roles in the department. Weakness in some actuarial tools was admitted, together with an intention to keep learning, and the offer followed.
what have I learned: Reinsurance was understood as risk transfer, capital support, and product design sitting behind direct insurance. Credibility theory and differences among group members were applied to quotations, and profit work used reserve assessment, profit testing, and solvency ideas from a loss-modelling class. Sum assured was distinguished from net amount at risk: face amount used in premium and price, versus face amount after deducting reserves as a measure of economic risk. Traceable Excel inputs, rather than copied numbers, made later review easier. Short written comments on what had changed, and a business comment on one quotation, were part of communication with Product Development and with a manager, and that quotation comment was accepted.
what do I need to improve: At the start, industry terms, internal systems, and processes were overwhelming, and Excel and AXIS were not yet known, which made it hard to see how to build the model. There was also a fear that asking basic questions would expose a lack of knowledge. Looking ahead, the named gaps to work on are data analysis and programming, specifically Python and SQL, and being more willing to ask questions and suggest improvements.
post-internship reflections: The pricing placement led to a wish to try internships in valuation and in product development, and also at a direct insurer, in order to see how individual customer needs differ. Actuarial exams are to strengthen technical knowledge. Further classes in data analysis and computer science are planned, with more contact with teachers, alongside becoming more proactive. A return to RGA after graduation would be welcome if a suitable opening appeared. The environment is described as friendly, with strong support for learning.
advice for future interns: Build a strong Excel base and learn commonly used actuarial software such as AXIS and Prophet, and master classes such as Financial Mathematics and Life Insurance. Follow insurance-industry news, including consumer demand, market trends, and regulation. Be willing to ask questions, keep records, and use feedback. Stay enthusiastic, because a proactive attitude draws more guidance from the team.
technical skills: Excel risk analysis and traceable workbooks; AXIS profit summaries; net amount at risk, sum assured, profit margin, and new-business embedded value; credibility theory and group pricing; facultative, catastrophe, and high-net-worth quotation types; manual testing of a disease-classification tool; and archiving of premium and transaction records. Python and SQL are named as skills still to be built, not as skills already used.
soft skills: Teamwork was practised in mock interviews before joining. On the job, communication with Product Development and with a manager, comments on how a tool felt to use, asking for feedback after each task, and keeping records are described.
courses mentioned: Principles of life insurance pricing and risk models were revised before the interview. A Credibility Theory course and a Loss Modelling class were applied at work. Advice to later applicants names Financial Mathematics and Life Insurance. Actuarial exams are part of the later plan. No HKU course code is given.
tools and software: Excel and AXIS were used on the job. A disease-classification tool that uses artificial intelligence was tested, but it is not named. Prophet is recommended for applicants and is not described as software used during the internship.

job description: The internship was a full-time placement at Deloitte Advisory, described as a client-based consulting firm, and it lasted six months, with part-time work continued afterward so a project could be finished. Consulting projects follow other companies' requests, such as help with reporting, checks of clients' calculation logic, or systems meant to streamline a client's process. The intern worked on assignments for an asset-liability management department and for a pricing team, and sometimes with accounting and finance colleagues. The report contrasts this with in-house actuaries, who sit in one department of an insurer and focus on a narrower set of calculations.
job duties: Researched whether a client data set had to be reported to the Insurance Authority, where no guideline existed and the Authority could not answer clearly, so other teams and seniors were asked and the plan slipped; helped with Risk-Based Capital reporting when values depended on policy-level personal data that the client had to tidy first; did asset-liability calculations for assets, reserves, and liabilities, and pricing work that needed premium calculations; worked with accounting and finance colleagues; joined client progress meetings that were often recorded; changed the plan when urgent questions or late files arrived, often working late near deadlines and submitting a best effort to be amended after submission.
pre-internship preparation: This was not a first internship. About two years earlier there had been half a year on the CTF Life pricing team, which had already shown what an actuarial intern is often asked to do. Preparation included Excel practice and YouTube tutorials on VBA and Access, the tools most used in that earlier role. Deloitte was researched before the interview, but the link to actuarial work was unclear because public descriptions stressed audit, tax, and financial advisory. When asked about expectations and knowledge of Deloitte, the answer given was that there was little idea. The interviewer explained likely tasks and the difference between in-house and consulting actuaries, and said that willingness to learn mattered more than existing knowledge or skill.
what have I learned: Three differences from in-house actuarial work are set out. Client requests make the load larger and less stable than the original timeline, and checking time is often squeezed, so a best effort may be submitted and amended afterward. Consulting calls for faster and broader learning, because the next project may be asset-liability management, pricing, or work beside accountants, and Insurance Authority requirements change often. Client communication is constant, including recorded meetings and care about not promising too easily when the two sides disagree on what is feasible. Meeting a hard deadline is described as satisfying, and colleagues were generous in sharing knowledge. A return offer was accepted.
what do I need to improve: Before the interview, the link between Deloitte's advisory business and actuarial work was a stated worry, and that lack of knowledge was admitted when the interviewer asked. During the placement, shifting client requests produced delays, a growing list of tasks, and late nights near deadlines, with less protected time for checking than in an insurance company.
post-internship reflections: When the six-month programme ended, a manager's invitation to continue part-time was accepted so the current project could be wrapped up. A return offer was also accepted, with the hope that later work would be similarly enjoyable even though the workload is heavy. A further hope is, after graduation, to share knowledge with later interns. The daily learning from unexpected questions is given as a reason the role felt worthwhile.
advice for future interns: Students who want to improve are recommended to take part in the internship programme at Deloitte. The report passes on the interviewer's line that willingness to learn is what matters: if you are willing to learn, Deloitte is the place for you.
technical skills: Excel was practised before the internship, and VBA and Access were studied from tutorials because they had been common tools on an earlier pricing internship. Work at Deloitte covered Risk-Based Capital reporting, premium calculations, calculations of assets, reserves, and liabilities, checks of client calculation logic, and a basic use of accounting when working with finance colleagues.
soft skills: Client communication, including progress meetings that are recorded and care not to promise too easily, curiosity and willingness to learn, and working with other teams and senior colleagues are described as central to consulting actuarial work.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Excel, VBA, Access, and YouTube tutorials used to practise VBA and Access. Those tools are tied to preparation and to an earlier CTF Life pricing internship as well as to readiness for Deloitte.

job description: Manulife (International) Limited is a Canadian multinational insurance and financial services company with more than 130 years of history, headquartered in Toronto. It operates as Manulife in Asia and Canada and as John Hancock in the United States, covering life and health insurance, wealth and asset management, pensions, and investment solutions. The full-time internship from July 2025 to January 2026 was on the IFRS 17 Reporting Team in Hong Kong Corporate Actuarial, a group of about 25 people. The role maintained Group Life and Health reporting under IFRS 17, where actuarial teams estimate future cash flows and provide financial results to management.
job duties: Prepared and maintained Excel and Access files for Group Life and Health products; produced monthly gain-and-loss analyses on claims and tracked gaps between expected and actual experience; updated the new-and-renewal business summary to judge profitability and premium adequacy; followed procedure guides, checked formulas and links, sent workings to a senior for review, and submitted the validated files; built VBA macros that shortened manual data conversion; tried running models in AXIS; reconciled figures across linked files and traced whether differences were personal errors or other causes; at quarter-end, added quarterly and ad hoc tasks, including steps explained only verbally, and kept notes so those steps could be repeated; chased late source files and warned downstream teams so month-end and quarter-end production could continue.
pre-internship preparation: The opening came through a Statistics and Actuarial Science Society firm visit, with an office walk-around and small-group talks with managers or directors. Preparation included Manulife's history and achievements, conversations with HKU seniors who had interned there, and questions on team differences, daily actuarial work, and SOA exams before graduation. The next day, school-recruitment HR messaged on WhatsApp and held a phone call on hours, salary, holidays, department choice, and availability. Hong Kong Corporate Actuarial was chosen from those conversations. The process was conversational rather than a formal interview. A SAAS corporate mentorship with an AXA pricing manager also covered valuation versus pricing and IFRS 4 versus IFRS 17.
what have I learned: Daily work built Excel skills, including pivot tables and logical and lookup formulas, plus Access, VBA, and early AXIS use, despite no formal Excel study beyond Python and R. HKU and SOA ideas such as earned premium, claim ratio, and present value helped catch data anomalies rather than only following guides. Review meetings required explaining manual adjustments and the business logic behind them. Contact with teammates, other actuarial teams, customer service, and IT was needed when files were late around public holidays. IFRS 17 terms such as risk adjustment, best estimate liability, and contractual service margin were set against IFRS 4, showing how an insurer balances profitability, risk, and compliance.
what do I need to improve: VBA and SQL had not been learned properly beforehand, so several weeks went into reading code and fixing macro and query errors. Linked-file outputs sometimes failed to reconcile, and tracing whether the cause was a personal mistake was slow and delayed colleagues. Some quarter-end procedures had no written guide and were explained only verbally. A closing feedback meeting mentioned areas to improve, but those areas are not named.
post-internship reflections: The internship confirmed a goal of becoming a life actuary and an interest in returning to Manulife after graduation because of the culture, colleagues, and learning. Four SOA exams are already passed, with a plan to finish five exams and all VEEs before graduation and to strengthen data-analytics and modelling skills through coursework and self-study.
advice for future interns: Ask questions confidently, because seniors will explain when they are free. Use the internship to practice time and workload management. Strengthen Excel and programming skills before starting so it is easier to adapt and contribute.
technical skills: Technical work used Excel, including pivot tables and logical and lookup formulas, Microsoft Access, VBA macros, AXIS model runs, SQL queries, monthly gain-and-loss analysis, and IFRS 17 items such as risk adjustment, best estimate liability, and contractual service margin.
soft skills: The report names workplace communication with teammates and other departments, time management, problem-solving, and asking seniors to explain adjustments and business logic.
courses mentioned: SOA exams are named, including four already passed and a plan to complete five exams and all VEEs. HKU knowledge is mentioned without a course code.
tools and software: Named tools are Excel, Microsoft Access, VBA, AXIS, SQL, Python, and R.

job description: Prudential Corporation Asia is the regional head office of Prudential plc and oversees direct insurance operations across local business units in Asia. The internship, from June to December 2025, was on the Heavy Model Team under the Group Internal Economic Capital Assessment Team. About two months were training, one month a dry run, and three months GIECA year-end production, with ad hoc user acceptance testing, housekeeping, and documentation. The Heavy Model Team runs actuarial models from local business units and produces outputs such as best estimate liability for the Lite Model Team to calibrate.
job duties: Studied operation manuals and replicated the previous year's production outputs; wrote detailed workspace notes and a Tips and Reminders guide; built and debugged Excel VBA tools, including small tools for local-business-unit adjustments; in user acceptance testing, found and fixed a functional bug and documented the solution; used Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise and viewed model code in diagram view without editing it; ran dry-run models on dummy inputs for a base scenario and a checking scenario, and investigated incorrect input from the India local business unit; in year-end production, ran assigned workspaces, including three workspaces in two weeks when submissions were late; calculated forward rates from spot rates to check yield-curve consistency; did housekeeping and repeated SQL uploads when storage and connections were unstable.
pre-internship preparation: The offer came from a Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science career fair. A CV was left at the Prudential Corporation Asia booth, and a short interview with a manager followed. Questions included how interest rates might move in a recession, from ECON1220 Introductory Macroeconomics, and an explanation of Markov chains, before STAT3903 Stochastic Models had been taken. A verbal offer was followed months later by an official email and assignment to the Heavy Model Team. Before onboarding there was a medical examination, updated glasses and professional attire, a mentorship with a pricing actuary at Reinsurance Group of America, and PCA training on insurance regulations and principles.
what have I learned: Training built Excel automation, VBA through debugging, and use of Prophet Professional and Prophet Enterprise. SQL uploads were highly automated, so coding exposure stayed limited. Dry runs showed the special adjustments each local business unit needs, and the value of finishing partial work when inputs are incomplete. Forward rates calculated from spot rates were used to check yield curves. Problems were reported by stating the issue, a hypothesis, attempts and results, then asking for solutions. Communication and workplace behaviour were part of the gain. Little exposure to investment and insurance-market information meant business sense did not develop.
what do I need to improve: A folder was permanently deleted during housekeeping. It was not a serious case, but the lesson was to check backups first. Workload became uneven when local business units submitted late. SQL coding exposure was limited, and the report calls the lack of investment and insurance-market exposure, and the resulting weak business sense, the biggest pity.
post-internship reflections: Capital modelling was enjoyable, but the plan is to explore part-time work in reinsurance pricing or consultancy finance and to test academic research next summer through an offered place on the Mitacs Global Research Internship Programme, while still looking for actuarial internships. Study at HKU is following the department's suggested course arrangements. The same experience was later shared as a student adviser for juniors admitted in 2025.
advice for future interns: Raise more meaningful questions with seniors or hiring managers so as to stand out. Network with actuarial professionals, because familiar faces reappear across companies. Join the corporate mentorship programme and the career fair.
technical skills: Technical work used Excel automation, VBA, Prophet Professional, Prophet Enterprise, user acceptance testing, actuarial model runs, forward-rate checks from spot rates, and limited SQL uploads.
soft skills: The report describes a structured way of reporting problems to a manager, collaboration with managers, and communication and workplace behaviour.
courses mentioned: ECON1220 Introductory Macroeconomics was used in an interview answer. STAT3903 Stochastic Models is named as not yet taken at that time. The department's suggested course arrangements are mentioned without listing codes.
tools and software: Named tools are Excel, VBA, Prophet Professional, Prophet Enterprise, and SQL.

job description: FWD Life Insurance Company (Bermuda) Limited is described as an insurer in which actuaries take part in product design, pricing, and risk modelling. The internship ran from 16 June 2025 to 2 January 2026 on the pricing and product development team, which designs new products, sets premium structures, and checks client information after purchase. The work covered monthly actual-versus-expected claim consolidation for Hong Kong and Macau, post-checking of medical and universal life products, and user acceptance testing for a new product, Imperial Life Fortune. During the internship the pricing department moved from Wan Chai to Devon House in Quarry Bay, renamed FWD Tower, and FWD listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
job duties: Did monthly actual-versus-expected consolidation for crisis and death claims in Hong Kong and Macau; used Microsoft Access to extract claim numbers, claim type, claim amount, and reinsurance recovery; compared those figures with the valuation team's report and manually adjusted duplicates when a client held more than one product; compared actual claims with expected claims, with assumptions usually updated quarterly; built charts and graphs for supervisors; post-checked medical and universal life products against pricing assumptions; looked up client information in IBM AS400 and found premium errors from IT and agent miscalculations; joined user acceptance testing for Imperial Life Fortune, checking how sex, smoker status, preferred-plus status, withdrawal, partial surrender, a quit-smoking initiative, and loading changed cost of insurance and premium.
pre-internship preparation: Applications were sent on LinkedIn in summer 2024. Before the FWD interview, research covered the company's place in life insurance and products aimed at younger customers, plus life contingencies, risk modelling, statistics, and the work of reporting, pricing, and valuation teams. The interview was about 30 minutes with human resources and then about an hour with three actuaries. A hard question was to define reserves without formulas, as if speaking to a client with no actuarial knowledge, after a first answer that used the present value of premiums and losses.
what have I learned: Pricing work was seen as forecasting, risk evaluation, and balancing profit with customer needs, not only calculation. Actual-versus-expected analysis and post-checking showed that assumptions must be reviewed against experience. Advanced Excel formulas, data handling, and VBA improved through self-study, including Microsoft Copilot, after formulas proved unfamiliar. IBM AS400 was used to read client records. Explaining reserves in plain language, studying old files when instructions were brief, and speaking up about issues were treated as necessary at work.
what do I need to improve: Excel formulas and functions were unfamiliar at the start, although most tasks depended on data handling and calculations. The fast pace was also difficult because busy seniors often gave only brief instructions, which caused struggle early in the internship.
post-internship reflections: The career goal is to become a qualified actuary, with stronger interest in pricing and product development, and a willingness to rejoin FWD Life Insurance Company after graduation. The plan is to sit more Society of Actuaries exams before graduation, study advanced Excel formulas and VBA on YouTube, practice shortcuts, and look for further part-time actuarial internships.
advice for future interns: Sit at least one or two SOA examinations to show commitment to the career. Build strong Excel skills, because analysis and automation matter in actuarial internship work. Stay curious and take a proactive approach to learning.
technical skills: Technical work used Microsoft Access extracts, Excel formulas, VBA, IBM AS400, actual-versus-expected consolidation, pricing post-checks, and user acceptance testing of premium and cost-of-insurance parameters.
soft skills: The report stresses explaining actuarial ideas without formulas, proactive communication when instructions were brief, and independent problem-solving while learning Excel.
courses mentioned: University study in probability theory, statistical analysis, life contingencies, and actuarial modelling is cited without course codes. Society of Actuaries exams are named as preparation for graduation and as advice to later students.
tools and software: Named tools are LinkedIn, Microsoft Access, Excel, VBA, IBM AS400, Microsoft Copilot, and YouTube.

job description: Prudential Hong Kong Limited writes life insurance. The six-month internship was on the Macau Risk-Based Capital team, which handles business planning, projection, and other work for the Macau market. The role prepared raw data for monthly and quarterly reports. Those inputs, including risk-free rates taken from bond yields, then went through a built-in Prophet model to produce mathematical reserves and solvency margins. Checking files were used to confirm that the model was working.
job duties: Prepared raw data for Macau monthly and quarterly reports and managed more than 100 Excel files, some with built-in formulas and add-ins; assembled risk-free rates for currencies such as HKD, USD, and CAD from bond yield to maturity; integrated, processed, and calculated further figures in Excel; used the built-in Prophet model to calculate mathematical reserves and solvency margins; maintained checking files and did manual calculations with fixed formulas and Excel functions to confirm that the model was functioning.
pre-internship preparation: Selection was one interview with three managers from different teams. Preparation covered why this company and department, why the candidate should be hired, a short self-introduction, a review of school actuarial material, and online reading on basic actuarial knowledge. One interviewer asked how to calculate reserves. An unexpected Excel question asked how to pull interest rates for different data sets from other workbooks. The report later names VLOOKUP as the model answer, which was not given in the interview.
what have I learned: The work showed the operational detail behind insurance calculations, with more factors than classroom formulas. Insurance terminology and calculation logic from an actuarial background made the duties easier to learn. Excel functions and add-ins became usable after repeated practice and sped up data processing. A stalled urgent task showed that asking questions immediately matters more than avoiding embarrassment, because later steps depended on the supporting data.
