In the second month, urgent same-day tasks given only by a short phone briefing were not finished, because questions stopped and an AI tool was used instead. The mentor took the work over, and the delay held up the team.
post-internship reflections: The six months clarified how a life insurer operates and opened interest in other insurance roles and in data-analysis jobs outside insurance, including risk management in finance. A finance course was taken this semester for that reason. Returning to Prudential Hong Kong Limited is possible but not decided, because other companies and roles are still being explored. The culture and working environment are described positively.
advice for future interns: Become fluent in a wide range of Excel shortcuts and formulas, because most of this role is done in Excel. Learn VBA so repetitive monthly and quarterly integration of files can be automated.
technical skills: Technical work used Excel functions, add-ins, and formulas, a built-in Prophet model, risk-free rates from bond yield to maturity, mathematical reserves, and solvency margins.
soft skills: The report describes asking a mentor questions in time, including about Excel shortcuts, after staying silent had delayed the team.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Named tools used are Excel and Prophet. VBA is recommended for future interns and is not described as used on the job.

company: AXA Hong Kong & Macau / Prudential Corporation Asia
job title: General Insurance (GI) pricing intern / capital management intern
job description: Two internships are reported. In the first half of 2025 the role was general insurance pricing intern at AXA Hong Kong & Macau. AXA is described as a French insurer in 51 markets serving 94 million customers, and as Hong Kong's largest general insurance provider, so the work followed property-and-casualty pricing. From July the role was capital management intern at Prudential Corporation Asia. Prudential plc is described as a British life insurer with its regional head office in Hong Kong. That team monitors local business unit solvency so capital can meet long-term liabilities.
job duties: At AXA, produced dashboards for general insurance products, priced renewal policies, analysed property-and-casualty portfolios, assisted user acceptance testing, and ran SAS programs; each month analysed employee compensation policies, extracted historical claims in SAS, filled pricing templates, and set technical premiums as pure premium plus variable expense per unit, then commented on prior-year results for underwriters; with reserving, studied seasonality in Personal Accident, Travel, Motor, and Household claims by the triangle method and compared CDF and ultimate loss ratios. At Prudential, pulled weekly interest rates and equity indexes from SQL and checked breakpoints; produced monthly solvency estimates, commentaries, and presentations; prepared quarterly capital packs on group solvency, FSR, hurdle rates, and WACC; helped approve expense payments, submitted service-tax invoices to the e-invoicing system, and completed IFRS 17, balance-sheet, and profit-and-loss reporting.
pre-internship preparation: In first year, a KPMG corporate mentorship with an experienced actuary covered careers, market segmentation, interview tips, and promotion, and those tips were used with KPMG Actuarial Advisory. Second year added CV writing sessions, simulated interviews, and aptitude tests, plus two Society of Actuaries exams and extracurricular activities. Recurring interview questions were refined across several rounds. Eight offers arrived in one day, and AXA and Prudential were chosen to see both general insurance and life insurance.
what have I learned: The internships deepened familiarity with insurance and with solvency concepts, and built connections with peers and professionals. Work across multicultural teams developed communication, a wider perspective, and the ability to work alone and with other departments. A shared Excel list of tasks, due dates, and assigners was used when several supervisors set work at once. Small technical mistakes led to more self-checking. Triangle development, CDF, and ultimate loss ratios were applied to general-insurance service lines.
what do I need to improve: Time pressure was a problem when duties arrived from different supervisors at the same time. Small technical mistakes happened, with a stated need for more self-learning and checking to fill gaps in professional knowledge. Cantonese speaking needed improvement for easier conversation with teammates.
post-internship reflections: The internships strengthened the aim of becoming a professional actuary. Studies are to finish in June, with a hope of an actuarial job in Hong Kong, a faster start, more industry and technical knowledge, and more professional exams in spare time. Longer term, the hope is to lead projects and teammates, while also considering a change of profession or a return to study. Future work is expected to cross paths with AXA and Prudential again.
advice for future interns: Take the lead, welcome challenges, and feel free to ask questions. The report tells later students that every experience, easy or difficult, is a step in improving.
technical skills: Technical work used SAS, SQL, dashboards, technical-premium and renewal pricing, triangle development, CDF and ultimate loss ratios, solvency monitoring, IFRS 17, balance-sheet and profit-and-loss reporting, and Excel task tracking.
soft skills: The report names communication, collaboration, adapting to different working styles, independent work across departments, and self-discipline. Cantonese speaking is named as still weak.
courses mentioned: STAT4903 is named as the source of the technical premium formula. Two Society of Actuaries exams are named as already passed, with a plan to take more professional tests.
tools and software: Named tools are SAS, SQL, Excel, and an e-invoicing system.

job description: AXA is described as a financial-services and insurance company offering health, life, property and casualty, and savings products, together with risk management and financial protection. The internship was in the Chief Life and Health Insurance Office. The intern was not placed on one team and instead did regular studies, ad hoc tasks, and projects across teams, with a focus on traditional pricing for wealth management, life, and health. In the report, pricing teams set mortality and incidence rates and build models, while valuation reviews participating and non-participating products and the asset-liability position.
job duties: Monitored product performance from monthly surrender and lapse records, estimated coming bonus and minor-claim payments, and tracked trends; answered client questions on value projections, charge breakdowns, and payback of paid-up policies; produced illustration summaries of discounted policies for agents and brokers; did SOA checking with the reinsurance team; prepared yearly assumption templates, handbooks, and PowerPoint decks; compared products using internal rate of return and gross internal rate of return and researched product background; helped prepare a deferred-annuity report for the Insurance Authority; enhanced a value-projection model for an extra health loading and pay mode, using SecureGPT and test projections; adjusted an assumption handbook, including mortality improvement; each month filed wealth-management and health reports and shared updated data; suggested non-price factors on a medical-indexation project.
pre-internship preparation: The AXA interview fell in Revision Week of Year 1 Semester 2, so preparation time was short. An April interview had shown that questions would follow courses then being studied. Company background was researched, and Chinese and English self-introductions were prepared. Three days prior, HR set an online Chinese interview with the Pricing Department senior manager. It covered a short introduction, reasons for choosing AXA, including its general-insurance standing in Hong Kong and the values Customer First, Integrity, Courage, and One AXA, business-competition and society experience, and a department choice. Pricing was chosen over valuation, general insurance, and employee benefits.
what have I learned: Regular and ad hoc work covered product analysis, data management, value projections, and lapse assumptions, and applied programme material to live products. Python packages pandas, os, and NumPy were used in analysis, building on COMP1117. STAT2902 and STAT3904 supported net present value, interest, and internal rate of return when products were compared. STAT3901 supported life-contingency features and pricing factors. Python, VBA, and Excel improved by working through models. Communication and time management grew across team deadlines. Comments on a medical-indexation project, invited by a senior, reduced an estimated error.
what do I need to improve: Time management was difficult because several teams and deadlines overlapped. Monthly data often arrived only at noon on the first working day, while two wealth-management reports and one health report were due, along with ad hoc tasks. Early on, the role was viewed as minor support work until seniors asked for opinions.
post-internship reflections: The industry picture is clearer, and the goal is to become a fellow actuary. The plan is to balance university study with SOA exams, earn more university exemption credits, and sit as many exams as possible. Rejoining the company after graduation is under consideration because the professionals, environment, and support fitted that aim.
advice for future interns: Revise life contingencies and financial mathematics before applying, because they are used at work. Learn Excel VBA and strengthen Python so more analytics tools are familiar. Take initiative and be proactive in the workplace.
technical skills: Technical work used Python with pandas, os, and NumPy, VBA, Excel, internal rate of return and gross internal rate of return, net present value, life-contingency product features, value-projection modelling, and mortality assumptions.
soft skills: The report names communication and time management from working across teams and deadlines, and speaking up when seniors asked for opinions.
courses mentioned: COMP1117 Computer Programming, STAT2902 Financial Mathematics, STAT3904 Corporate Finance for Actuarial Science, and STAT3901 Life Contingency I are named as courses used on the job. SOA exams and university exemption credits are also named.
tools and software: Named tools are Python, pandas, os, NumPy, VBA, Excel, PowerPoint, and SecureGPT.

job description: The internship was at Ernst & Young, which provides assurance, consulting, strategy, tax, and transaction advisory across industries. The placement was in the actuarial consulting team. Unlike an in-house insurer actuary, the team advises external clients, including insurers, reinsurers, and other corporations, on risk quantification, strategic planning, and regulatory compliance. Three projects were involved. Before the internship, actuarial work had been linked mainly to premiums, reserves, and solvency inside insurance. The placement showed the same methods used in wider business decisions.
job duties: Conducted research and reviewed client materials, including modelling documentation and insurance product specifications, then summarized findings for the project manager; investigated how policyholders respond to market returns and the risk-free rate, using articles and industry reports, market numbers, and investor-behaviour data; consolidated that comparison in a spreadsheet, plotted trend graphs, and measured the gap between assumed and actual behaviour so the project manager could use it in decisions; on a live project with short deadlines, asked other interns about onboarding steps and checked task problems with project colleagues while setting aside non-urgent induction items.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation covered company and role research, including a teamwork culture, plus practice of a self-introduction and expected behavioural questions by revisiting technical points on the CV and actuarial coursework rather than repeating the CV. Selection began with a face-to-face interview and then an online assessment that included English and behavioural parts. One question asked how to prioritize several urgent tasks from different projects. The answer used deadlines and task dependencies, especially work that would block teammates or the next project phase.
what have I learned: Industry frameworks rarely covered in class, especially IFRS 17 and HKRBC, became familiar, along with the structure of some products. Research tasks drew on corporate-finance and financial-derivatives ideas such as behaviour under different risk attitudes and market volatility. Assignments arrived as high-level objectives, so solutions had to be found without step-by-step instructions. Communication, teamwork, and relationships grew, including at department gatherings where seniors discussed careers and projects. A direct start on a live project made peer help and time management necessary.
what do I need to improve: NA
post-internship reflections: The career goal is to become a qualified actuary specializing in risk management, using quantitative work to support business decisions. The plan is to complete as many professional examinations as possible and to seek further internships in insurance companies, including life valuation and pricing, so experience is not limited to consulting. Rejoining Ernst & Young after graduation would be welcome because of the mentorship, culture, and variety, but other sectors will be explored first.
advice for future interns: For a similar consulting role, keep a strong technical base and be comfortable with Microsoft Office, especially Excel, because those tools are heavily used. Communication matters, because findings have to be understood and acted on. A basic grasp of industry developments and regulation helps, but it is not required.
technical skills: Technical work used research and review of modelling documents and product specifications, spreadsheet analysis, trend graphs, comparisons of assumed and actual policyholder behaviour, and frameworks including IFRS 17 and HKRBC, with corporate-finance and financial-derivatives ideas applied to risk attitudes and volatility.
soft skills: The report names communication, teamwork, critical thinking, proactiveness, peer support, and time management.
courses mentioned: A corporate finance course and financial derivatives from the programme are named as knowledge used at work. Professional examinations are mentioned without a syllabus name.
tools and software: Microsoft Office and Excel are named as tools heavily used in the consulting work. Findings were also put into a spreadsheet.

job description: The six-month internship was at Manulife, on the Local Team of Hong Kong Corporate Actuarial. That team supports compliance with Hong Kong's Risk-Based Capital framework through calculations, stress tests, scenario analysis, reporting, and modelling for capital adequacy and reserves. The intern also prepared and analysed Macau Insurance Ordinance figures, including reserve movement analysis. An intern project with Regional Actuarial Services summarized participating funds. Reserves are described as amounts set aside for future liabilities and as a window on solvency.
job duties: Did Macau Insurance Ordinance preparation and reserve movement analysis for 1.5 Full Preliminary Term, Premium Deficiency Reserve, and Excess Cash Value; ran the premium-deficiency programme in SQL about twice a month, valued the three reserve types under different bonds and interest rates, and turned the results into solvency-margin and reserve figures; used SQL and AXIS, checking that codes and assumptions were right before a run; at quarter-end and year-end, helped with model change management for new products, paid-up policies, and assumption changes; with Regional Actuarial Services, researched participating-fund dividends, Asset Share, and the Experience Fluctuation Account, summarized them, and the group won a best-team prize.
pre-internship preparation: There was no traditional interview. The offer followed a company visit in first year, when actuarial work and insurance were still unclear. Preliminary reading identified pricing and valuation as two pillars, but not how they fit together. Fresh graduates and current students were consulted, and managers were spoken with during the visit. Human resources then called, and the offer was accepted. Hong Kong Corporate Actuarial was chosen in order to see corporate operations in Hong Kong. The report credits the offer to interest shown and a proactive manner at the visit.
what have I learned: SQL and AXIS became the tools for running models and handling large sets of assumptions and results, which also practiced coding. STAT3901 material on premiums and reserves was applied, but workplace figures were split across many items and had to be interpreted, with lapse, mortality, and morbidity all affecting reserves. Model change management showed how new products, paid-up policies, and assumption changes move policy values. The participating-fund project introduced Asset Share and the Experience Fluctuation Account. Lunch-and-learn sessions added further actuarial background.
what do I need to improve: The first model-change-management run was started in SQL without updating the new assumptions, so the results were wrong and a senior had to repair the run overnight. The stated lesson was to confirm every step before starting a run so the same mistake would not happen again.
post-internship reflections: The internship clarified that examinations, internship experience, and soft skills all belong in a personal portfolio, and that more actuarial activities would widen that base. Manulife is described as comfortable, with supportive colleagues, lunch-and-learn talks, and intern projects that give a view of other teams.
advice for future interns: Do not rely only on actuarial exams. Learn how actuarial concepts and models are used in finance, for example through ASHK events or by consulting seniors and professors. Become familiar with AI tools, because the report treats them as a concern for large companies and as help for future candidates.
technical skills: Technical work used SQL, AXIS, reserve movement analysis, premium-deficiency calculations, solvency-margin figures, model change management, and participating-fund measures including Asset Share and the Experience Fluctuation Account.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: STAT3901 is named as material applied to premiums and reserves in the daily work. Actuarial exams are mentioned without a syllabus name.
tools and software: Named tools used are SQL and AXIS. AI tools are recommended without a product name.

job description: Chubb Life is described as a US-based insurance company. The internship was as a Product Pricing Team Intern and began shortly after a new agency system launched. Daily work was user acceptance testing and support for that change, covering new products still on the previous system and the company's best-selling basic and rider plans at the same time. Other tasks compared whole-life savings plans across insurers and checked campaign discounts for arbitrage. Monthly pricing meetings added context on launches, experience studies, and pricing assumptions.
job duties: Built test plans across insured profiles and policy options, and prepared new-business illustrations from specifications and brochures for plans such as the Voluntary Health Insurance Scheme, investment-linked assurance, and waiver of premium; generated proposals and checked displayed premiums against an Excel illustration; sent test plans, illustrations, and old-system PDFs to the project team, then compared counts and values with PDFs from the new agency system; for market comparison, extracted guaranteed cash value and total cash value from proposal PDFs and calculated guaranteed and total internal rates of return and break-even years; checked that day-one guaranteed cash value plus commission did not exceed a campaign-discounted premium; wrote VBA macros to price many cases, enter test cases into the agency system, generate PDFs, and edit the code when the system changed.

Prepared questions asked about challenges, skills to build before the start, and typical pricing-intern tasks.
what have I learned: The main technical gain was VBA, from cell selection, copy and paste, and opening workbooks through loops that automated Excel work and pushed test cases into the agency system. Reading specifications built a clearer view of product features and restrictions. post-internship reflections: The internship created a strong interest in a full-time pricing role. The assigned work was mainly testing, but team meetings showed a broader pricing function. Valuation is also of interest, and a valuation and pricing internship at another insurer is planned so the two sides can be compared. Part-time work at Chubb continues in the first half of 2026, and a full-time return would be welcome.
advice for future interns: Before a product-pricing internship, build Excel functions and basic VBA so large sets of data and illustrations are manageable. Take time to understand different product types. Ask colleagues questions and show a willingness to learn and grow.
technical skills: Technical work used Excel functions and illustrations, VBA macros, user acceptance testing, PDF comparison, and pricing metrics including guaranteed and total internal rates of return and break-even years.
soft skills: The report describes asking colleagues for help after first trying an internal AI tool, taking notes in pricing meetings, and following up with questions.

company: Chubb Life HK / HSBC Insurance (Asia) Limited

post-internship reflections: The HSBC internship is described as useful for career planning, and rejoining the company after graduation would be considered. Experience from both internships is only in valuation, which now feels suitable and is the preferred area of future work.
advice for future interns: Be proactive and do not hesitate to ask managers or supervisors questions, including questions about the actuarial industry, career planning, and life advice. The report says most of them would be willing to help.

job description: The host reinsurance company is not named. Its clients are direct insurers. It takes ceded premium to help them manage risk and cedes premium onward to transfer risk, and it updates and tests models for existing treaties. The report describes this field as still developing and not very well known in Hong Kong. The internship was on the Hong Kong valuation team while the company was moving regular runs to a faster tool. The role covered pre-quarter-end cash-flow reports, scenario testing, and Long-Duration Targeted Improvements reporting.
job duties: Ran macros and prepared cash-flow reports for the pre-quarter-end position; tested data under scenarios that changed assumptions such as interest rates, lapse, catalyzing factors, and longevity, and judged whether results looked reasonable; worked on Long-Duration Targeted Improvements, learned the net premium ratio quickly from prior GAAP study, and calculated present values of cash flows; built a VBA tool that measures the quarter-to-quarter change in present values of premiums and benefits by the company's method, and teammates used that tool; compared a new faster tool with the old one, found an unreasonable old-tool result caused by the input data, showed the supervisor the evidence, and the model was rerun.

what have I learned: Excel had rarely been used at university and became a main skill, including shortcuts, filters, pivot tables, and VBA templates. Programme knowledge of product types made cash-flow patterns easier to follow, and changes in interest, lapse, and longevity were easier to judge for reasonableness. GAAP reporting studied in the programme made Long-Duration Targeted Improvements and the net premium ratio easier to learn. Programming logic made VBA quick to pick up. what do I need to improve: After the internship, actuarial knowledge is described as not broad enough, with a need to study different models and insurance policies harder. In the first days the intern was too shy to talk with colleagues and did not know how to build those relationships.
post-internship reflections: Most of the tasks experienced were regular tasks, so rejoining is of interest mainly in order to try the company's project-based work. The environment, the view, and the colleagues are described positively. Further study of different models and insurance policies is planned.
advice for future interns: Learn Excel, SQL, and Alteryx before joining so the work is easier to pick up and colleagues spend less time teaching tools. Use known shortcuts. Prepare questions for experienced colleagues on career paths, the team's purpose, and how departments work together. Be willing to talk with people, including directors or team heads, and ask them for advice.

soft skills: The report describes overcoming early shyness, getting to know colleagues, and explaining a data error to a supervisor with supporting evidence.
