job description: The 6.5-month internship was at Manulife Financial Asia Limited, as an actuarial intern in Regional Actuarial Services at the Singapore Valuation Shared Services Center. Reports and assumptions are produced quarterly for the Singapore business unit, with differences such as basic model changes in the third quarter and extra annual reports in the fourth. Each quarter has user acceptance testing, model change management, and production, when official reserves are calculated. Colleagues in that center work from the Philippines, so daily contact was through Teams. During production the intern owned medium-term reserve sensitivity.
job duties: In production, ran medium-term sensitivity by calculating reserves under scenarios such as higher interest rates, lower risk-free rates, higher lapses, lower mortality, and lower morbidity, and compared them with the prior quarter; in user acceptance testing, tried the next quarter's changes, estimated impact and profit, and compared trends with the production just finished, without adding new products; in model change management, applied model changes, calculated reserves against production, and put new products into the model; set up each run in Moody's AXIS from instruction documents and rewrote missing steps so the next person could find the right screens; built checking files used in production and wrote progress notes; on a group project about AI in financial risk management, helped cut time on some Asia Risk Management tasks and then used AI on daily files.
pre-internship preparation: Career fairs, firm visits, and mentorship events were attended while looking for an internship. A place was offered in the HKU Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science corporate mentorship programme, with a Manulife mentor and eight meetings. Before each meeting a topic was assigned, including the Voluntary Health Insurance Scheme and a qualifying deferred annuity policy, and it was researched and presented for comment. When the internship search came up, the mentor contacted human resources and an offer followed.
what have I learned: Seeing user acceptance testing, model change management, and production showed how reserves are calculated and what valuation work involves. Moody's AXIS and SQL were learned, and Excel improved enough to create checking files that production actually used. Named soft-skill gains are asking necessary and clear questions, finishing complex work in a short time with few errors, and submitting several tasks on time. Clear progress notes were also learned. A group project on AI in financial risk management cut time for some Asia Risk Management tasks and led to AI use on daily files.
what do I need to improve: Model setup in AXIS was the hardest part of the role. The interface is layered, senior guides often skipped how to reach a screen and sometimes showed only a screenshot, and a small mistake forces a rerun. Fitting in was also a worry at the start because teammates worked from the Philippines and could be reached only on Teams.
post-internship reflections: Valuation feels comfortable after 6.5 months, but choosing a field is described as too early after seeing only one. If the next role can be chosen, a different area such as pricing, reinsurance, or retirement would be preferred. More SOA exams are planned during the undergraduate degree.
advice for future interns: Be comfortable with repetitive quarterly work, because the same files and steps return each quarter, including four waves of medium-term sensitivity. Someone looking for a constantly challenging job may find valuation dull. Learn basic Excel first, especially shortcuts and functions such as SUMIF, COUNTIF, and lookup. Advanced VBA or macros were not required in this role.
technical skills: Technical work used Moody's AXIS, SQL, Excel including SUMIF, COUNTIF, lookup, and shortcuts, reserve sensitivity testing, model setup, checking files, documentation, and AI applied to financial risk management tasks.
soft skills: The report names asking clear questions, time management, completing several tasks on time with few errors, and building a working relationship with remote teammates.
courses mentioned: SOA exams are named as a study plan during the undergraduate degree. The Voluntary Health Insurance Scheme and a qualifying deferred annuity policy were mentorship topics, not HKU course codes.
tools and software: Named tools are Moody's AXIS, SQL, Excel, and Microsoft Teams. AI was used in the group project and on daily files, without a product name.

job description: The report covers two six-month internships. AXA is a French multinational insurer, mainly a primary insurer, with reinsurance only a minor part of the business. From 2 January to 30 June 2025 the role was Life Product Intern on the product team. Hang Seng Insurance Company (HSIC), which the report calls HSBC Insurance and links to Hang Seng Bank as a principal member of the HSBC Group, hosted the second role from 23 July to 31 December 2025 on the Actuarial Analytics team. Actuarial work is described as managing risk for the insurer, policy owner, and reinsurer by estimating claims and reserves and setting interest and premium assumptions.
job duties: At AXA, prepared special quotations for overage clients or for an instant discount or extra rebate, and created proposals and supplementary forms by hand when the wording differed from standard proposals; assisted with the English and Chinese launch kit and with user-acceptance checks of wording and validations for a savings product launched in late May 2025; compared market returns with cash-flow and internal-rate-of-return calculations. At Hang Seng, applied factors to morbidity assumptions and ran Prophet; ran Prophet after changing assumptions and rates from the IFRS17 team; prepared monthly reports on premium-financing policies for different channels and calculated dividends; built an Excel VBA routine to extract data from Prophet.
pre-internship preparation: Several hours were spent revising STAT3901, described as the prerequisite for STAT4767, but the AXA interview did not use that material. AXA was a ten-minute phone call with a one-minute self-introduction, scenarios on communication and adapting to a new setting, three strengths and three weaknesses, and how to manage time when many tasks arrive together. The manager then explained intern duties and working hours. Before Hang Seng, applications went to more than five companies through JobsDB and the HKU internship system. Fubon Insurance asked about mortality, interest rates, internal rate of return, and the definitions of dividend and bonus. Hannover Re asked about attentiveness, loyalty, and what a low GPA says about personality. The Hang Seng interview used complicated questions tied mostly to STAT3901 and STAT3904, while the human-resources questions were easier.
what have I learned: On the product team, trusted work led to a wider mix of tasks, and an early difficulty speaking at team lunches because of the age gap eased after colleagues asked about everyday life and hobbies. At Hang Seng, the most valued gain was Excel VBA for extracting Prophet data, together with Prophet runs for morbidity factors and IFRS17 assumption changes, premium-financing reports, and dividend calculations. Urgent work outside the syllabus was handled by reading instructions, asking colleagues on Teams, and researching the actuarial points involved. The experience also showed that an actuarial student can do more than only become an actuary.
what do I need to improve: Time management, task difficulty, and interpersonal relationships are named as difficulties at Hang Seng. Several urgent tasks often arrived on the same day and had to be understood from the instructions before work could start. For one week the hours ran from 9:00 a.m. until 7:00 a.m. the next morning because the work was hard and urgent. At AXA in the first month, communication felt weak and almost nothing was said at daily team lunches because of the age gap with full-time staff.
post-internship reflections: Before these internships, actuarial study felt boring, and the worry was that actuaries were introverted, worked overtime, and had no social events. The later aim is to start a business using mathematical and financial knowledge, but first to work as an actuary and pursue Society of Actuaries exams, and to turn to the business after saving enough capital. Two semesters of leave mean a five-year degree, one year deferred. A return to AXA after graduation is under consideration because the office is close to home and the environment, including team lunches, was better than expected.
advice for future interns: Use the internship to test whether an actuarial career really fits. Interact more with colleagues, because some of the learning is not the work that was expected. Trying something outside a comfort zone is what makes those experiences possible.
technical skills: Special quotations, manual proposal forms, launch-kit and user-acceptance checks, cash-flow and internal-rate-of-return comparisons, Prophet runs, morbidity assumption factors, premium-financing reports, dividend calculations, and Excel VBA extraction from Prophet.
soft skills: The AXA interview tested communication and adaptability. The report later describes learning to speak with older colleagues, building trust with a manager, and handling several urgent tasks at once.
courses mentioned: STAT3901, STAT3904, and STAT4767 are named. Society of Actuaries exams are the planned next professional step.
tools and software: Prophet, Excel VBA, and Microsoft Teams.

job description: AXA Hong Kong is described as one of the biggest insurers in Hong Kong, offering life insurance to individuals and businesses, including protection, savings, retirement, and investment products. The six-month internship, from July to December 2025, was in the Participating Product Team, which manages participating life policies that pay guaranteed benefits such as cash value and non-guaranteed bonuses. The role supported monthly asset-share reporting and policyholder complaint cases about bonuses or benefit amounts.
job duties: Assisted monthly asset-share calculations in Excel by extracting data from different systems, importing them into working files, and correcting errors so final asset-share numbers, bonuses, and performance reviews could be produced; from August to November, ran parallel comparisons of an older VBA cash-flow extraction and a new Python method, investigated differences, and adjusted monthly files until the outputs matched, after which the Python method was approved for routine use in November; for complaints, recalculated policy values or benefits with re-illustration tools, reset model parameters when client information was wrong, and sent the results to the complaint-handling team.
pre-internship preparation: With no prior internship, preparation included reading the AXA website and reviewing STAT3901 Life Contingencies I so product knowledge was fresh, covering whole life, endowment, and annuity business. A CV and cover letter went through the internship system. A week later, interviewers asked about the importance of interest rates, familiarity with insurance products, and pricing methods. The answers linked interest rates to discounting future cash flows and to investment returns on reserves. The interview ended with a choice among valuation, pricing, and investment, and a human-resources offer came the same day.
what have I learned: Coursework on cash flows and bonuses made the monthly asset-share process easier to follow. Complaint cases showed how sensitive present values are to age and gender, and how an unpaid premium can be deducted from policy value, as with an automatic policy loan or lapse, which connected to FINA 2342. Excel moved from basic formulas to large datasets, cash-flow tables, macros, and hotkeys. In the office, Excel and Prophet were far more common than R, which lectures emphasise, and were used for monthly review, scenario analysis, and assumption modelling. A colleague's response to an early mistake also showed the value of owning the error and fixing it.
what do I need to improve: Early on, unfamiliarity with the process led to mistakes that created extra work for colleagues. In one case a colleague stayed late to fix an error, which prompted an apology. The lesson taken from that was to accept the mistake, take responsibility, and focus on the fix rather than panic. Before the internship, Excel was limited to basic formulas, with little knowledge of useful hotkeys.
post-internship reflections: Before the internship, the picture of an actuary came only from lectures and examinations. Seeing colleagues' work, and doing part of it, gave a clearer view of a full-time actuarial role and of how a life insurer operates. Because Excel and Prophet mattered more in practice than R, the plan is to build those tools into later study. The hope is to rejoin AXA after graduation and continue an actuarial career, with more confidence in both the technical work and workplace relationships.
advice for future interns: Do not hesitate to ask questions. An internship is a chance to learn from mistakes in a setting where colleagues expect newcomers to know less and will explain basic points. Be proactive, take notes, and try work that is interesting. Pretending to know everything helps less than accepting a gap. Making a mistake is acceptable; repeating the same mistake is the problem.
technical skills: Excel for large datasets, cash-flow tables, macros, and hotkeys; comparison of VBA and Python cash-flow extraction; asset-share and bonus calculations; re-illustration of policy values; and adjustment of model parameters such as age and gender. Prophet is described as widely used for monthly review, scenario analysis, and assumption modelling.
soft skills: The report names communication skills, asking questions, taking responsibility for mistakes, and greater confidence in workplace relationships. Daily lunches and a supportive team are described as part of fitting in.
courses mentioned: STAT3901 (Life Contingencies I) was reviewed before the interview. FINA 2342 (Insurance: Theory and Practice) is linked to an unpaid-premium case.
tools and software: Excel, VBA, Python, Prophet, R, and re-illustration tools.

job description: HSBC is described as a global bank and financial services organisation operating in more than 60 countries. The internship was in the Global Insurance Section, a group function that monitors insurance entities worldwide, including HSBC Life in Hong Kong, Singapore, Shanghai, Mexico, Malta, and other places. That section manages group assets and liabilities, regulatory requirements, and financial results, mixing underwriting, reserving, and risk assessment with asset management, capital allocation, and market-linked investments. The placement was on the Global Integrated Reporting team, supporting consolidated monthly reports and occasional analysis.
job duties: Updated monthly report files by taking market data from Bloomberg terminals, including yield curves, exchange rates, and index performance, and by incorporating entity files shared by regional teams; checked the data, performed straightforward reconciliations, and prepared documentation for senior review; helped monitor asset-liability mismatches and supported variance explanations; built a CSM walk waterfall chart in Excel; when two teams set overlapping deadlines, arranged a call with both managers and agreed a revised priority; for an entity with US-dollar assets and Hong Kong-dollar liabilities, pulled Bloomberg yield and index data, compared the US-dollar 10-year bond rate with the Hong Kong-dollar 10-year swap rate and the US-dollar/Hong Kong-dollar spread, and supplied visuals that went into a report used with senior management.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation focused on the HSBC interview because hiring managers sometimes see the whole candidate pool in one day. It included the SAAS Workplace Etiquette Workshop for actuarial students and CEDARS Career Readiness Training on professional behaviour, confidentiality, active listening, teamwork, and misconduct such as poor communication or misusing work hours. Academic review ran from basic accounting through life contingencies and risk modelling, with practice explaining major models. Selection was an online application, resume screening, and virtual interviews. One question asked for the Black-Scholes model, its use in option pricing, and all six inputs: underlying price, strike, time to expiration, risk-free rate, dividend yield, and volatility. Five were recalled. The interviewer supplied the missing input and linked the model to embedded options in insurance, which matched studies in financial derivatives.
what have I learned: ACCT coursework helped with balance-sheet and profit-and-loss items under international standards, and actuarial mathematics supplied terms such as reserves, premiums, and solvency ratios. IFRS 17 was learned in more detail, especially revenue recognition and risk adjustment. The placement also showed HSBC's layered structure and how teams in different time zones, including Singapore and Mexico, feed group reporting. A failed homemade waterfall chart led to using Excel's own feature and to asking for help sooner. A currency study, comparing US-dollar and Hong Kong-dollar rates, was used in a senior discussion of asset reallocation. Open teamwork and praise for accurate data were the most enjoyed parts of the work.
what do I need to improve: Technical recall under pressure was incomplete: only five of the six Black-Scholes variables were remembered in the interview. Excel and PowerPoint were weak at the start. A CSM walk chart was attempted with stacked normal and inverted bars because the waterfall feature was unknown, and the chart broke when the manager tried to edit it. That gap is described as something still to work on, because actuarial reporting needs solid Excel skill.
post-internship reflections: The career aim is a banking role that uses actuarial skills for financial risk management and strategic planning. The study plan is to add finance courses such as advanced financial derivatives, investment analysis, and banking regulations, and to prepare for the CFA as well as actuarial exams. A return to HSBC after graduation is of interest because of its global presence, work on insurance-product innovation, and a friendly environment. Group-level work made the room to develop inside the firm clearer.
advice for future interns: Become proficient in Excel early, including pivot tables, VLOOKUP, charts such as waterfall and scenario charts, and macros, using tutorials or projects on realistic datasets. Network through university career events and LinkedIn to learn company cultures. Review technical concepts often, because interviews test recall under pressure. Treat the internship with humility, ask questions, and use difficulties as chances to learn.
technical skills: Bloomberg market data, data checks and reconciliations, asset-liability mismatch monitoring, variance explanations, CSM walk waterfall charts, IFRS 17 reporting concepts, and a US-dollar versus Hong Kong-dollar rate comparison.
soft skills: The report highlights teamwork, active listening, confidentiality, and communication used to resolve two teams' overlapping deadlines. Asking for help on the chart, and recognition for accuracy, are also described.
courses mentioned: ACCT classes, life contingencies, risk modelling, and financial derivatives were reviewed or used. Planned study includes advanced financial derivatives, investment analysis, banking regulations, the CFA, and actuarial exams.
tools and software: Excel, PowerPoint, Bloomberg terminals, pivot tables, VLOOKUP, and macros.

job description: The internship was in the Reinsurance Hub of the Chief Life and Health Office at AXA. The hub helps insurers in mainland China and Southeast Asia reinsure risks, and it sits under the pricing team rather than as a separate pricing placement. The role supported health and critical-illness quotations for China and Southeast Asian countries and product development as the team tried to expand those markets in 2025. Markets such as Vietnam were new to the team, so pricing bases had to be built up from sourced data and adjustments.
job duties: Supported pricing of health and critical-illness quotations for China and Southeast Asia; worked with underwriting to turn cedent needs into product concepts; researched pricing assumptions, including critical-illness incidence rates, and adjusted rates for how severe the disease definition was; ran experience studies of claim cost and exposure against the cedent's target reinsurance rate; wrote technical notes for internal approval and sensitivity tests of profit margin, including a 1-in-200 disability shock and a higher profit-tax rate; prepared second-opinion reports on product features and pricing assumptions from other AXA branches; proposed elderly diseases for a Singapore critical-illness product using competitor research and Hong Kong in-house claims, exposure, and frequency; simplified long formulas in earlier interns' files and added notes.
pre-internship preparation: Preparation started with the resume, especially case-competition lines, and a fresh pass through the parts of those competitions personally worked on. A self-introduction and answers were drafted for strengths and weaknesses, reasons for joining the company, and reasons for fitting the role. Current industry topics were tied back to school, including new insurance products, reserve calculations, and why reserves matter. Human resources first held a phone interview on background and preferred team, then scheduled a pricing-manager interview. That interview asked for a walkthrough of the case competition, including how online data were proxied and turned into analysis. The questions were within what had been prepared, and the manager said human resources would continue the application.
what have I learned: Excel functions and shortcuts, plus basic VBA for repetitive tasks and custom functions, were learned on the job. Reinsurance concepts, structures, and treaty terms became concrete. Incidence rates for major cancers used mortality and survival, and continuous cancer benefits used present value. Communication and presentation improved by explaining workings to seniors and joining product discussions across teams. A very tight reinsurance-proposal deadline, alongside other deadlines, showed why time management matters. Judgement on thin incidence data, and weekend study of IBNR and IBNP with senior guidance, deepened the picture of risk management.
what do I need to improve: Actuarial judgement was the hardest part, especially when incidence data were not split by gender and age and sources disagreed. It was difficult to decide whether a rate was low, accurate, and conservative enough in markets where the team had no experience. IBNR and IBNP had not been studied before and had to be learned during experience studies of claim patterns. Some earlier interns' formulas were too long to follow until they were simplified and annotated.
post-internship reflections: The career aim is to see more of the insurance industry than reinsurance alone. The plan is further part-time internships at other reinsurers and a full-time internship in direct pricing, because the two pricing settings are related but not the same. More Society of Actuaries exams are planned before graduation. Rejoining AXA is of interest because of the culture, the collaborative setting, and seniors who encouraged proactive comments.
advice for future interns: Prepare well. Actuarial knowledge and strong Excel skills are essential, and it helps to follow industry news, especially new product launches. For a reinsurance internship, learn some reinsurance basics first. Being prepared is described as raising the chance of success.
technical skills: Excel functions and shortcuts, VBA automation and custom functions, pricing assumptions, incidence-rate adjustments, experience studies, sensitivity tests, present value, mortality and survival, and IBNR and IBNP.
soft skills: Communication and presentation improved by explaining work to seniors and discussing product design with other teams. Time management under simultaneous deadlines is also named.
courses mentioned: School knowledge of mortality, survival, and present value was applied, without course codes. More Society of Actuaries exams are planned before graduation.
tools and software: Excel and VBA.

job description: The six-month internship was on the Group Internal Economics Capital Analysis (GIECA) team at Prudential. The report describes the company, citing Prudential Hong Kong, as providing financial-planning services and products such as individual life insurance, investment-linked insurance, retirement solutions, health and medical protection, and general insurance, with actuarial work covering underwriting, reserving, pricing, and regulatory compliance. The intern's tasks centred on capital adequacy, support for model validation, and data preparation, including Universal Life model runs and summaries used to check economic capital against regional-group requirements.
job duties: Prepared data, assisted actuarial model runs, and wrote summary reports and other tasks requested by senior actuaries; for the Universal Life model, prepared Prophet tables, run settings, and run structure, validated scenarios, and extracted and summarised results; changed business and economic assumptions to trace the impact on output; built scenario comparisons of asset share and liability to look for abnormal results and to analyse movements, so policy economic capital could be checked against the regional group requirement; traced a workflow error with a small effect, corrected it, and reran the results; presented the internship, including a technical question session, as part of return-offer selection.
pre-internship preparation: Registration for the Corporate Mentorship Programme came before the internship. Extra technical study was skipped because the interview was described as a test of interpersonal and communication skills rather than of material that a CV can show. Preparation was a CV, a mock interview with a mentor, and formal dress for the career fair. At the fair, CVs went to interested companies, intern roles were discussed, and terms such as RBC and regional office were picked up. Some interviews happened at the fair and resembled the mock: hobbies, the kinds of tasks, and views on the actuarial industry, with no technical challenge questions. The message was that an intern would not be expected to arrive with much practical skill, but would need to learn by trial and error.
what have I learned: Probability and statistics, financial mathematics, and life contingencies gave background for discounting, capital requirements, policy reserves, and asset share, even though no single university formula was applied directly. Practical gains were Microsoft Office, especially Excel macros, formulas, and file handling, and a first exposure to Prophet run settings, procedures, and error checks. Communication with a supervisor, including polite English in daily messages, and a view of the GIECA framework were also gained. Debugging missing data and inconsistent formats trained patience and a habit of tracing errors to the cause. The return-offer presentation, which did not lead to an offer, was practice in explaining technical work.
what do I need to improve: With no prior work experience, instructions from the supervisor were often hard to follow at the start, as were company Excel templates, tight deadlines, and shortcuts. Model runs frequently failed because of missing data, inconsistent formats, and other errors. The company expected interns to try to solve problems before asking, so general Microsoft Office questions were looked up online or with generative AI, while template and Prophet questions went to the supervisor.
post-internship reflections: The aim is to become a qualified actuary in insurance. The study plan was changed to take a heavier course load in the current semester so a later semester has only four courses, leaving room for a part-time or full-time internship. That change follows from seeing how much practice-specific knowledge is learned only at work. Rejoining is of interest if a suitable role is open after graduation. Prudential is described as giving teams flexibility on schedules and work from home.
advice for future interns: In insurance internships, be proactive and ask about both the procedure and the idea behind it, and read files when that is allowed, because the business knowledge is hard to get elsewhere. At Prudential, watch every step and document the contribution carefully, because that record is used in the internship presentation that affects a return offer.
technical skills: Excel macros, formulas, and file handling; Prophet table setup, run settings, scenario validation, and error checking; Universal Life model runs; asset-share and liability scenario comparisons; and economic-capital checks under the GIECA framework.
soft skills: The report stresses clear communication, care with detail, explaining quantitative results in business terms, polite written English with a supervisor, presentation in a return-offer session, patience, and systematic problem-solving.
courses mentioned: Probability and statistics courses, financial mathematics, and life contingencies are named as background for the work. No course codes are given.
tools and software: Microsoft Office, Excel, Excel macros, Prophet, and generative AI for general Microsoft Office questions.

job description: The internship was in the Pricing Department of Manulife (International) Limited from 2 July to 16 January, about 6.5 months. Pricing is described as first-line contact with policyholders, where the task is to balance the company's returns with customer needs. Many complex models were already built and needed only simple inputs. Day-to-day work was policy-value quotation, checks on market campaigns for agencies, banks, and brokers, and user-acceptance testing, including the year-end Dividend Scale Change. A project with Regional Actuarial Services covered participating business across the region.
job duties: Quoted policy values by rolling anniversary figures to the quotation date with prescribed interest rates, and rebuilt older plans that had no single method; measured sales mix and campaign results for agencies, banks, and brokers, including a cancelled 5 percent commission uplift that did not lift critical-illness sales by low-sales agents; monitored costs of prepayment, special policy loans, and a contingent life insured; for the Dividend Scale Change, loaded dividend recommendations into rate files, ran user-acceptance tests, and traced formulas such as the terminal dividend rolled forward at the earned rate; compared the Experience Fluctuation Account and Asset Share and read GL34 material on participating-business committees in Hong Kong; built Excel tools, learned VBA from earlier code and artificial intelligence, and highlighted only notable statistical changes.
pre-internship preparation: In year one, the SAAS Career Fair was used to ask exhibitors what they wanted, even when most had no junior openings. The lesson taken was that prior experience was often less important than a firm handshake and confident speaking. A later SAAS visit to Manulife introduced senior actuaries and available roles and led to an interest in pricing, followed by an application to the Corporate Mentorship Programme with the company. A mentor who was a senior committee member and a graduate of the HKU actuarial programme discussed a health product that failed because of weak features. That conversation framed pricing as more than covering profit and solvency: customer value and staying competitive also matter.
what have I learned: Financial mathematics supplied the present-value step in quotations, and age, gender, and income were seen to change premiums. The Dividend Scale Change made participating business and dividends concrete, including how the terminal dividend is rolled forward. Regional practice uses either an Experience Fluctuation Account or asset share to pass gains and losses to policyholders with limited fluctuation. GL34 in Hong Kong, on participating-business committees, was part of that regulatory reading. Excel formula tracing and self-taught VBA sped up repetitive copy-and-paste work. Feedback also shifted daily habits toward telling colleagues the status of work before leaving.
what do I need to improve: Negative feedback was to be more accountable for the work. There was no user-acceptance-testing experience before the Dividend Scale Change, and questions were avoided at first for fear of looking unprepared, which led to a missed deadline until a supervisor provided a walkthrough and past documentation. Weak grades in statistics courses had also been a reason for hesitation about continuing.
post-internship reflections: Seeing actuaries sit higher exams while working, including an alumna who failed an FSA exam and kept preparing, shifted the study plan toward Society of Actuaries exams. Rejoining Manulife (International) Limited after graduation is the hope, but non-pricing experience is wanted first. A talk by the Chief Pricing Officer is cited for the idea of filling gaps: reserves, enterprise risk management, and modelling systems are the areas to explore through further internships.
advice for future interns: Join career activities early, because networking matters as actuarial hiring gets more competitive. Strengthen technical and language skills. Besides university computer courses, a few Excel shortcuts and simple VBA from YouTube are useful. Be able to organise complex mathematical results and explain them in plain language.
technical skills: Present-value policy quotations, sales-mix and campaign analysis, dividend rate files, user-acceptance testing, Excel formula tracing, and Excel VBA automation of repetitive updates.
soft skills: Confident speaking was what career-fair exhibitors were said to look for. On the job, accountability, telling colleagues about progress, and explaining results clearly are the interpersonal points named. An intern manager collected feedback from collaborating actuaries.
courses mentioned: The Financial Mathematics course was used for quotations. Statistics courses, Society of Actuaries exams, an FSA exam, and university computer courses are also named.
tools and software: Excel, Excel VBA, and artificial intelligence used while learning VBA.

job title: Intern of Actuarial Section in the RBC Reporting Team
job description: Prudential Hong Kong Limited is described as a long-established Hong Kong insurer offering individual life insurance, retirement solutions, health and medical products, and general insurance. Its actuarial department covers financial and regulatory reporting, product pricing, and risk management. From 2 July 2025 to 16 January 2026 the internship was in the risk-based capital reporting team, gaining practice in capital management and reporting. The stated duties were market inputs for liability discounting, risk metrics, analysis of model movement, and on-schedule regulatory returns.
job duties: Processed financial data into consistent market inputs for liability discounting; calculated risk metrics such as the SAR factor; analysed model movement to measure the effect of model changes; prepared and submitted scheduled regulatory returns; built an Excel VBA template that compared extracted results with the prior year, with a control page that showed True when every worksheet matched and otherwise named the worksheet and highlighted wrong cells in red; read Risk-Based Capital Methodology and Valuation repeatedly while moving from risk-free yield curves to risk capital by module and the asset-calculation consolidation workbook.
pre-internship preparation: The application went through the department's Internship/Job Online-application System, and a CV was also sent to The Actuarial Society of Hong Kong. Three interview invitations followed. Preparation covered each company's mission, values, annual report, recent news, market position, and products, plus a review of predictive modelling and probability theory, the job description, and current challenges in actuarial work. Interviews were online video or phone calls, opening with a short self-introduction and questions on the insurance industry. One question was how an insurer makes money. The answer covered premiums, investment in bonds and stocks, claim risk, diversification through scale and pricing, and how a reporting team monitors capital adequacy and reserves. The interviewer noted the clarity.
what have I learned: Financial mathematics was used for future-value discounting and economic valuation, and earlier Python made colleagues' scripts easier to read and debug. Self-taught Excel VBA automated repetitive checks. The RBC picture grew from the three-pillar framework to the five Prescribed Capital Amount modules, market risk, life insurance risk, general insurance risk, counterparty default risk, and operational risk, and to Best Estimate Liability, Matching Adjustment, and Solvency Ratio. Product familiarity included the Prudential Entrust Multi-Currency Plan. Attention to detail, debugging messy data, and explaining a mistake, its cause, and a fix to colleagues were the working habits gained. Reading the methodology until the full reporting cycle made sense was the most satisfying part.
what do I need to improve: Time management was the main difficulty. Regular data preparation, returns, and ad hoc tasks overlapped, and the time required was underestimated, which caused a late submission. The response was to split work into smaller steps, check progress, ask colleagues about upcoming tasks and procedure notes, and warn them early with status updates if a deadline was at risk. The work also required much closer attention to detail because a small error could flow into later calculations and reports.
post-internship reflections: The internship confirmed an interest in continuing as an actuary. The short-term goal is to pass the SOA actuarial examinations while keeping up university results. The longer aim is to follow industry developments and seek more internships. Elective courses in finance and programming are planned because both were useful at work, and a mentorship programme is planned for contact with senior actuaries.
advice for future interns: Before interviews, research the company's insurance products and recent news. During the internship, stay curious, ask thoughtful questions, and treat the placement as a learning opportunity. Afterward, keep in touch with colleagues and human resources, because those contacts may help with part-time work or a graduate role.
technical skills: Excel VBA automation, reading and debugging Python scripts, SAR-factor and model-movement analysis, regulatory returns, and RBC concepts including the three pillars, five Prescribed Capital Amount risk modules, Best Estimate Liability, Matching Adjustment, and Solvency Ratio.
soft skills: Attention to detail, analytical problem-solving, and communication while collaborating with colleagues are named, including summarising a mistake, its cause, and how to prevent it, and giving early progress updates.
courses mentioned: Predictive modelling and probability theory were reviewed before interviews. Financial Mathematics was used at work. Planned steps are SOA actuarial examinations and elective courses in finance and programming.
tools and software: Excel, VBA, and Python.

job description: SunLife HK Limited is described as focused on healthy lifestyles and long-term financial stability, with protection, wealth management, retirement planning, and healthcare cover for an aging society. The internship, from July to December 2025, was in the Life Product Pricing and Development area, on the Pricing team, which prices new life and health products designed by the Product team. Pricing is described as risk assessment, product features, and profitability, and as the bridge from technical models to real cases. The team handles Indexed Universal Life, a permanent policy with a death benefit and cash value linked to market indices.
job duties: Prepared Premium Discount Letters for high-net-worth and corporate clients, including first-year premium discounts and overage cases, using an Excel tool to produce a PDF and checking product name, discount, insured details, and funding source, sometimes within one hour; ran user-acceptance tests on Ingenium before launches, creating policies for partial withdrawal, split premium, top-up, and rider claims, then comparing guaranteed cash value, cash surrender value, and interest value with expected results; prepared in-force illustrations of cash value and death benefit, including interpolation of guaranteed cash value and total-premium-paid flooring; took index history such as the S&P 500 and Hang Seng Index from Bloomberg and compared 15-year, 20-year, and 25-year performance, volatility, and fund returns; built an Excel IF template so a death-benefit quote no longer depended on finding the last worker's file.
pre-internship preparation: Department talks by senior students who had finished actuarial internships covered what actuaries do, how departments differ, and tools such as Excel and Bloomberg terminals. Applications went through LinkedIn and produced interviews at Manulife and SunLife. Preparation used recent product launches, annual reports, market position, and the difference between pricing and valuation. In one interview a probability question had to be solved without paper. After a nervous start, the solution was explained step by step and was correct. The offer was from SunLife, in Life Product and Pricing.
what have I learned: Excel and Ingenium became much more familiar, including shortcuts, charts for market comparisons, and consistent formatting for the pricing team. Drafting steps in a text file and walking a supervisor through them improved explanations when something was unclear. User-acceptance work contributed to a system change that shortened illustration turnaround for clients. A team-meeting presentation brought feedback on the working pattern. When Ingenium errors blocked test cases, documenting screenshots and reproduction steps and escalating to IT early, while doing other tasks in parallel, kept the testing moving.
what do I need to improve: In user-acceptance testing, system errors that stopped a case from being created were investigated alone for a long time. Waiting to ask IT made the testing much slower. The change was to log the error with screenshots and steps and escalate sooner, and to work on other tasks while waiting. The interview probability question was also a nervous moment before the reasoning was slowed down and explained aloud.
post-internship reflections: The career goal remains an actuarial role, ideally in life and health development. Preparation for Society of Actuaries exams will continue, along with learning more kinds of insurance products. Rejoining SunLife after graduation is of strong interest because of the supportive culture, attention to employee development, and the focus on insurance solutions.
advice for future interns: Strengthen technical skills, especially life insurance statistics. During the internship, ask for feedback and ask questions, because the answers are useful later in a career.
technical skills: Excel, including shortcuts, charts, and IF formulas; Ingenium user-acceptance testing and policy scenarios; in-force illustration of guaranteed cash value, surrender value, and death benefit; and Bloomberg index comparisons covering return and volatility.
soft skills: Explaining complex results to a supervisor, presenting findings in a team meeting, prioritising urgent letters, and asking for feedback are the communication points described.
courses mentioned: Statistical modelling is cited as training used to design test cases. Society of Actuaries exams are the planned professional exams, and life insurance statistics is the skill future interns are told to strengthen.
tools and software: Excel, Ingenium, Bloomberg terminal, and LinkedIn.

job description: AIA Group Limited is described as a Hong Kong insurer covering life insurance, health insurance, savings, retirement, group schemes, and wealth management. The internship was with the Prophet Change Management Team, which develops and maintains AIA's Prophet model. The team takes updates from business units, builds variables and formulas, and integrates the model for pricing, financial reporting, and strategic decisions. The role centred on impact analysis of model changes and on merging separate ordinary-life and universal-life analysis tools into one Python tool.
job duties: Reviewed change logs from business units, applied the changes in Prophet, ran projections, and compared policy value, cash flow, and reserves between the original and modified models; when results missed the expected outcome, traced the formulas and variables at fault; used Product Diagram View to project a variable such as renewal expenses and to see its formula, inputs, and dependents; built simple variables and set assumptions in tables; combined the ordinary-life and universal-life impact tools into one Python tool using Pandas, Dask, and NumPy; wrote a developer manual and user guide after the code became hard to maintain; designed faulty Prophet models as class exercises for the HKU Prophet Project with AIA, for STAT3957, including a wrong data type in a parametric table.
pre-internship preparation: From mid-October 2024, preparation for AIA reviewed Financial Mathematics and Life Contingencies and the company's annual reports, products, and market position, and used practice questions generated with AI. The interview was on Microsoft Teams with a senior actuary, split between actuarial questions and workplace expectations at AIA. The hardest question was to describe the pattern of human mortality: high in infancy, lowest around age 10, rising from about 15 to 25, then increasing steeply from about age 40. The interviewer encouraged deeper knowledge of insurance and of AIA, suggested pursuing ATPA after graduation because the exam is expensive and taking an actuarial job, and described his own internship. An offer arrived after a week.
what have I learned: Prophet was the main new tool: Product Diagram View, formulas, data types, assumption tables, user guides, the internal debugger, study videos, a manual, and the Modelling Star forum. STAT3901 helped when reading recursive policy-value and annuity expressions in change requests. COMP1117 and STAT3907 helped in understanding earlier tools and finishing the Python impact tool. Debugging Prophet was described as the most enjoyable challenge. Designing STAT3957 class exercises from those Prophet errors turned the same skill toward teaching. A written manual, which the manager asked to expand into a developer manual and user guide, made the tool easier to keep.
what do I need to improve: Prophet programming was new, so failed runs and unclear error messages were frustrating at the start. The ways through that were user guides and the internal debugger, asking the manager after being stuck, and self-study from AIA videos, the manual, and Modelling Star. Separately, the impact-analysis code became too complicated to maintain, which is why a manual was written.
post-internship reflections: The internship made an actuarial career more certain. The plan is to earn as much University Earn Credit as possible to exempt some Society of Actuaries exams, and to add working experience through a part-time internship in year 4. Rejoining AIA after graduation is of strong interest because colleagues were professional and supportive and seniors gave guidance to a newcomer.
advice for future interns: Strengthen hard skills before a similar internship. This role required Python, Prophet, and Excel VBA. Prophet needs a user licence, so most actuarial students will not have used it beforehand. Excel VBA and Python are the skills recommended to build in advance.
technical skills: Prophet model changes, projections, Product Diagram View, variable building, and debugging; impact analysis of policy value, cash flow, and reserves; Python with Pandas, Dask, and NumPy; and documentation of a modelling tool. Excel VBA is named as required for the role.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: Financial Mathematics and Life Contingencies were reviewed before the interview. STAT3901 Life Contingencies, COMP1117 Computer Programming, and STAT3907 Linear models and forecasting were used on the job. STAT3957 Essential principles in actuarial modelling is the HKU course for which class exercises were designed. ATPA, University Earn Credit, and Society of Actuaries exams are also named.
tools and software: Prophet, Python, Pandas, Dask, NumPy, Excel VBA, Microsoft Teams, Modelling Star, and AI-generated interview questions.

job description: Prudential Hong Kong Limited offers a range of insurance plans. Its actuarial department includes pricing, participating business, assets and liability management, and valuation, and valuation is split into embedded-value and IFRS17 reporting teams. The half-year internship, July to December 2025, was on the IFRS17 reporting team. The work supported financial reporting under IFRS17, including a Best Estimate Liability and Underlying Items project under the Variable Fee Approach, quarterly report checks, and an attempt to replicate Premium Deposit Account reserves.
job duties: On the Best Estimate Liability and Underlying Items project, handled many variables and checked them so they matched the transfer impact under the Variable Fee Approach model; updated links for the new quarter; downloaded financial-report files and copied files from the PMCS platform to another platform; cross-checked quarterly reports across the General Measurement Model and the Variable Fee Approach, and across Liability for Remaining Coverage and Liability for Incurred Claims; tried to replicate reserve calculations for the Premium Deposit Account; wrote formulas that checked and connected variables. Prophet models were not run personally, but tasks used variables and results that Prophet had produced.
pre-internship preparation: Interview preparation included background research on the companies applied to, their products, and their vision, plus a review of annuities and life contingencies in case technical questions came up. The Prudential Hong Kong Limited interview was a phone call covering the reason for applying and expectations for the internship. The interviewer also described the kinds of tasks and the steps before the start. The process is described as smooth.
what have I learned: The main domain gain was IFRS17: the models the team runs, the steps, the variables, and the daily reporting routine, including contractual service margin and analysis of movement. Excel skills grew through complex formulas, filters, and shortcuts used in reserve calculations and report checks. Prophet was learned from the variables and results it produces and from the steps used in production, and PMCS and WinSCP became familiar. An introductory Python course made VBA code easier to follow. Discount rates, annuities, mortality, and premiums were needed to understand reserve work rather than only to operate the files.
what do I need to improve: Many technical terms and acronyms were new and were not in lectures, including CSM for contractual service margin and AOM for analysis of movement, so an early Excel file was hard to understand. Learning PMCS and Prophet was a second difficulty. The approach was to collect questions and clarify them in one meeting, and to ask for instructions while trying the software.
post-internship reflections: The aim is still to be an actuary, with an interest in teams other than reporting and valuation, possibly assets and liability management or the participating team, because each team has its own work. Further internships or jobs are planned, along with a professional actuarial qualification and more proficiency in VBA and Excel. Work experience is described as necessary because some skills are not learned in lectures.
advice for future interns: Learn some coding, and become familiar with Excel shortcuts and functions, because both are useful when helping with internship tasks.
technical skills: Excel formulas, filters, and shortcuts; reading VBA with help from Python; IFRS17 reporting under the General Measurement Model and Variable Fee Approach; Best Estimate Liability, Underlying Items, Liability for Remaining Coverage, Liability for Incurred Claims, and Premium Deposit Account reserves; and use of Prophet outputs, PMCS, and WinSCP.
soft skills: Communication and collaboration improved by asking questions, discussing tasks, and updating colleagues. Analytical and logical thinking, and closer attention to detail on verification and on downloading the correct quarter and format, are also named.
courses mentioned: Annuities and life contingencies were reviewed before the interview. An introductory computer programming course at HKU, taught in Python, helped with reading VBA. A professional qualification in actuarial science is planned. No course codes are given.
tools and software: Excel, Prophet, PMCS, WinSCP, VBA, and Python.

job description: Ernst & Young is a global professional-services firm in assurance, consulting, and advisory work. Its actuarial team supports insurers and reinsurers on IFRS 17 reporting, audit, product modelling, asset-liability management, and process automation. From 2 July to 31 December 2025 the role was risk consulting intern (actuarial). Work came as client and internal projects: a liquidity review for a China-based insurer, IFRS 17 audits, an HKRBC automation pitch, actuarial pitch decks, a pre-close audit, and an AI research project. A licence-application engagement and some other projects were left out of the report for confidentiality, and some client names were withheld.
job duties: On a liquidity review for a China-based insurer, mapped pricing-model, Prophet, income-statement, and balance-sheet outputs into projected cash flows; tested commissions, campaign costs, and fund charges; and assessed Indexed Universal Life as a lower-strain product. On IFRS 17 second-quarter audits for FWD and Peak Re, helped calculate Best Estimate Liability, Contractual Service Margin, and Risk Adjustment; standardised Excel templates; checked data, assumptions, and treaties against the prior quarter; and updated the Actuarial Summary and Review Memorandum. Edited HKRBC slides and helped build a demo in Excel VBA, Power Apps, and Power Automate. Supported four pitch decks on indexed universal life modelling, Prophet optimisation, participating funds, and asset-liability management. For FWD's 2025 fourth-quarter pre-close, reviewed assumption changes, compared Alteryx with Prophet, and checked ESG inputs such as implied volatility and credit spreads. Researched AI extraction from financial reports for audit support.
pre-internship preparation: The application was made at the SAAS departmental career fair. Preparation was a concise CV covering academic background and an earlier internship. Before the interview, that earlier life-insurance actuarial internship was reviewed, along with a light pass over common insurance products and introductory IFRS 17 ideas. Before the start date, Excel and PowerPoint were refreshed because both are used often in actuarial consulting.
what have I learned: The stated gains are a professional habit of being proactive, reliable, and responsive to feedback across projects; a working grasp of Best Estimate Liability, Contractual Service Margin, Risk Adjustment, and IFRS 17 in audit; financial analysis that ties cash flows, the income statement, and the balance sheet to profit and cost; hands-on automation with Excel, VBA, Power Automate, and Power Apps, including HKRBC production steps; and clearer client-ready slides. ESG inputs and a tight liquidity timeline also required judgement about which cash-flow drivers mattered most. The AI project showed how newer tools can sit beside traditional actuarial checks.
what do I need to improve: IFRS 17 concepts and logic were unfamiliar at the start of the audits and were learned through self-study and senior guidance. VBA and Power Apps were also new when the HKRBC demo was built. ESG methods and their data steps were another new area and were checked against industry practice and other insurers. On the liquidity project, the short timeline meant judging which cash-flow drivers were material instead of reviewing every item equally.
post-internship reflections: The internship confirmed a plan to stay in actuarial work, while also raising interest in roles closer to financial markets, such as market risk or quantitative work in banks. Rejoining Ernst & Young after graduation is under consideration because of the supportive culture and guidance from senior colleagues. The next step described is more relevant coursework and technical practice, plus roles that widen industry exposure.
advice for future interns: Build a strong academic record, because recruitment treats it as a sign of responsibility and willingness to learn. Develop communication, since consulting means working across teams and, later, with clients. Being proactive, adaptable, and able to explain an idea clearly is presented as important both in the internship and afterward.
technical skills: Cash-flow checks and scenario testing, IFRS 17 audit calculations for Best Estimate Liability, Contractual Service Margin, and Risk Adjustment, Excel template standardisation, HKRBC workflow automation, comparison of Alteryx and Prophet, ESG input review, and research on AI extraction from reports and workbooks.
soft skills: Professionalism, being proactive and reliable, responding to feedback, contributing inside project teams, and presenting analytical findings clearly to stakeholders are the skills the report lists.
courses mentioned: NA
tools and software: Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, Prophet, Excel VBA, Power Apps, Power Automate, and Alteryx.

company: AXA China Region Insurance Company Limited
job description: The internship at AXA China Region Insurance Company Limited ran from 2 July to 31 December 2025, with the office in Wong Chuk Hang. AXA is described as an insurance company. The placement was on the IFRS17 team, one of the valuation teams, which matched the team requested at interview because of an interest in data analytics. Much of the work was repeated Prophet runs and data extracts, supported by templates, macros, and checks. Scenario jobs also gave a rough sense of whether a result was on track before the numbers were final.
job duties: Monthly work was GOC mapping with Power Query, including debugging, and DOD SD by extracting system data and running Power Query. Quarter-end work generated ESG simulations for Prophet and ETI/RPU profit estimates. Ad hoc work automated Prophet tables with macros and edited Excel templates with formulas. Housekeeping backed up Prophet results with batch files and copied files across drives. Audit work broke links and cleared comments and notes before handover. Other help extracted Prophet results, compared run logs to confirm the file, updated templates, and flowed summaries. For assumption changes, ALS and deterministic Prophet models were run, summarised in Excel, consolidated on an FCF sheet, and flowed into templates of the BEL summary and CSM release; scenarios were rerun until managers accepted the impact.
pre-internship preparation: After the resume was sent, preparation was a rehearsed self-introduction about interest in actuarial science, and likely questions such as why that field was chosen. A previous brokerage internship was used to think through questions on tasks, tools, and skills learned. An assistant manager then called without notice for a phone interview of about ten minutes. It covered the self-introduction, the earlier internship, knowledge of AXA, the choice of actuarial science because of mathematics, data analytics, and a stable path, what the various teams do, VBA experience, and a preferred team. Valuation was chosen. The caller said this phone call was the only interview. Human resources made an offer about an hour later.
what have I learned: The IFRS17 routine became familiar: setting Prophet runs, extracting results, and consolidating them, including what CSM is and how it is calculated. Colleagues explained tasks in detail and also talked about Society of Actuaries progress and career paths, including an FSA route described as having easier papers and higher pass rates. Assumption-change cycles showed how economic scenarios move BEL and CSM. Lunches and a party-room gathering with actuarial colleagues were the social parts remembered most.
what do I need to improve: Very large Excel files could be handled only on a remote desktop, but getting one took months, so a senior's machine was borrowed. That failed when both people had urgent work, and working from home was worse because the laptop VPN was slow and often disconnected, sometimes before a file could be saved. A second difficulty was several colleagues assigning tasks at once. The response was to ask which tasks were urgent and to say what was already in progress.
post-internship reflections: The goal is to become an actuary. Exam P and Exam FM have been passed, with university earn credit on FM, and FAM, SRM, and ALTAM are planned before graduation, with university earn credit hoped for on SRM and ALTAM. The conclusion also lists ALTAM or ASTAM and PA toward ASA. Rejoining the company is under consideration because of the working atmosphere, a work-from-home policy of twice a week, and an office location that does not take long to reach. Shuttle buses to Aberdeen at lunch are also mentioned.
advice for future interns: Take the phone interview when the call comes, because waiting can mean the intern places are already filled. Ask whenever a step is unclear, because a small error can become a larger one. Join colleague events such as farewell parties or party rooms, which are a chance to learn what the role expects.
technical skills: Prophet runs, including ALS and deterministic models, run-log checks, and ESG simulations; Power Query for GOC mapping and DOD SD; Excel formulas, macros, and impact summaries for BEL and CSM; batch-file backups; and ETI/RPU profit estimates.
soft skills: NA
courses mentioned: Exam P and Exam FM, with university earn credit on FM, are already passed. Planned exams named are FAM, SRM, ALTAM, ASTAM, and PA toward ASA, plus an FSA path suggested by colleagues.
tools and software: Prophet, Power Query, Excel, VBA, macros, batch files, remote desktop, and VPN.

job description: Sun Life's business is life insurance, including term, whole life, and universal life, plus health insurance, wealth management, asset management, and retirement planning. The report links that business to actuarial work because the timing of death and claims is uncertain, and statistics, finance, and mathematics are used to estimate present values. The internship supported the team rather than making decisions. Quarter-end work estimated the present value of Amount of Deposits under sensitivity scenarios in the AXIS model. Other work was checking, analysing, and presenting data, improving a repetitive file process, and writing VBA for another team. The report does not name which reporting team was joined.
job duties: At quarter-end, estimated the present value of Amount of Deposits under sensitivity scenarios in the AXIS model, checking that inputs were appropriate and that results looked reasonable; checked the accuracy of data provided by the manager, analysed it, and set it out so colleagues could read it and decide more quickly; reorganised the file structure of one repetitive task so the process took at least half as long; wrote VBA from scratch for another team's new files, using online references and similar existing files, despite not having learned VBA before and not initially knowing where to enter the code.
pre-internship preparation: The interview was with three senior staff from different teams. Preparation was a thirty-second self-introduction and a review of concepts from statistics courses that might matter at work. The process was that interview plus a call with human resources, with no case analysis. The opening question was which course had been most difficult. The answer was Life Contingencies, followed by how many types of insurance were known, how a higher interest rate changes present value, and whether an older person should be charged more or less. A question about which reporting team to join was unexpected. Only reporting versus product was known beforehand, and that IFRS17 sat on the reporting side, so the available reporting teams and their tasks had to be asked about. The interviewers explained them.
what have I learned: University statistics and financial mathematics stayed theoretical until the AXIS work showed that a calculation also needs a purpose, suitable inputs, and a reasonableness check. Excel at the start was only arithmetic. A first task was redone several times because calculation was set to automatic and linked data refreshed incorrectly; a colleague explained that this task needed manual calculation. VBA for another team was learned from online material and from similar files, and was finished on time. Reorganising one repetitive file structure cut the time by at least half. Four other interns on the same floor, on different teams, were a source of mutual support.
what do I need to improve: Excel at the start was limited to addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Not knowing that automatic calculation would refresh links caused the first task to be redone three or four times before a colleague pointed out the manual setting. VBA had never been learned, and the request to build code from nothing, without knowing where the code panel was, caused panic until examples and testing made the task possible.
post-internship reflections: The goal is still to become an FSA and work as an actuary in an insurance company. What changed is the plan to do more internships before graduation, because the practical skills from this placement showed that industry experience matters alongside books and lectures. Rejoining Sun Life is the intention if a suitable opening exists, because the office location is convenient and coworkers explained tasks, tips, and shortcuts willingly.
advice for future interns: Ask questions as soon as a task is confusing. Become familiar with Excel functions such as SUMIF and SUMPRODUCT, because that makes it easier to settle into the work.
technical skills: AXIS present-value and sensitivity calculations for Amount of Deposits, data checking and cleaner presentation, Excel calculation settings, and VBA written for another team's files. SUMIF and SUMPRODUCT are the functions recommended for similar work.
soft skills: The report describes asking a colleague for help when an Excel result would not match, and support among four interns on different teams who ran into similar difficulties.
courses mentioned: Statistics courses were reviewed before the interview. Life Contingencies was discussed in the interview. Financial mathematics is named as university study used to understand insurance present values. The career goal named is FSA.
tools and software: AXIS, Excel, VBA, SUMIF, and SUMPRODUCT.
